concepts: Scalar and vector products of vectors
questions.question: Let $\vec{a}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}$. If $\vec{c}$ is a vector such that $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}=|\vec{c}|$, $|\vec{c}-\vec{a}|=2\sqrt{2}$ and the angle between $(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})$ and $\vec{c}$ is $\frac{\pi}{6}$, then the value of $|(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})\times\vec{c}|$ is:
questions.key_idea: Expanding $|\vec{c}-\vec{a}|^2$ with $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}=|\vec{c}|$ gives a perfect square $(|\vec{c}|-1)^2=0$, so $|\vec{c}|=1$.
useful_results: $|\vec{u}-\vec{v}|^2=|\vec{u}|^2+|\vec{v}|^2-2\,\vec{u}\cdot\vec{v}$; a condition mixing $|\vec{c}|$ and $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}$ often becomes a perfect square.
$|\vec{u}\times\vec{v}|=|\vec{u}||\vec{v}|\sin\theta$ where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{u}$ and $\vec{v}$ (here $\vec{u}=\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$, $\vec{v}=\vec{c}$).
$|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|^2=|\vec{a}|^2|\vec{b}|^2-(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})^2$; here $9\cdot2-9=9$, so $|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|=3$ (check).

concepts: Projection of a vector and dot product
questions.question: In a triangle $ABC$, if $|\overrightarrow{BC}|=3$, $|\overrightarrow{CA}|=5$ and $|\overrightarrow{BA}|=7$, then the projection of the vector $\overrightarrow{BA}$ on $\overrightarrow{BC}$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Both vectors start at $B$, so the projection is $|\overrightarrow{BA}|\cos\angle ABC$, and the cosine rule gives $\cos\angle ABC$.
solution: Projection of $\overrightarrow{BA}$ on $\overrightarrow{BC}$ $=|\overrightarrow{BA}|\cos\angle ABC$, as both vectors issue from $B$.
The side opposite $\angle B$ is $CA=5$, with $BC=3$ and $BA=7$ adjacent to it.

alternate_solutions.idea: Place $B$ at the origin and $C$ on the $x$-axis; the projection on $\overrightarrow{BC}$ is just the $x$-coordinate of $A$.
solution: $\overrightarrow{BC}$ points along the positive $x$-axis, so the projection of $\overrightarrow{BA}$ on it equals $x=\frac{11}{2}$.

useful_results: Projection (scalar) of $\vec{u}$ on $\vec{v}$ is $\frac{\vec{u}\cdot\vec{v}}{|\vec{v}|}$; the vector projection is $\frac{\vec{u}\cdot\vec{v}}{|\vec{v}|^2}\vec{v}$.

In triangle $ABC$: $\overrightarrow{BA}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}=\frac{BA^2+BC^2-CA^2}{2}$ (cosine rule in dot-product form); here $\frac{49+9-25}{2}=\frac{33}{2}$, divided by $|BC|=3$ gives $\frac{11}{2}$.
Take care that vectors start at the same point before reading the angle between them.

concepts: Coplanar vectors and scalar triple product
questions.question: Let a vector $\vec{a}$ be coplanar with vectors $\vec{b}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c}=\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}$. If $\vec{a}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{d}=3\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+6\hat{k}$, and $|\vec{a}|=\sqrt{10}$, then a possible value of $[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{c}]+[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{d}]+[\vec{a}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{d}]$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Coplanarity gives $\vec{a}=\lambda\vec{b}+\mu\vec{c}$ and $[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{c}]=0$; $\vec{a}\perp\vec{d}$ and $|\vec{a}|=\sqrt{10}$ then fix $\vec{a}=\pm(3\hat{j}-\hat{k})$.
solution: Sum $=0-28-14=-42$ (for $-\vec{a}$ the sum would be $+42$, not among the options). Option (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $\vec{a}\parallel(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})\times\vec{d}$ (perpendicular to the plane normal and to $\vec{d}$), and combine the last two triple products into one.
solution: $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}=2\hat{i}-\hat{j}-3\hat{k}$ is normal to the plane of $\vec{b},\vec{c}$; $\vec{a}$ lies in that plane, so $\vec{a}\perp\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$, and $\vec{a}\perp\vec{d}$.

useful_results: $\vec{a}$ coplanar with $\vec{b},\vec{c}$ (non-parallel) $\iff\vec{a}=\lambda\vec{b}+\mu\vec{c}\iff[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{c}]=0$.
$[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{d}]+[\vec{a}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{d}]=[\vec{a}\ (\vec{b}+\vec{c})\ \vec{d}]$, since the triple product is linear in each slot.
A vector perpendicular to both $\vec{n}$ and $\vec{d}$ is along $\vec{n}\times\vec{d}$; use it to find the line of a plane vector perpendicular to a given direction.

concepts: Vector and scalar triple products
questions.question: Let three vectors $\vec{a},\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ be such that $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}=\vec{c}$, $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}=\vec{a}$ and $|\vec{a}|=2$. Then which one of the following is not true?
questions.key_idea: The two cross-product relations force $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$ to be mutually perpendicular with $|\vec{b}|=1$, $|\vec{c}|=2$; then every option is a one-line check.
solution: (A): $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}=\vec{a}$, so the projection of $\vec{a}$ on it is $\frac{\vec{a}\cdot\vec{a}}{|\vec{a}|}=|\vec{a}|=2$. True.
Hence the statement that is not true is (B).
questions.correction_note: The PDF verifies only options (A) and (B) (its check of (A) is garbled: it writes sin and cos of an unspecified angle) and never checks (C) and (D). Its derivation of orthogonality and |b|=1, |c|=2 and its verdict on (B) are correct; (A) was re-derived simply as a.a/|a|=2 and (C), (D) were added.

alternate_solutions.idea: The relations describe a right-handed orthogonal triad, so take $\vec{a}=2\hat{i}$, $\vec{b}=\hat{j}$, $\vec{c}=2\hat{k}$ and compute each option in components.
solution: $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}=\vec{c}$ and $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}=\vec{a}$ with $|\vec{a}|=2$ give mutually perpendicular vectors with $|\vec{b}|=1,|\vec{c}|=2$ (as in the main solution); choose axes along them: $\vec{a}=2\hat{i}$, $\vec{b}=\hat{j}$, $\vec{c}=2\hat{k}$.
(A): $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}=2\hat{i}$; projection of $2\hat{i}$ on it is $2$. True.
(C): $(\vec{b}+\vec{c})\times(\vec{b}-\vec{c})=(0,1,2)\times(0,1,-2)=(-4,0,0)$, parallel to $\vec{a}$, so the cross with $\vec{a}$ is $\vec{0}$. True.
(D): $[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{c}]=\left|\begin{matrix}2&0&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&2\end{matrix}\right|=4$, and $[\vec{c}\ \vec{a}\ \vec{b}]=4$ (cyclic); sum $=8$. True. The untrue statement is (B).

useful_results: If $\vec{u}\times\vec{v}=\vec{w}$ and $\vec{v}\times\vec{w}=\vec{u}$, then $\vec{u},\vec{v},\vec{w}$ are mutually perpendicular, $|\vec{w}|=|\vec{u}||\vec{v}|$ and $|\vec{u}|=|\vec{v}||\vec{w}|$, so $|\vec{v}|=1$.
The triple product is unchanged by cyclic permutation: $[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{c}]=[\vec{c}\ \vec{a}\ \vec{b}]=[\vec{b}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{a}]$.
$(\vec{b}+\vec{c})\times(\vec{b}-\vec{c})=-2\,\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$ (expand; $\vec{b}\times\vec{b}=\vec{0}$ and $\vec{c}\times\vec{b}=-\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$).
For mutually perpendicular vectors, $|x\vec{a}+y\vec{b}+z\vec{c}|^2=x^2|\vec{a}|^2+y^2|\vec{b}|^2+z^2|\vec{c}|^2$.

Properties of determinants
questions.question: Let the vectors $(2+a+b)\hat{i}+(a+2b+c)\hat{j}-(b+c)\hat{k}$, $(1+b)\hat{i}+2b\hat{j}-b\hat{k}$ and $(2+b)\hat{i}+2b\hat{j}+(1-b)\hat{k}$, $a,b,c\in\mathbb{R}$ be co-planar. Then which of the following is true?
questions.key_idea: Coplanar means the $3\times3$ determinant of components is $0$; two row/column operations reduce it to one non-zero cofactor.
solution: Coplanar vectors have scalar triple product $0$: $\left|\begin{matrix}2+a+b&a+2b+c&-b-c\\1+b&2b&-b\\2+b&2b&1-b\end{matrix}\right|=0$.
useful_results: Three vectors are coplanar $\iff$ the determinant of their components is $0$.
Row and column operations $R_i\to R_i-R_j$ or $C_i\to C_i-C_j$ do not change a determinant; use them to create zeros before expanding.
Look for rows that differ by a simple vector (here $R_3-R_2=(1,0,1)$) to shorten the work.

concepts: Coplanar vectors and scalar triple product
questions.question: Let $a,b$ and $c$ be distinct positive numbers. If the vectors $a\hat{i}+a\hat{j}+c\hat{k}$, $\hat{i}+\hat{k}$ and $c\hat{i}+c\hat{j}+b\hat{k}$ are co-planar, then $c$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Co-planarity gives a zero determinant that collapses to $c^2=ab$, so $c$ is the geometric mean.
solution: Expand along the first row: $a(0\cdot b-1\cdot c)-a(1\cdot b-1\cdot c)+c(1\cdot c-0\cdot c)=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write the first vector as a combination $\alpha(\hat{i}+\hat{k})+\beta(c\hat{i}+c\hat{j}+b\hat{k})$; the $\hat{j}$ component decouples at once.
solution: $\hat{i}+\hat{k}$ and $c\hat{i}+c\hat{j}+b\hat{k}$ are not parallel ($c>0$), so coplanarity means $a\hat{i}+a\hat{j}+c\hat{k}=\alpha(\hat{i}+\hat{k})+\beta(c\hat{i}+c\hat{j}+b\hat{k})$.

useful_results: Three vectors are coplanar $\iff$ $[\vec{u}\ \vec{v}\ \vec{w}]=0\iff$ one is a combination of the other two (when those two are not parallel).
If one vector has a zero component, the corresponding scalar equation often fixes a coefficient immediately.
Such a condition typically produces the geometric mean: $c^2=ab$ (distinct positive $a,b$ means $\min<c<\max$).

concepts: Scalar and vector products of vectors
questions.question: If $|\vec{a}|=2$, $|\vec{b}|=5$ and $|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|=8$, then $|\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}|$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|$ gives $\sin\theta=\frac{4}{5}$, hence $|\cos\theta|=\frac{3}{5}$, and then $|\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}|=|\vec{a}||\vec{b}||\cos\theta|$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Lagrange's identity $|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|^2+(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})^2=|\vec{a}|^2|\vec{b}|^2$ gives the answer without any angle.

useful_results: $|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|^2+(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})^2=|\vec{a}|^2|\vec{b}|^2$ for all vectors (check: $\vec{a}=\hat{i}$, $\vec{b}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}$ gives $1+1=1\cdot2$).
Only $|\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}|$ is determined, because the sign of $\cos\theta$ is not fixed by $\sin\theta$.
Recognise $\sin\theta=\frac{4}{5}\leftrightarrow\cos\theta=\pm\frac{3}{5}$ (Pythagorean triple) to save time.

concepts: Vector triple product
questions.question: Let $\vec{a}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b}=-\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$. Then the vector product $(\vec{a}+\vec{b})\times\Big(\big(\vec{a}\times((\vec{a}-\vec{b})\times\vec{b})\big)\times\vec{b}\Big)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $(\vec{a}-\vec{b})\times\vec{b}=\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$ collapses the nesting; then repeated BAC-CAB with $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=7$, $|\vec{a}|^2=6$, $|\vec{b}|^2=14$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Skip the identities and evaluate each cross product in components, starting from $(\vec{a}-\vec{b})\times\vec{b}$.

useful_results: BAC-CAB: $\vec{a}\times(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})=(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c})\vec{b}-(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})\vec{c}$ and $(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})\times\vec{c}=(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c})\vec{b}-(\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c})\vec{a}$; the vector triple product is not associative.
$(\vec{u}-\vec{v})\times\vec{v}=\vec{u}\times\vec{v}$: subtracting a multiple of the second factor does not change a cross product.
$(\vec{a}+\vec{b})\times(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})=(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}+|\vec{b}|^2)\vec{a}-(|\vec{a}|^2+\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})\vec{b}$; here $21\vec{a}-13\vec{b}$.
$(x\vec{a}+y\vec{b})\times\vec{b}=x\,\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$ whenever the first factor lies in the plane of $\vec{a},\vec{b}$.

questions.question: Let $\vec{a},\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ be three vectors such that $\vec{a}=\vec{b}\times(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$. If the magnitudes of the vectors $\vec{a},\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ are $\sqrt{2},1$ and $2$ respectively and the angle between $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ is $\theta$ $\left(0<\theta<\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$, then the value of $1+\tan\theta$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: BAC-CAB turns $\vec{a}$ into $2\cos\theta\,\vec{b}-\vec{c}$; then $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=0$ and $|\vec{a}|^2=2$ (or $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}$) fix $\cos\theta$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's outline (expand by BAC-CAB, dot with b, a and c) is right but it has errors: it writes 'cos^2(theta) = +-1/sqrt2' where cos^2(theta)=1/2 (cos(theta)=1/sqrt2) is correct, it states a.b=0 without reason, and it drops the -|c|^2 term when dotting with c ('2 = 4cos^2(theta)' is correct only after moving the -4). Steps were re-derived and written out cleanly.

alternate_solutions.idea: Since $\vec{b}\perp(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$, $|\vec{a}|=|\vec{b}|\,|\vec{b}\times\vec{c}|$ directly gives $\sin\theta$.

useful_results: $|\vec{b}\times(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})|=|\vec{b}|^2|\vec{c}|\sin\theta$: the vector $\vec{b}\times(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$ equals $-|\vec{b}|^2$ times the component of $\vec{c}$ perpendicular to $\vec{b}$.
$\vec{a}=\vec{b}\times(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$ lies in the plane of $\vec{b},\vec{c}$ and is perpendicular to $\vec{b}$.
Dotting a vector identity with the vectors that appear in it (here $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{c}$) gives scalar equations in the unknown $\cos\theta$.

concepts: Shortest distance between skew lines
questions.question: If the shortest distance between the lines $\vec{r}_1=\alpha\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}+\lambda(\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+2\hat{k})$, $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$, $\alpha>0$ and $\vec{r}_2=-4\hat{i}-\hat{k}+\mu(3\hat{i}-2\hat{j}-2\hat{k})$, $\mu\in\mathbb{R}$ is $9$, then $\alpha$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: The shortest distance is the projection of the joining vector on $\vec{p}\times\vec{q}$, a linear equation $|2\alpha+15|=27$ in $\alpha$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Shortest distance equals the distance from a point of $L_1$ to the plane through $L_2$ parallel to $L_1$.
solution: The plane through $(-4,0,-1)$ containing the direction of $L_2$ and parallel to $L_1$ has normal $\vec{p}\times\vec{q}\parallel(2,2,1)$.
$L_1$ is parallel to this plane, so every point of $L_1$ is at the same distance; take $(\alpha,2,2)$.

useful_results: Shortest distance between skew lines $\vec{r}=\vec{a}+\lambda\vec{p}$ and $\vec{r}=\vec{b}+\mu\vec{q}$ is $\frac{|(\vec{a}-\vec{b})\cdot(\vec{p}\times\vec{q})|}{|\vec{p}\times\vec{q}|}=\frac{|[\vec{a}-\vec{b}\ \ \vec{p}\ \ \vec{q}]|}{|\vec{p}\times\vec{q}|}$.
The lines intersect (or are coplanar) iff $[\vec{a}-\vec{b}\ \ \vec{p}\ \ \vec{q}]=0$; here that gives $\alpha=-\frac{15}{2}$.
For parallel lines use $\frac{|(\vec{a}-\vec{b})\times\vec{p}|}{|\vec{p}|}$.
Dividing $\vec{p}\times\vec{q}$ by a common factor first (here $4$) keeps the numbers small.

concepts: Scalar and vector products of vectors
questions.question: Let $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$ be three mutually perpendicular vectors of the same magnitude and equally inclined at an angle $\theta$ with the vector $\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}$. Then $36\cos^2 2\theta$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: For mutually perpendicular equal vectors, $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}|=r\sqrt{3}$, so $\cos\theta=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Take $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$ along the axes; the angle is that of the diagonal $(1,1,1)$ with an axis, and direction cosines satisfy $\sum\cos^2=1$.
solution: Choose axes along the three vectors: they are $r\hat{i},r\hat{j},r\hat{k}$ and the sum is along $(1,1,1)$.
The sum makes equal angles $\theta$ with all three axes, so $\cos^2\theta+\cos^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$ (direction cosines).

useful_results: Direction cosines of any line satisfy $l^2+m^2+n^2=1$; equal angles with three perpendicular axes give $\cos\theta=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$.
For mutually perpendicular vectors, $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}|^2=|\vec{a}|^2+|\vec{b}|^2+|\vec{c}|^2$ (all cross terms vanish).
$\cos2\theta=2\cos^2\theta-1$; with $\cos^2\theta=\frac{1}{3}$ this is $-\frac{1}{3}$.

concepts: Scalar and vector products of vectors
questions.question: For $p>0$, a vector $\vec{v}_2=2\hat{i}+(p+1)\hat{j}$ is obtained by rotating the vector $\vec{v}_1=\sqrt{3}p\hat{i}+\hat{j}$ by an angle $\theta$ about origin in counter clockwise direction. If $\tan\theta=\dfrac{\alpha\sqrt{3}-2}{4\sqrt{3}+3}$, then the value of $\alpha$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Rotation preserves length, which fixes $p=2$; then $\tan\theta=\frac{\text{cross}}{\text{dot}}$ of $\vec{v}_1,\vec{v}_2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Treat the vectors as complex numbers: $e^{i\theta}\propto\vec{v}_2\,\overline{\vec{v}_1}$, whose argument is $\theta$.
solution: $z_2=z_1e^{i\theta}$, so $e^{i\theta}\propto z_2\overline{z_1}$ with a positive real factor $\frac{1}{|z_1|^2}$.

useful_results: A rotation about the origin preserves magnitude; equal-length conditions often fix an unknown parameter.
For plane vectors, $\tan\theta=\frac{x_1y_2-x_2y_1}{x_1x_2+y_1y_2}$ is the tangent of the anticlockwise angle from $\vec{v}_1$ to $\vec{v}_2$ (cross product over dot product).
In complex form, the angle from $z_1$ to $z_2$ is $\arg\big(z_2\overline{z_1}\big)$.

concepts: Scalar and vector products of vectors
questions.question: Let $\vec{p}=2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ and $\vec{q}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ be two vectors. If a vector $\vec{r}=\alpha\hat{i}+\beta\hat{j}+\gamma\hat{k}$ is perpendicular to each of the vectors $(\vec{p}+\vec{q})$ and $(\vec{p}-\vec{q})$, and $|\vec{r}|=\sqrt{3}$, then $|\alpha|+|\beta|+|\gamma|$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Two perpendicularity conditions give $\vec{r}=\alpha(\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k})$, and $|\vec{r}|=\sqrt{3}$ forces $|\alpha|=1$.

alternate_solutions.idea: A vector perpendicular to both $\vec{p}+\vec{q}$ and $\vec{p}-\vec{q}$ is parallel to their cross product, which equals $-2\,\vec{p}\times\vec{q}$.

useful_results: A vector perpendicular to two non-parallel vectors $\vec{u},\vec{v}$ is parallel to $\vec{u}\times\vec{v}$.
$(\vec{p}+\vec{q})\times(\vec{p}-\vec{q})=-2\,\vec{p}\times\vec{q}$, so $\vec{r}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{p}$ and $\vec{q}$ as well.
With a magnitude given, a direction vector $\pm\vec{n}$ gives exactly two possibilities for $\vec{r}$; $|\alpha|+|\beta|+|\gamma|$ is the same for both.

concepts: Scalar and vector products of vectors
questions.question: If $(\vec{a}+3\vec{b})$ is perpendicular to $(7\vec{a}-5\vec{b})$ and $(\vec{a}-4\vec{b})$ is perpendicular to $(7\vec{a}-2\vec{b})$, then the angle between $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ (in degrees) is ______.
questions.key_idea: Each perpendicularity is a relation among $|\vec{a}|^2$, $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}$, $|\vec{b}|^2$; two of them give $|\vec{a}|=|\vec{b}|$ and $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=\frac{|\vec{b}|^2}{2}$.
useful_results: Perpendicularity $\Rightarrow$ dot product $=0$; expanding gives homogeneous equations in $|\vec{a}|^2$, $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}$, $|\vec{b}|^2$.
Two such equations determine the ratios, hence $\cos\theta$, even though the lengths are unknown.
Remember $(x\vec{a}+y\vec{b})\cdot(u\vec{a}+v\vec{b})=xu|\vec{a}|^2+(xv+yu)\,\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}+yv|\vec{b}|^2$.

concepts: Scalar triple product and projection of a vector
questions.question: Let $\vec{a}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}$, $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}=\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ be three vectors such that $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}=\vec{c}$ and $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=1$. If the length of the projection vector of the vector $\vec{b}$ on the vector $\vec{a}\times\vec{c}$ is $l$, then the value of $3l^2$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Dotting $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}=\vec{c}$ with $\vec{c}$ gives the triple product $[\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}]=|\vec{c}|^2$ without ever finding $\vec{b}$.
solution: The length of the projection of $\vec{b}$ on $\vec{a}\times\vec{c}$ is $l=\frac{|\vec{b}\cdot(\vec{a}\times\vec{c})|}{|\vec{a}\times\vec{c}|}=\frac{|[\vec{b},\vec{a},\vec{c}]|}{|\vec{a}\times\vec{c}|}=\frac{|[\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}]|}{|\vec{a}\times\vec{c}|}$.
Given $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}=\vec{c}$; take the dot product with $\vec{c}$: $(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})\cdot\vec{c}=\vec{c}\cdot\vec{c}$.
Interchanging two vectors only changes the sign of a triple product, so $|[\vec{b},\vec{a},\vec{c}]|=|[\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}]|=2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Solve for $\vec{b}$ explicitly from $\vec{a}\times(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})$, then dot with $\vec{a}\times\vec{c}$.

useful_results: $(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})\cdot\vec{c}=[\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}]$; if $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}=\vec{c}$ this equals $|\vec{c}|^2$ at once.
Interchanging any two vectors in a scalar triple product changes only its sign; a cyclic shift changes nothing.
Length of the projection of $\vec{u}$ on $\vec{v}$ is $\frac{|\vec{u}\cdot\vec{v}|}{|\vec{v}|}$.
$\vec{a}\times(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})=(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})\vec{a}-|\vec{a}|^2\vec{b}$ recovers $\vec{b}$ from $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$ and $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}$ (here $\vec{b}=\hat{i}$).

concepts: Dot product and scalar triple product of vectors
questions.question: Let $\vec{a}=\hat{i}-\alpha\hat{j}+\beta\hat{k}$, $\vec{b}=3\hat{i}+\beta\hat{j}-\alpha\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c}=-\alpha\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$, where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are integers. If $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=-1$ and $\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c}=10$, then $(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})\cdot\vec{c}$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: The two dot-product conditions give $\alpha\beta=2$ and $2\alpha+\beta=-5$; integrality picks one root, then expand the determinant.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes $\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c}$ as $3\alpha-2\beta-\alpha$ and $\vec{c}$ as $-\alpha\hat{j}-2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ (typos). Correct: $\vec{c}=-\alpha\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c}=-3\alpha-2\beta-\alpha=-4\alpha-2\beta$; the PDF's equation (2) and answer 9 are right.
useful_results: For $\vec{u}=(u_1,u_2,u_3)$ etc., $(\vec{u}\times\vec{v})\cdot\vec{w}$ is the $3\times3$ determinant of the three coefficient rows (in that order).
A pair of conditions of the form $\alpha\beta=m$ and $p\alpha+q\beta=n$ reduces to a quadratic; the word 'integers' discards the non-integral root.
Always substitute the solved parameters back and recheck both given dot products before expanding the determinant.

concepts: Coplanarity of two lines in space
questions.question: The lines $x=ay-1=z-2$ and $x=3y-2=bz-2$ $(ab\neq0)$ are coplanar, if:
questions.key_idea: Write both lines in symmetric form (dividing the $y$ and $z$ parts so that $x$ has denominator 1), then use the coplanarity determinant.
solution: The $a$-terms cancel: this simplifies to $\frac{b-1}{ab}=0$, i.e. $b=1$ (with $a\neq0$ arbitrary).
Check with $b=1$: the third row becomes $\left(1,\frac{1}{3},1\right)$ and the first row has only a middle entry, giving determinant $\propto(1\cdot1-1\cdot1)=0$ for every $a$.
Options (B), (C): $b\neq1$, not coplanar; option (D) allows $b\neq1$, so it is wrong. Answer: (A).
questions.correction_note: The PDF's expansion line '$3b-4a+4ab=3$' is wrong (the determinant simplifies to $\frac{b-1}{ab}=0$); it only happens to be satisfied by $b=1$ for all $a$. Final answer (A) $b=1,\ a\in\mathbb{R}-\{0\}$ is correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Coplanar lines either meet or are parallel, so equate the points for the same $x=t$ and see what is forced.
solution: Put $x=t$. Line 1: $\left(t,\frac{t+1}{a},t+2\right)$. Line 2: $\left(t,\frac{t+2}{3},\frac{t+2}{b}\right)$ (same $x$ means same parameter).
With $b=1$ equal $y$ gives $\frac{t+1}{a}=\frac{t+2}{3}$, which has a solution for every $a\neq3$ (lines meet).
For $a=3$ and $b=1$ the directions coincide, so the lines are parallel and still coplanar. Hence $b=1$, $a\in\mathbb{R}-\{0\}$: (A).

useful_results: Lines through $A$, $B$ with directions $\vec{p}$, $\vec{q}$ are coplanar iff $[\overrightarrow{AB},\vec{p},\vec{q}]=0$ (they meet, or are parallel).
Rewrite a line given as $x=ay-1=z-2$ by dividing: $\frac{x}{1}=\frac{y-1/a}{1/a}=\frac{z-2}{1}$. Direction ratios are the reciprocals of the coefficients.
If two lines are skew the shortest distance is $\frac{|[\overrightarrow{AB},\vec{p},\vec{q}]|}{|\vec{p}\times\vec{q}|}\neq0$.

concepts: Image of a point in a line
Equation of a plane perpendicular to a line
questions.question: Consider the line $L$ given by $\frac{x-3}{2}=\frac{y-1}{1}=\frac{z-2}{1}$. Let $Q$ be the mirror image of the point $(2,3,-1)$ with respect to $L$. Let a plane $P$ be such that it passes through $Q$, and the line $L$ is perpendicular to $P$. Then which of the following points is on the plane $P$?
questions.key_idea: The plane is $2x+y+z=d$ since $L$ is its normal; find $Q$ (via the foot of the perpendicular) and substitute to get $d$.
solution: Let $A=(2,3,-1)$ and let $B=(2\lambda+3,\lambda+1,\lambda+2)$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $L$; direction $\vec{p}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}$.
Plane $P$ has normal $\vec{p}=(2,1,1)$ and passes through $Q$: $2(x-2)+(y+2)+(z-4)=0$, i.e. $2x+y+z=6$.
Test the options: $(1,2,2)$ gives $2+2+2=6$, so it lies on $P$; $(1,1,2)\to5$ and $(-1,1,2)\to1$ do not. Answer (B).
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes the image coordinates as $\beta=2,\gamma=2$ (typo); the midpoint equations give $\beta=-2$, $\gamma=4$, $Q=(2,-2,4)$, which is what the PDF's plane $2x+y+z=6$ actually uses. Also options (A) and (C) are both printed as $(1,1,2)$ in the paper.

alternate_solutions.idea: A rotation by $180^\circ$ about $L$ (reflection in $L$) maps every plane perpendicular to $L$ onto itself, so $Q$ lies in the plane through $A$ perpendicular to $L$.
solution: Reflection in the line $L$ is a half-turn about $L$; it keeps the plane through $A$ perpendicular to $L$ fixed (as a set).
So $Q$ lies in the plane through $A$ with normal $\vec{p}=(2,1,1)$, and $P$ (through $Q$, normal $\vec{p}$) is exactly that plane.
Only $(1,2,2)$ satisfies $2x+y+z=6$. Answer (B); $Q$ never had to be computed.

useful_results: Reflection in a line is a $180^\circ$ rotation about it, so each plane perpendicular to the line is mapped into itself.
Foot of perpendicular from $A$ to $\frac{x-x_1}{l}=\frac{y-y_1}{m}=\frac{z-z_1}{n}$: put a general point and impose $\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot(l,m,n)=0$.
Image of $A$ in a line: $Q=2B-A$, where $B$ is the foot of the perpendicular.
Plane through a point $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ perpendicular to a line with direction $(l,m,n)$: $l(x-x_0)+m(y-y_0)+n(z-z_0)=0$.

concepts: Line of intersection of two planes
Foot of perpendicular from a point to a line
questions.question: Let $L$ be the line of intersection of the planes $\vec{r}\cdot(\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k})=2$ and $\vec{r}\cdot(2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k})=2$. If $P(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ is the foot of the perpendicular on $L$ from the point $(1,2,0)$, then the value of $35(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Direction of $L$ is $\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2$; take a general point of $L$ and impose perpendicularity of the join to the point.
solution: Put $z=0$ in (1) and (2): $x=\frac{4}{3}$, $y=-\frac{2}{3}$, so $\left(\frac{4}{3},-\frac{2}{3},0\right)$ is on $L$.

alternate_solutions.idea: $\overrightarrow{PN}\perp L$ means $\overrightarrow{PN}$ lies in the span of the two normals, so $N=P+u\vec{n}_1+v\vec{n}_2$ with $N$ on both planes.

useful_results: A vector perpendicular to the line of intersection of two planes lies in the span of their normals $\vec{n}_1,\vec{n}_2$ (since $L\parallel\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2$).
To get a point on the line of intersection, set one coordinate to $0$ and solve the two plane equations.
Foot of perpendicular from $P$ to a line through $A$ with direction $\vec{p}$: $N=A+\frac{(P-A)\cdot\vec{p}}{|\vec{p}|^2}\vec{p}$.

concepts: Shortest distance between skew lines
questions.question: If the shortest distance between the straight lines $3(x-1)=6(y-2)=2(z-1)$ and $4(x-2)=2(y-\lambda)=(z-3)$, $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$ is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{38}}$, then the integral value of $\lambda$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Convert to symmetric form to read directions $\vec{p},\vec{q}$ and points, then use $d=\frac{|\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot(\vec{p}\times\vec{q})|}{|\vec{p}\times\vec{q}|}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Distance between two parallel planes: the plane through each line, both with normal $\vec{p}\times\vec{q}$.
solution: Both planes contain a line each and are parallel, so $d=\frac{|(5\lambda-5)-9|}{\sqrt{38}}=\frac{|5\lambda-14|}{\sqrt{38}}$.

useful_results: Shortest distance between skew lines $\vec{r}=\vec{a}_1+s\vec{p}$, $\vec{r}=\vec{a}_2+t\vec{q}$ is $\frac{|(\vec{a}_2-\vec{a}_1)\cdot(\vec{p}\times\vec{q})|}{|\vec{p}\times\vec{q}|}$.
It equals the distance between the two parallel planes containing the lines, both with normal $\vec{p}\times\vec{q}$.
Convert $a(x-x_1)=b(y-y_1)=c(z-z_1)$ to direction ratios $\left(\frac{1}{a},\frac{1}{b},\frac{1}{c}\right)$ before using the formula.

concepts: Foot of perpendicular and line parallel to a plane
Angle between two lines
questions.question: Let the foot of perpendicular from a point $P(1,2,-1)$ to the straight line $L:\frac{x}{1}=\frac{y}{0}=\frac{z}{-1}$ be $N$. Let a line be drawn from $P$ parallel to the plane $x+y+2z=0$ which meets $L$ at the point $Q$. If $\alpha$ is the acute angle between the lines $PN$ and $PQ$, then $\cos\alpha$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $PN\perp L$ makes $\triangle PNQ$ right-angled at $N$, so $\alpha$ is the angle at $P$ and $\cos\alpha=\frac{PN}{PQ}$; alternatively use $\angle PQN=90^\circ-\alpha$ with the direction of $L$.
solution: $PQ$ is parallel to the plane $x+y+2z=0$, so $\overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot(1,1,2)=0$.
In the right triangle $PNQ$, the angle at $Q$ between $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ and $L$ is $90^\circ-\alpha$ (as $PN\perp L$).
questions.correction_note: The PDF's final line gives $Q(-1,0,-1)$, which is not on $L$; the correct point is $Q(-1,0,1)$ (i.e. $\lambda=-1$ in $(\lambda,0,-\lambda)$). The PDF's $\overrightarrow{PQ}=(-2,-2,2)$ and answer $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ are correct. The English text layer also loses the minus sign of $z/(-1)$; the Hindi stem shows $\frac{z}{-1}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Find $N$ explicitly and use the right triangle $PNQ$: $\cos\alpha=\frac{PN}{PQ}$.

useful_results: Line $PQ$ is parallel to a plane with normal $\vec{n}$ iff $\overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot\vec{n}=0$.
If $PN\perp L$ with $N,Q\in L$, then $\triangle PNQ$ is right-angled at $N$, so $\cos\angle NPQ=\frac{PN}{PQ}$ and $\sin\angle NPQ=\frac{NQ}{PQ}$.
Angle between the line $PQ$ and a line of direction $\vec{p}$: $\cos\theta=\frac{|\overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot\vec{p}|}{|\overrightarrow{PQ}||\vec{p}|}$.

concepts: Plane perpendicular to two given planes
questions.question: Let the plane passing through the point $(-1,0,-2)$ and perpendicular to each of the planes $2x+y-z=2$ and $x-y-z=3$ be $ax+by+cz+8=0$. Then the value of $a+b+c$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The normal of a plane perpendicular to two planes is the cross product of their normals.
solution: Required plane is perpendicular to both, so its normal is $\vec{n}=\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2$.
useful_results: A plane perpendicular to two planes has normal $\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2$ (it is parallel to both normals); the same vector is the direction of their line of intersection.
Plane through $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ with normal $(l,m,n)$: $l(x-x_0)+m(y-y_0)+n(z-z_0)=0$; scale it so the constant term is the one asked for.

concepts: Point of intersection of two lines
Point lying on a plane
questions.question: For real numbers $\alpha$ and $\beta\neq0$, if the point of intersection of the straight lines $\frac{x-\alpha}{1}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z-1}{3}$ and $\frac{x-4}{\beta}=\frac{y-6}{3}=\frac{z-7}{3}$ lies on the plane $x+2y-z=8$, then $\alpha-\beta$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Equate the general points of the two lines; the $y$ and $z$ equations fix both parameters, then use the plane.
solution: The intersection point in terms of $\alpha$ is $(\alpha+1,\,3,\,4)$; it lies on $x+2y-z=8$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's last lines read '$1+\alpha+6-4=8,\ \alpha=5,\ \beta=2,\ \alpha-\beta=7$'. With $\alpha+\beta=3$ and $\alpha=5$, $\beta=-2$ (not $2$); then $\alpha-\beta=7$. The PDF's answer (B) $7$ is correct; the stated $\beta=2$ was a slip.

alternate_solutions.idea: Every point of $L_2$ satisfies $z-y=1$, which immediately fixes the parameter of $L_1$.
solution: On $L_2$: $y-6=z-7$ (both equal $3t_2$), so every point of $L_2$ satisfies $z-y=1$.
On $L_1$: $z-y=(1+3t_1)-(1+2t_1)=t_1$. So at the common point $t_1=1$ and the point is $(\alpha+1,3,4)$.
Plane: $\alpha+1+6-4=8$ gives $\alpha=5$, so the point is $(6,3,4)$.

useful_results: If two lines have direction ratios with equal $y$- and $z$-components, the combination $z-y$ is constant on that line; look for such invariants to cut down the elimination.
For lines meeting at a point, use separate parameters $t_1,t_2$ and solve any two coordinate equations first; the third is then a consistency check.
After finding the point, substitute it in the plane to fix the remaining unknown.

concepts: Plane through three points
Vector triple product
questions.question: Let $P$ be a plane passing through the points $(1,0,1)$, $(1,-2,1)$ and $(0,1,-2)$. Let a vector $\vec{a}=\alpha\hat{i}+\beta\hat{j}+\gamma\hat{k}$ be such that $\vec{a}$ is parallel to the plane $P$, perpendicular to $(\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+3\hat{k})$ and $\vec{a}\cdot(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+2\hat{k})=2$, then $(\alpha-\beta+\gamma)^2$ equals ______.
questions.key_idea: $\vec{a}$ lies in the plane of $\vec{p},\vec{q}$ and is perpendicular to $\vec{r}$, so $\vec{a}=\lambda\,(\vec{p}\times\vec{q})\times\vec{r}$.
solution: Let $A(1,0,1)$, $B(1,-2,1)$, $C(0,1,-2)$. $\overrightarrow{AB}=-2\hat{j}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}=-\hat{i}+\hat{j}-3\hat{k}$; only directions matter, so take $\vec{p}=2\hat{j}$ and $\vec{q}=-\hat{i}+\hat{j}-3\hat{k}$.
Let $\vec{r}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$. $\vec{a}$ is parallel to the plane (in the plane of $\vec{p},\vec{q}$) and perpendicular to $\vec{r}$.
A vector in the plane of $\vec{p},\vec{q}$ perpendicular to $\vec{r}$ is $\vec{a}=\lambda(\vec{p}\times\vec{q})\times\vec{r}$ (it is perpendicular to $\vec{p}\times\vec{q}$ and to $\vec{r}$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the normal $\vec{n}=\vec{p}\times\vec{q}$ of the plane: parallel to $P$ means $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{n}=0$, giving a plain linear system.

useful_results: For vectors $\vec{p},\vec{q}$ spanning a plane and any $\vec{r}$, the vector $(\vec{p}\times\vec{q})\times\vec{r}$ lies in that plane and is perpendicular to $\vec{r}$.
$(\vec{x}\times\vec{y})\times\vec{z}=(\vec{x}\cdot\vec{z})\vec{y}-(\vec{y}\cdot\vec{z})\vec{x}$.
A vector is parallel to a plane iff it is perpendicular to the plane's normal, which gives a linear equation; three independent conditions fix the vector.

concepts: Coplanarity of two lines in space
questions.question: If the lines $\frac{x-k}{1}=\frac{y-2}{2}=\frac{z-3}{3}$ and $\frac{x+1}{3}=\frac{y+2}{2}=\frac{z+3}{1}$ are co-planar, then the value of $k$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: Coplanarity is the single condition $[\overrightarrow{AB},\vec{p},\vec{q}]=0$, which is linear in $k$.
solution: Line 1 passes through $A(k,2,3)$ with direction $\vec{p}=(1,2,3)$; line 2 passes through $B(-1,-2,-3)$ with direction $\vec{q}=(3,2,1)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Coplanar non-parallel lines must meet: solve for the common point.
solution: Line 1: $(k+\lambda,\,2+2\lambda,\,3+3\lambda)$; line 2: $(-1+3\mu,\,-2+2\mu,\,-3+\mu)$. The lines are not parallel.

useful_results: Two non-parallel lines are coplanar iff they intersect; the determinant condition $[\overrightarrow{AB},\vec{p},\vec{q}]=0$ is the compact test.
When only one unknown appears in the determinant, the condition is linear in it, so exactly one value works.
Coplanarity is unaffected by the sign or scale of $\overrightarrow{AB}$, $\vec{p}$, $\vec{q}$.

concepts: Plane containing a line and a point
Distance of a point from a plane
questions.question: Let a plane $P$ pass through the point $(3,7,-7)$ and contain the line $\frac{x-2}{-3}=\frac{y-3}{2}=\frac{z+2}{1}$. If the distance of the plane $P$ from the origin is $d$, then $d^2$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: The plane contains $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and the line's direction, so its normal is their cross product; then use the point-plane distance.
solution: The line passes through $A(2,3,-2)$ with direction $\vec{p}=-3\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$; let $B=(3,7,-7)$, so $\overrightarrow{AB}=\hat{i}+4\hat{j}-5\hat{k}$.
For a general point $R(x,y,z)$ of the plane, $\overrightarrow{AR}$, $\overrightarrow{AB}$, $\vec{p}$ are coplanar.
Check: $A$ gives $2+3-2=3$ and $B$ gives $3+7-7=3$, so both lie on the plane.
questions.correction_note: The PDF says '$\overrightarrow{AR},\overrightarrow{AB},\vec{P}$ are collinear vectors'; it should be coplanar (the determinant is the coplanarity condition). The working and answer $3$ are correct.
useful_results: Plane through a point $B$ containing a line (point $A$, direction $\vec{p}$): normal $\vec{n}=\overrightarrow{AB}\times\vec{p}$.
Distance of the origin from $ax+by+cz+e=0$ is $\frac{|e|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}$.
Expanding the $3\times3$ determinant is the same as the cross product $\overrightarrow{AB}\times\vec{p}$ (here $14(1,1,1)$).

concepts: Intersection of a line and a plane
Distance between two points
questions.question: The distance of the point $P(3,4,4)$ from the point of intersection of the line joining the points $Q(3,-4,-5)$ and $R(2,-3,1)$ and the plane $2x+y+z=7$, is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Put the general point of line $QR$ in the plane to find the intersection, then take the distance.

alternate_solutions.idea: Section formula with signed plane values: the point divides $QR$ in the ratio of the values of $f=2x+y+z-7$ at $Q$ and $R$.
solution: $f(Q)=6-4-5-7=-10$ and $f(R)=4-3+1-7=-5$ (same sign, so the point lies outside $QR$).
The intersection $T$ divides $QR$ externally in the ratio $|f(Q)|:|f(R)|=10:5=2:1$, i.e. $T=2R-Q$.

useful_results: A line meets a plane $f(x,y,z)=0$ where its general point satisfies $f=0$; for a linear $f$ this is a single linear equation in the parameter.
The line $QR$ meets $f=0$ at the point dividing $QR$ in the ratio $-f(Q):f(R)$ (a negative ratio means external division).
Distance between $(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ and $(x_2,y_2,z_2)$ is $\sqrt{\sum(x_1-x_2)^2}$.

concepts: Vector triple product and scalar triple product
questions.question: Let $\vec{a}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b}=\hat{j}-\hat{k}$. If $\vec{c}$ is a vector such that $\vec{a}\times\vec{c}=\vec{b}$ and $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}=3$, then $\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Cross $\vec{a}$ with $\vec{a}\times\vec{c}=\vec{b}$ to express $\vec{c}$ via $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$, then dot with $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Cyclic property of the scalar triple product: $\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})=\vec{b}\cdot(\vec{c}\times\vec{a})=-\vec{b}\cdot(\vec{a}\times\vec{c})$.
solution: Check: such $\vec{c}$ exists since $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=0$; e.g. $\vec{c}=\left(\frac{5}{3},\frac{2}{3},\frac{2}{3}\right)$ has $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}=3$ and $\vec{a}\times\vec{c}=\vec{b}$. The condition $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}=3$ is not even needed.

useful_results: $[\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}]$ is unchanged by cyclic permutation and changes sign on swapping two vectors.
If $\vec{a}\times\vec{c}=\vec{b}$, then $[\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}]=\vec{b}\cdot(\vec{c}\times\vec{a})=-|\vec{b}|^2$ immediately.
$\vec{a}\times\vec{c}=\vec{b}$ is solvable only if $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=0$, and then $\vec{c}=\frac{(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c})\vec{a}-\vec{a}\times\vec{b}}{|\vec{a}|^2}$.
$\vec{a}\times(\vec{a}\times\vec{x})=(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{x})\vec{a}-|\vec{a}|^2\vec{x}$.

concepts: Dot product and magnitude of a sum of vectors
questions.question: Let $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ be two vectors such that $|2\vec{a}+3\vec{b}|=|3\vec{a}+\vec{b}|$ and the angle between $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ is $60^\circ$. If $\frac{1}{8}\vec{a}$ is a unit vector, then $|\vec{b}|$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Square the equal-magnitude condition and use $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos60^\circ$ to get a quadratic in $|\vec{b}|$.
solution: $\frac{1}{8}\vec{a}$ is a unit vector, so $|\vec{a}|=8$. Write $a=|\vec{a}|$, $b=|\vec{b}|$; the angle between them is $60^\circ$, so $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=ab\cos60^\circ$.
Factorise: $(b+8)(b-5)=0$. Since $b>0$, $b=5$, so $|\vec{b}|=5$ and the answer is (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the difference of squares: $|\vec{u}|^2=|\vec{v}|^2\iff(\vec{u}-\vec{v})\cdot(\vec{u}+\vec{v})=0$.

useful_results: $|\vec{u}|=|\vec{v}|\iff(\vec{u}+\vec{v})\cdot(\vec{u}-\vec{v})=0$: the diagonals of the parallelogram on $\vec{u},\vec{v}$ are perpendicular exactly when $|\vec{u}|=|\vec{v}|$.
$|\vec{x}+\vec{y}|^2=|\vec{x}|^2+|\vec{y}|^2+2\,\vec{x}\cdot\vec{y}$ with $\vec{x}\cdot\vec{y}=|\vec{x}||\vec{y}|\cos\theta$ turns most magnitude conditions into one quadratic.
A unit-vector hint such as '$\frac{1}{8}\vec{a}$ is a unit vector' simply means $|\vec{a}|=8$; always reject the negative root of a length equation.

concepts: Vector triple product
Linear combination of mutually perpendicular vectors
questions.question: Let $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$ be three vectors mutually perpendicular to each other and have the same magnitude. If a vector $\vec{r}$ satisfies $\vec{a}\times\{(\vec{r}-\vec{b})\times\vec{a}\}+\vec{b}\times\{(\vec{r}-\vec{c})\times\vec{b}\}+\vec{c}\times\{(\vec{r}-\vec{a})\times\vec{c}\}=\vec{0}$, then $\vec{r}$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $\vec{a}\times(\vec{x}\times\vec{a})=|\vec{a}|^2\vec{x}-(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{x})\vec{a}$ is $|\vec{a}|^2$ times the part of $\vec{x}$ perpendicular to $\vec{a}$; expand $\vec{r}$ in the triad.
solution: Since $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$ are mutually perpendicular, write $\vec{r}=x\vec{a}+y\vec{b}+z\vec{c}$ with $|\vec{a}|=|\vec{b}|=|\vec{c}|=k$.
In the same way the second term is $k^2(\vec{r}-\vec{c})-k^2y\vec{b}$ and the third is $k^2(\vec{r}-\vec{a})-k^2z\vec{c}$.
Add the three terms and divide by $k^2$: $(\vec{r}-\vec{b})-x\vec{a}+(\vec{r}-\vec{c})-y\vec{b}+(\vec{r}-\vec{a})-z\vec{c}=\vec{0}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Read $\vec{a}\times(\vec{x}\times\vec{a})$ as $k^2$ times the component of $\vec{x}$ perpendicular to $\vec{a}$ and work in coordinates along the triad.
solution: Take $\vec{a}=k\vec{e}_1$, $\vec{b}=k\vec{e}_2$, $\vec{c}=k\vec{e}_3$ for an orthonormal triad and $\vec{r}=(x,y,z)$ in this triad (components in units of $\vec{e}_i$).
$\vec{a}\times\{\vec{p}\times\vec{a}\}=k^2\times$ (component of $\vec{p}$ perpendicular to $\vec{e}_1$), i.e. $k^2$ times $\vec{p}$ with its $\vec{e}_1$-part deleted.
$\vec{r}-\vec{c}=(x,y,z-k)$; deleting the $\vec{e}_2$-part gives $(x,0,z-k)$. $\vec{r}-\vec{a}=(x-k,y,z)$; deleting the $\vec{e}_3$-part gives $(x-k,y,0)$.

useful_results: $\vec{a}\times(\vec{x}\times\vec{a})=|\vec{a}|^2\vec{x}-(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{x})\vec{a}$: it is $|\vec{a}|^2$ times the projection of $\vec{x}$ onto the plane perpendicular to $\vec{a}$.
BAC-CAB rule: $\vec{a}\times(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})=(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c})\vec{b}-(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})\vec{c}$ (the middle vector times the dot of the outer two, minus the other).
For mutually perpendicular vectors, expand an unknown $\vec{r}$ as $x\vec{a}+y\vec{b}+z\vec{c}$; dot products then isolate the coefficients.

concepts: Projection of a vector
questions.question: If the projection of the vector $\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ on the sum of the two vectors $2\hat{i}+4\hat{j}-5\hat{k}$ and $-\lambda\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ is $1$, then $\lambda$ is equal to ____.
questions.key_idea: Add the two vectors, then use projection of $\vec{p}$ on $\vec{q}$ $=\frac{\vec{p}\cdot\vec{q}}{|\vec{q}|}$; the squared equation turns out linear in $\lambda$.
solution: Projection of $\vec{v}_1$ on $\vec{v}_4$ is $\vec{v}_1\cdot\frac{\vec{v}_4}{|\vec{v}_4|}$, and it equals $1$.
So $20\lambda=100$ and $\lambda=5$. Check: $12-\lambda=7>0$, so the projection is $+1$ and no root is lost or added.
useful_results: Scalar projection of $\vec{p}$ on $\vec{q}$ is $\frac{\vec{p}\cdot\vec{q}}{|\vec{q}|}$ (signed); the vector projection is $\frac{\vec{p}\cdot\vec{q}}{|\vec{q}|^2}\vec{q}$.
Squaring a projection equation can bring in the wrong sign: always check that $\vec{p}\cdot\vec{q}$ has the sign of the required projection.
When the unknown appears in both numerator and under the root as $\lambda$ with the same coefficient, the $\lambda^2$ terms cancel and the equation is linear.

concepts: Cross product magnitude (Lagrange identity)
Perpendicular vectors
questions.question: Let $\vec{a}=\hat{i}+5\hat{j}+\alpha\hat{k}$, $\vec{b}=\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+\beta\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c}=-\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-3\hat{k}$ be three vectors such that $|\vec{b}\times\vec{c}|=5\sqrt{3}$ and $\vec{a}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{b}$. Then the greatest amongst the values of $|\vec{a}|^2$ is ____.
questions.key_idea: $|\vec{b}\times\vec{c}|^2=|\vec{b}|^2|\vec{c}|^2-(\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c})^2$ gives $\beta$; then $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=0$ gives $\alpha$ for each $\beta$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Compute $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$ directly as a determinant instead of using the Lagrange identity.

useful_results: Lagrange's identity: $|\vec{b}\times\vec{c}|^2=|\vec{b}|^2|\vec{c}|^2-(\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c})^2$, i.e. $(|\vec{b}||\vec{c}|\sin\theta)^2$; it avoids computing the cross product.
A quadratic in the unknown component usually gives two values; 'greatest' or 'least' in the stem is the signal to carry both branches to the end.
$\vec{a}\perp\vec{b}\iff\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=0$ is linear in the unknown component of $\vec{a}$ once $\vec{b}$ is fixed.

concepts: Vector in the plane of two vectors (triple product)
Projection of a vector
questions.question: Let $\vec{a}=2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-\hat{k}$. Let a vector $\vec{v}$ be in the plane containing $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$. If $\vec{v}$ is perpendicular to the vector $3\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and its projection on $\vec{a}$ is $19$ units, then $|2\vec{v}|^2$ is equal to ____.
questions.key_idea: A vector in the plane of $\vec{a},\vec{b}$ and perpendicular to $\vec{c}$ is parallel to $\vec{c}\times(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})=(\vec{c}\cdot\vec{b})\vec{a}-(\vec{c}\cdot\vec{a})\vec{b}$.
solution: Let $\vec{c}=3\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-\hat{k}$. $\vec{v}$ lies in the plane of $\vec{a},\vec{b}$ and is perpendicular to $\vec{c}$, so $\vec{v}=\lambda\{\vec{c}\times(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})\}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $\vec{v}=p\vec{a}+q\vec{b}$ and use the two conditions to find $p,q$.
solution: $\vec{v}$ lies in the plane of $\vec{a},\vec{b}$, so $\vec{v}=p\vec{a}+q\vec{b}$. Dot products: $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{a}=9$, $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=-2$, $\vec{c}\cdot\vec{a}=2$, $\vec{c}\cdot\vec{b}=8$ with $\vec{c}=3\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-\hat{k}$.

useful_results: A vector in the plane of $\vec{a},\vec{b}$ is $p\vec{a}+q\vec{b}$; it is also perpendicular to $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$.

The vector in the plane of $\vec{a},\vec{b}$ perpendicular to $\vec{c}$ is along $\vec{c}\times(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})=(\vec{c}\cdot\vec{b})\vec{a}-(\vec{c}\cdot\vec{a})\vec{b}$ (use it as a shortcut for the direction).
Projection of $\vec{v}$ on $\vec{a}$ equals $\vec{v}\cdot\hat{a}$, so the given value is $\vec{v}\cdot\vec{a}/|\vec{a}|$, not $\vec{v}\cdot\vec{a}$.

concepts: Family of planes through a line
Perpendicular planes
questions.question: A plane $P$ contains the line $x+2y+3z+1=0=x-y-z-6$, and is perpendicular to the plane $-2x+y+z+8=0$. Then which of the following points lies on $P$?
questions.key_idea: Use the family $\pi_1+\lambda\pi_2=0$ and impose perpendicularity of normals to fix $\lambda$.
solution: Only $(0,1,1)$ lies on $P$, so the answer is (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Normal of $P$ is perpendicular both to the line direction and to the normal of the given plane.
solution: $P$ contains the line, so its normal $\perp(1,4,-3)$; $P\perp$ the plane with normal $(-2,1,1)$, so its normal $\perp(-2,1,1)$.
A point on the line (put $z=0$): $x+2y=-1$, $x-y=6$ gives $\left(\frac{11}{3},-\frac{7}{3},0\right)$.

useful_results: A plane through the line of intersection of $\pi_1=0$ and $\pi_2=0$ has the form $\pi_1+\lambda\pi_2=0$ (excluding $\pi_2$ itself).
Two planes are perpendicular iff $\vec{n}_1\cdot\vec{n}_2=0$; the normal of the family is $\vec{n}_1+\lambda\vec{n}_2$.
A plane containing a line and perpendicular to another plane has normal $\vec{n}_{\text{given}}\times\vec{d}_{\text{line}}$.

concepts: Family of planes through a line
questions.question: Let $P$ be the plane passing through the point $(1,2,3)$ and the line of intersection of the planes $\vec{r}\cdot(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+4\hat{k})=16$ and $\vec{r}\cdot(-\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})=6$. Then which of the following points does NOT lie on $P$?
questions.key_idea: The required plane is $\pi_1+\lambda\pi_2=0$, with $\lambda$ fixed by the given point.
solution: Cartesian form of the two planes: $x+y+4z-16=0$ and $-x+y+z-6=0$.
Plane through their line of intersection: $(x+y+4z-16)+\lambda(-x+y+z-6)=0$.
$(4,2,2)$: $12+2+14=28\neq26$, so it does not lie on $P$. Answer (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Take three points that lie on $P$ (the given point and two points on the line) and find the normal by a cross product.
solution: Adding the two plane equations: $2y+5z=22$. Take $z=0$: $y=11$, $x=5$, giving $(5,11,0)$. Take $z=2$: $y=6$, $x=2$, giving $(2,6,2)$.
Both points satisfy $x+y+4z=16$ and $-x+y+z=6$, so they lie on the line.

useful_results: Plane through the intersection of $\pi_1=0$, $\pi_2=0$ and a given point $Q$: $\pi_1+\lambda\pi_2=0$ with $\lambda=-\pi_1(Q)/\pi_2(Q)$.
When the point is given, the family trick is faster than finding a point and the direction of the line.
A point lies on $P$ iff $\pi_1(X)/\pi_2(X)=\pi_1(Q)/\pi_2(Q)$ (with the same ratio) - useful for testing options quickly.

concepts: Family of planes through a line
Distance of a point from a plane
questions.question: Equation of a plane at a distance $\sqrt{\frac{2}{21}}$ from the origin, which contains the line of intersection of the planes $x-y-z-1=0$ and $2x+y-3z+4=0$, is:
questions.key_idea: Write the plane as $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$ and equate its distance from the origin to $\sqrt{2/21}$ to find $\lambda$.
solution: The other root $\lambda=\frac{15}{154}$ gives a second valid plane that is not among the options.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the options: keep only planes that contain the line (normal $\perp$ line direction, a point of the line on it), then check the distance.
solution: Direction of the line: $(1,-1,-1)\times(2,1,-3)=(4,1,3)$; a point on it ($z=0$): $(-1,-2,0)$.
(A) and (C) both contain the point $(-1,-2,0)$: $-3+3=0$ and $-4+2+2=0$, so both contain the line.

useful_results: Distance of $ax+by+cz+d=0$ from the origin is $\frac{|d|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}$.
The distance condition gives a quadratic in $\lambda$, so there are generally two planes in the family at the required distance; options (or extra conditions) pick one.
To test whether a plane contains a line: its normal is perpendicular to the line direction AND one point of the line lies on it.

concepts: Distance of a point from a plane measured along a direction
questions.question: The distance of the point $(1,-2,3)$ from the plane $x-y+z=5$ measured parallel to a line, whose direction ratios are $2,3,-6$ is:
questions.key_idea: Move from the point along the given direction until the plane is hit; the parameter times $|(2,3,-6)|=7$ is the distance.
solution: Let $A=(1,-2,3)$ and let $B$ be the point where the line through $A$ with direction ratios $2,3,-6$ meets the plane.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the slant-distance formula $\dfrac{|\vec{n}\cdot A-p|\,|\vec{d}|}{|\vec{n}\cdot\vec{d}|}$ for a point $A$, plane $\vec{n}\cdot\vec{r}=p$ and direction $\vec{d}$.
solution: Perpendicular distance of $A$ from the plane is $\frac{|1+2+3-5|}{\sqrt3}=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$.
Cosine of the angle between the direction $(2,3,-6)$ and the normal $(1,-1,1)$: $\frac{|2-3-6|}{7\sqrt3}=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$.
Distance along the direction = perpendicular distance divided by this cosine: $\frac{1/\sqrt3}{1/\sqrt3}=1$.

useful_results: Distance of $A$ from the plane $\vec{n}\cdot\vec{r}=p$ measured along $\vec{d}$ is $\frac{|\vec{n}\cdot\vec{a}-p|\,|\vec{d}|}{|\vec{n}\cdot\vec{d}|}$.
It equals the perpendicular distance divided by $\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{d}$ and the normal; it is never less than the perpendicular distance.
If $\vec{n}\cdot\vec{d}=0$ the direction is parallel to the plane and the distance is undefined (infinite).

concepts: Family of planes through a line
Plane parallel to a coordinate axis
questions.question: The equation of the plane passing through the line of intersection of the planes $\vec{r}\cdot(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})=1$ and $\vec{r}\cdot(2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-\hat{k})+4=0$ and parallel to the $x$-axis is:
questions.key_idea: A plane parallel to the $x$-axis has no $x$ term, so choose $\lambda$ in the family to kill the $x$-coefficient.
solution: Parallel to the $x$-axis means its normal is perpendicular to $\hat{i}$: $(1+2\lambda)\cdot1+(1+3\lambda)\cdot0+(1-\lambda)\cdot0=0$.
In vector form this is $\vec{r}\cdot(\hat{j}-3\hat{k})+6=0$, option (A).
questions.correction_note: The PDF labels the parameter value as $d=-\frac12$; it is $\lambda=-\frac12$ (the parameter of the family). It also stops at the dot-product condition and omits the final substitution into the family; the substitution is shown here and gives $y-3z+6=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Eliminate $x$ between the two plane equations; the result is a plane through the line of intersection with no $x$ term.
solution: This gives $-y+3z-6=0$, i.e. $y-3z+6=0$. It has no $x$ term, so it is parallel to the $x$-axis, and it passes through the line of intersection.

useful_results: A plane parallel to the $x$-axis has no $x$ term ($ax+by+cz+d=0$ with $a=0$); similarly for the $y$- and $z$-axes.
A plane through the line of intersection of two planes that is parallel to a coordinate axis is found by eliminating that variable between the two equations.
Plane $\parallel$ line with direction $\vec{d}$ means $\vec{n}\cdot\vec{d}=0$.

concepts: Direction cosines of a line
Angle between two lines
questions.question: The angle between the straight lines, whose direction cosines are given by the equations $2l+2m-n=0$ and $mn+nl+lm=0$, is:
questions.key_idea: Eliminate $n$ to get $2l^2+5lm+2m^2=0$, which factorises into two lines; find their direction ratios and the angle.
solution: Case II, $l=-\frac{m}{2}$: $n=2\left(\frac m2\right)=m$, direction ratios $\left(-\frac m2,m,m\right)\sim(-1,2,2)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Treat $r=l/m$ as the unknown: the two roots $r_1,r_2$ of the quadratic give the lines, and Vieta's relations give the dot product without solving.
solution: Eliminating $n$ gives $2l^2+5lm+2m^2=0$, i.e. $2r^2+5r+2=0$ with $r=\frac lm$; so $r_1+r_2=-\frac52$, $r_1r_2=1$.
For each root, a direction ratio vector is $(r,1,2(r+1))$ (since $n=2(l+m)$ and $m=1$).

useful_results: Direction cosines satisfy $l^2+m^2+n^2=1$; only their ratios matter for the angle, so use direction ratios $(l:m:n)$.
Eliminating one variable from a linear and a homogeneous quadratic condition gives a homogeneous quadratic in the other two, i.e. two lines.
Angle between lines with direction ratios $\vec{d}_1,\vec{d}_2$: $\cos\theta=\frac{|\vec{d}_1\cdot\vec{d}_2|}{|\vec{d}_1||\vec{d}_2|}$ (for the acute angle).

concepts: Family of planes through a line
questions.question: Let the equation of the plane, that passes through the point $(1,4,-3)$ and contains the line of intersection of the planes $3x-2y+4z-7=0$ and $x+5y-2z+9=0$, be $\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z+3=0$, then $\alpha+\beta+\gamma$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Family $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$ with $\lambda$ fixed by the given point, then rescale so the constant term is $3$.
solution: The given form has constant term $+3$, so multiply by $-1$: $-11x-4y-8z+3=0$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=-11-4-8=-23$ before it has found the plane (the line appears twice) and never shows the determination of $\lambda$ from the point $(1,4,-3)$. $\lambda=\frac23$ is derived above; the plane and answer $-23$ are as in the PDF.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the plane's normal $\perp$ the line's direction, and one point on the line, together with the given point.
solution: Direction of the line: $(3,-2,4)\times(1,5,-2)=(-16,10,17)$. A point on the line ($z=0$): $3x-2y=7$, $x+5y=-9$ gives $(1,-2,0)$.
The plane $\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z+3=0$ contains $(1,-2,0)$: $\alpha-2\beta+3=0$.
Its normal is perpendicular to the line direction: $-16\alpha+10\beta+17\gamma=0$.
From the first, $\alpha=2\beta-3$. The second then gives $6\beta-3\gamma=0$, so $\gamma=2\beta$.

useful_results: The pencil $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$ covers every plane through the line except $P_2$; if the target is $P_2$ itself use it directly.
If $\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z+3=0$ is fixed by the constant 3, rescale the plane found (including a sign flip) before reading $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$.
The line of intersection of $\vec{n}_1\cdot\vec{r}=p_1$, $\vec{n}_2\cdot\vec{r}=p_2$ has direction $\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2$.

concepts: Line as intersection of two planes
Distance of a point from a line
questions.question: The distance of the point $(-1,2,-2)$ from the line of intersection of the planes $2x+3y+2z=0$ and $x-2y+z=0$ is:
questions.key_idea: The direction of the line is $\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2$; the foot of the perpendicular satisfies $\overrightarrow{PR}\cdot\vec{b}=0$.
solution: The origin satisfies both plane equations, so the line passes through $(0,0,0)$: $\vec{r}=\lambda(7\hat{i}-7\hat{k})=7\lambda(\hat{i}-\hat{k})$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes the foot as $R=\left(-\frac12,0,-\frac12\right)$. With $\lambda=\frac1{14}$ and $R=(7\lambda,0,-7\lambda)$ it is $\left(\frac12,0,-\frac12\right)$. The distance $\sqrt{17/2}=\sqrt{34}/2$ and the answer (B) are unaffected (the PDF's distance uses the correct vector $\left(\frac32,-2,\frac32\right)$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Distance of a point from a line through the origin: $\dfrac{|\overrightarrow{OP}\times\vec{b}|}{|\vec{b}|}$.
solution: Direction of the line (from the cross product of normals): $\vec{b}\parallel(1,0,-1)$, and the line passes through $O$.

useful_results: Direction of the line of intersection of two planes is $\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2$; if both planes are homogeneous (constant $0$), the line passes through the origin.
Distance of $P$ from the line through $A$ with direction $\vec{b}$ is $\frac{|\overrightarrow{AP}\times\vec{b}|}{|\vec{b}|}$.
The foot $R$ of the perpendicular satisfies $\overrightarrow{PR}\cdot\vec{b}=0$; it is the point of the line closest to $P$.

concepts: Line as intersection of two planes
Distance of a point from a line
questions.question: The distance of the line $3y-2z-1=0=3x-z+4$ from the point $(2,-1,6)$ is:
questions.key_idea: Find the direction ratios and a point of the line, then use the foot of the perpendicular (or the cross-product formula).
solution: Let the direction ratios of the line be $\langle a,b,c\rangle$. It lies in both planes, so $0a+3b-2c=0$ and $3a+0b-c=0$.
A point on the line: put $x=0$; then $z=4$ from $3x-z+4=0$ and $y=3$ from $3y-2z-1=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the point-to-line formula $\dfrac{|\overrightarrow{AQ}\times\vec{d}|}{|\vec{d}|}$ with the point $A=(0,3,4)$ and direction $(1,2,3)$.
solution: Direction of the line: $(0,3,-2)\times(3,0,-1)=(-3,-6,-9)\parallel(1,2,3)$; a point on it: $A=(0,3,4)$ (check: $9-8-1=0$ and $0-4+4=0$).

useful_results: Distance of $Q$ from the line through $A$ with direction $\vec{d}$: $\frac{|\overrightarrow{AQ}\times\vec{d}|}{|\vec{d}|}$, or $\sqrt{|\overrightarrow{AQ}|^2-\left(\frac{\overrightarrow{AQ}\cdot\vec{d}}{|\vec{d}|}\right)^2}$.
For a line given as two planes, its direction is the cross product of the normals and a point is found by setting one coordinate to a convenient value.
Here $\overrightarrow{AQ}\cdot\vec{d}=2-8+6=0$, so the chosen point $A=(0,3,4)$ is already the foot of the perpendicular.

concepts: Angle bisectors of two planes
questions.question: Let the acute angle bisector of the two planes $x-2y-2z+1=0$ and $2x-3y-6z+1=0$ be the plane $P$. Then which of the following points lies on $P$?
questions.key_idea: Bisector: $\frac{L_1}{|n_1|}=\pm\frac{L_2}{|n_2|}$; $\vec n_1\cdot\vec n_2>0$ makes the minus sign the acute bisector.
solution: Here $a_1a_2+b_1b_2+c_1c_2=2+6+12=20>0$, so the negative sign gives the acute angle bisector.
The other options do not: (B) gives $-46+128+10=92$, (C) gives $39-23+16+10=42$, (D) gives $52+64+10=126$, all non-zero.
Therefore the required point is $\left(-2,0,-\frac12\right)$, option (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: Any bisector plane contains the line of intersection of the two planes, so a point lying on both planes is on $P$ whichever bisector it is.
solution: Both bisector planes of $P_1,P_2$ pass through the common line $P_1\cap P_2$, so every point with $L_1=0$ and $L_2=0$ lies on $P$, acute or obtuse.
For (A) $\left(-2,0,-\frac12\right)$: $L_1=-2-0+1+1=0$ and $L_2=-4-0+3+1=0$. So (A) lies on both planes, hence on $P$.

For (B) $(0,2,-4)$: $L_1=0-4+8+1=5
eq0$. For (C): $L_1=3-2+1+1=3
eq0$. For (D): $L_1=4+0+4+1=9
eq0$, so none lies on the common line.
Since exactly one option is correct and (A) is certain to lie on $P$, the answer is (A); no need to decide which bisector is acute.
Check of the full result: $13x-23y-32z+10$ at (A) is $-26+16+10=0$, in agreement.

useful_results: Bisector planes: $\frac{a_1x+b_1y+c_1z+d_1}{\sqrt{a_1^2+b_1^2+c_1^2}}=\pm\frac{a_2x+b_2y+c_2z+d_2}{\sqrt{a_2^2+b_2^2+c_2^2}}$. The two bisectors are perpendicular to each other and both contain the common line of the planes.

With the form $\frac{L_1}{|n_1|}=-\frac{L_2}{|n_2|}$ the normal is $\hat n_1+\hat n_2$, so this plane bisects the acute angle when $\vec n_1\cdot\vec n_2>0$ and the obtuse angle when $\vec n_1\cdot\vec n_2<0$.
Here $\cos\theta=\frac{20}{21}$ between the normals; the acute bisector makes angle $\frac{\theta}{2}$ with each plane (about $8.9^\circ$), the obtuse one about $81.1^\circ$.
Points on the common line of the two planes lie on every bisector plane, a quick way to eliminate or confirm options.

concepts: Line lying in a plane
questions.question: Suppose the line $\frac{x-2}{\alpha}=\frac{y-2}{-5}=\frac{z+2}{2}$ lies on the plane $x+3y-2z+\beta=0$. Then $(\alpha+\beta)$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Line in plane means $\vec b\cdot\vec n=0$ and the given point of the line satisfies the plane.
solution: Direction of the line: $\vec b=\alpha\hat i-5\hat j+2\hat k$. Normal of the plane: $\vec n=\hat i+3\hat j-2\hat k$.
The line lies in the plane, so $\vec b\cdot\vec n=0$.
The point $(2,2,-2)$ of the line must satisfy the plane: $2+6+4+\beta=0$.
useful_results: The line $\vec r=\vec r_0+\lambda\vec b$ lies in the plane $\vec n\cdot\vec r=d$ iff $\vec b\cdot\vec n=0$ and $\vec r_0\cdot\vec n=d$.
If $\vec b\cdot\vec n=0$ but $\vec r_0\cdot\vec n\neq d$, the line is parallel to the plane and not in it; if $\vec b\cdot\vec n\neq0$ it meets the plane at exactly one point.
Equivalent check: substitute $(2+\alpha t,\,2-5t,\,-2+2t)$ in the plane; the coefficient of $t$ gives $\alpha=19$ and the constant gives $\beta=-12$.

concepts: Intersection of a line and a plane
Distance between two points
questions.question: The square of the distance of the point of intersection of the line $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-2}{3}=\frac{z+1}{6}$ and the plane $2x-y+z=6$ from the point $(-1,-1,2)$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: A general point of the line is $(1+2\lambda,2+3\lambda,-1+6\lambda)$; substitute it in the plane to find $\lambda$.
solution: Let $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-2}{3}=\frac{z+1}{6}=\lambda$. A general point of the line is $A(1+2\lambda,\,2+3\lambda,\,-1+6\lambda)$.
So the point of intersection is $A(3,5,5)$.
useful_results: Line-plane intersection: substitute $\vec r_0+\lambda\vec b$ in $\vec n\cdot\vec r=d$; $\lambda=\frac{d-\vec n\cdot\vec r_0}{\vec n\cdot\vec b}$ (needs $\vec n\cdot\vec b\neq0$). Here $\lambda=\frac{6-(2-2-1)}{7}=1$.
Squared distance avoids the square root: $AB^2=\sum(\Delta x)^2$, which is the usual integer answer in numerical-type questions.

concepts: Image of a point in a plane
questions.question: Let $S$ be the mirror image of the point $Q(1,3,4)$ with respect to the plane $2x-y+z+3=0$ and let $R(3,5,\lambda)$ be a point of this plane. Then the square of the length of the line segment $SR$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: $R$ lies on the mirror plane, so $RS=RQ$; alternatively find $S$ by the foot of the perpendicular and midpoint.
solution: $R(3,5,\lambda)$ is on the plane: $2(3)-5+\lambda+3=0$, so $\lambda=-4$ and $R(3,5,-4)$.
The line $QS$ is perpendicular to the plane, so $\vec r=(1,3,4)+t(2,-1,1)$; its general point is $P(1+2t,\,3-t,\,4+t)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Every point of a mirror plane is equidistant from an object point and its image, so $SR=QR$ and $S$ is never needed.
solution: $R$ lies on the plane $2x-y+z+3=0$, which is the perpendicular bisector plane of $QS$.
Every point of the perpendicular bisector plane of a segment is equidistant from its ends, so $RS=RQ$.
$R(3,5,\lambda)$ on the plane gives $6-5+\lambda+3=0$, so $\lambda=-4$ and $R=(3,5,-4)$.
Hence $SR^2=RQ^2=72$, matching the direct computation with $S(-3,5,2)$.

useful_results: Image of $Q$ in the plane $\vec n\cdot\vec x+d=0$: $S=Q-\frac{2(\vec n\cdot Q+d)}{|\vec n|^2}\,\vec n$. Here $\vec n\cdot Q+d=6$ and $|\vec n|^2=6$, so $S=Q-2\vec n=(-3,5,2)$.
The mirror plane is the perpendicular bisector plane of $QS$: every point $R$ of it has $RQ=RS$, and the midpoint of $QS$ lies on it.
Distance of $Q$ from the plane is $\frac{|\vec n\cdot Q+d|}{|\vec n|}=\sqrt6$, so $QS=2\sqrt6$.

concepts: Projection of a line on a plane
Distance of a point from a line
questions.question: Let the line $L$ be the projection of the line $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-3}{1}=\frac{z-4}{2}$ in the plane $x-2y-z=3$. If $d$ is the distance of the point $(0,0,6)$ from $L$, then $d^2$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: The projection passes through the point where the line meets the plane and the foot of a perpendicular from the line.
solution: Let $P(1,3,4)$ be a point of the given line $L_1$. Its general point is $(1+2\gamma,\,3+\gamma,\,4+2\gamma)$.
$R$ = point where $L_1$ meets the plane: $1+2\gamma-2(3+\gamma)-(4+2\gamma)=3$, so $-9-2\gamma=3$ and $\gamma=-6$.
$Q$ = foot of the perpendicular from $P$ on the plane: $Q(1+\mu,\,3-2\mu,\,4-\mu)$.
It satisfies the plane: $1+\mu-2(3-2\mu)-(4-\mu)=3\Rightarrow 6\mu-9=3$, so $\mu=2$ and $Q(3,-1,2)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: $L$ is the intersection of two perpendicular planes, so $d^2$ is the sum of the squared distances of the point from those planes.
solution: The plane $\Pi_1: x-2y-z=3$ has normal $\vec n=(1,-2,-1)$; the line $L_1$ has direction $\vec d=(2,1,2)$.
The plane $\Pi_2$ through $L_1$ perpendicular to $\Pi_1$ has normal $\vec d\times\vec n=(3,4,-5)$; through $(1,3,4)$ it is $3x+4y-5z=-5$.
For a point and the line of intersection of two perpendicular planes, $d^2=d_1^2+d_2^2$ (distances to the two planes).

useful_results: Projection of a line on a plane $\Pi$: the intersection of $\Pi$ with the plane containing the line and perpendicular to $\Pi$ (normal $\vec d\times\vec n$).

Foot of perpendicular from $P$ on $\vec n\cdot\vec x=k$: $P-\frac{\vec n\cdot P-k}{|\vec n|^2}\vec n$. For $P(1,3,4)$ and $x-2y-z=3$: $\vec n\cdot P-k=-12$, so $Q=P+2\vec n=(3,-1,2)$, the same as $\mu=2$.

questions.question: Let $Q$ be the foot of the perpendicular from the point $P(7,-2,13)$ on the plane containing the lines $\frac{x+1}{6}=\frac{y-1}{7}=\frac{z-3}{8}$ and $\frac{x-1}{3}=\frac{y-2}{5}=\frac{z-3}{7}$. Then $(PQ)^2$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: The plane through two coplanar lines has normal $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$; $PQ$ is the point-plane distance.
solution: The plane contains the point $(1,2,3)$ and the directions $(6,7,8)$ and $(3,5,7)$.
$PQ$ is the perpendicular distance of $P(7,-2,13)$ from this plane: $PQ=\frac{|7+4+13|}{\sqrt{1+4+1}}=\frac{24}{\sqrt6}$.
useful_results: Plane through two coplanar lines with point $A$ and directions $\vec d_1,\vec d_2$: $(\vec r-\vec A)\cdot(\vec d_1\times\vec d_2)=0$.
Distance of $P$ from plane $\vec n\cdot\vec x=k$ is $\frac{|\vec n\cdot P-k|}{|\vec n|}$; the foot $Q$ is not needed for $(PQ)^2$.
Equivalent form: $PQ=\frac{|[\overrightarrow{AP},\vec d_1,\vec d_2]|}{|\vec d_1\times\vec d_2|}$. Here $[\ ]=-216$ and $|\vec d_1\times\vec d_2|=9\sqrt6$, giving $PQ^2=\frac{216^2}{486}=96$.

questions.key_idea: $\vec c$ is perpendicular to $\vec c\times\hat a$, so $|\hat b|^2=|\vec c|^2+4|\vec c\times\hat a|^2$ with no cross term.
solution: Let $|\vec c|=x$. Given $\hat b=\vec c+2(\vec c\times\hat a)$ and $|\hat b|=1$.
Square: $|\vec c|^2+4|\vec c\times\hat a|^2+4\,\vec c\cdot(\vec c\times\hat a)=1$.
Since $\vec c\cdot(\vec c\times\hat a)=0$ and $|\vec c\times\hat a|=x\sin15^\circ$: $x^2+4x^2\sin^2 15^\circ=1$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's first line writes $\hat b=\vec c+(\vec c\times\hat a)$ without the factor 2; the next lines (and the question) use $\hat b=\vec c+2(\vec c\times\hat a)$ and are correct. Restored the factor 2 and the intermediate $4\sin^2 15^\circ=2-\sqrt3$ step.
useful_results: For any $\vec c$ and $\hat a$: $\vec c\perp(\vec c\times\hat a)$, so $|\vec c+k(\vec c\times\hat a)|^2=|\vec c|^2+k^2|\vec c\times\hat a|^2=|\vec c|^2\left(1+k^2\sin^2\phi\right)$ for unit $\hat a$ at angle $\phi$ to $\vec c$.
Half-angle values: $\sin^2 15^\circ=\frac{2-\sqrt3}{4}$, $\cos^2 15^\circ=\frac{2+\sqrt3}{4}$.
Rationalising: $\frac{1}{3-\sqrt3}=\frac{3+\sqrt3}{6}$.
Here $|\vec c|^2=\frac{3+\sqrt3}{6}\approx0.789$; check: $0.789\left(1+4\cdot0.0670\right)=1.000$.

questions.question: Let $\hat a$ and $\hat b$ be two unit vectors such that $\left|(\hat a+\hat b)+2(\hat a\times\hat b)\right|=2$. If $\theta\in(0,\pi)$ is the angle between $\hat a$ and $\hat b$, then among the statements: (S1) $2|\hat a\times\hat b|=|\hat a-\hat b|$, (S2) the projection of $\hat a$ on $(\hat a+\hat b)$ is $\frac12$.
questions.key_idea: $\hat a+\hat b$ is perpendicular to $\hat a\times\hat b$, so the cross term vanishes and $\cos\theta=-\frac12$ follows.
solution: Square the given relation: $|\hat a+\hat b|^2+4|\hat a\times\hat b|^2+4(\hat a+\hat b)\cdot(\hat a\times\hat b)=4$.
$(\hat a+\hat b)\cdot(\hat a\times\hat b)=0$, $|\hat a+\hat b|^2=1+1+2\cos\theta$ and $|\hat a\times\hat b|^2=\sin^2\theta$, so $2+2\cos\theta+4\sin^2\theta=4$.
(S1): $2|\hat a\times\hat b|=2\sin\frac{2\pi}{3}=\sqrt3$ and $|\hat a-\hat b|=\sqrt{1+1-2\cos\theta}=\sqrt{1+1+1}=\sqrt3$. Equal, so (S1) is true.
(S2): projection of $\hat a$ on $\hat a+\hat b$ is $\frac{\hat a\cdot(\hat a+\hat b)}{|\hat a+\hat b|}=\frac{1+\cos\theta}{\sqrt{2+2\cos\theta}}$.
With $\cos\theta=-\frac12$: $|\hat a+\hat b|=\sqrt{2-1}=1$ and $\hat a\cdot(\hat a+\hat b)=1-\frac12=\frac12$, so the projection is $\frac12$. (S2) is true.
useful_results: For any vectors, $(\vec a+\vec b)\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)=0$, so $|p(\vec a+\vec b)+q(\vec a\times\vec b)|^2=p^2|\vec a+\vec b|^2+q^2|\vec a\times\vec b|^2$.

For unit vectors at angle $\theta$: $|\hat a+\hat b|=2\cos\frac\theta2$, $|\hat a-\hat b|=2\sin\frac\theta2$, $|\hat a\times\hat b|=\sin\theta$, and the projection of $\hat a$ on $\hat a+\hat b$ is $\cos\frac\theta2$.
Hence for $\theta\in(0,\pi)$ both (S1) and (S2) are equivalent to $\cos\frac\theta2=\frac12$, i.e. $\theta=\frac{2\pi}{3}$, which is exactly what the given condition forces.
The root $\cos\theta=1$ of the quadratic is rejected because $\theta\in(0,\pi)$.

questions.question: Let $\vec a=a_1\hat i+a_2\hat j+a_3\hat k$, $a_i>0$, $i=1,2,3$ be a vector which makes equal angles with the coordinate axes $OX$, $OY$ and $OZ$. Also let the projection of $\vec a$ on the vector $3\hat i+4\hat j$ be $7$. Let $\vec b$ be a vector obtained by rotating $\vec a$ with $90^\circ$. If $\vec a$, $\vec b$ and the $x$-axis are coplanar, then the projection of the vector $\vec b$ on $3\hat i+4\hat j$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $\vec b$ lies in the plane of $\vec a$ and $\hat i$, is perpendicular to $\vec a$ and has the same length as $\vec a$.
solution: Equal angles with the axes and $a_i>0$ give $\vec a=\lambda\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\hat i+\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\hat j+\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\hat k\right)=\frac{\lambda}{\sqrt3}(\hat i+\hat j+\hat k)$.
Projection on $\vec c=3\hat i+4\hat j$ is $\frac{\vec a\cdot\vec c}{|\vec c|}=7$: $\frac{\lambda}{\sqrt3}\cdot\frac{3+4}{5}=7$, so $\lambda=5\sqrt3$.
Hence $\vec a=5(\hat i+\hat j+\hat k)$ and $|\vec a|=5\sqrt3$.
$\vec b$ is coplanar with $\vec a$ and $\hat i$: $\vec b=5\alpha(\hat i+\hat j+\hat k)+\beta\hat i$.
Then $\vec b=5\alpha(\hat i+\hat j+\hat k)-15\alpha\hat i=5\alpha(-2\hat i+\hat j+\hat k)$.
Rotation preserves length: $|\vec b|=|\vec a|=5\sqrt3$, so $5|\alpha|\sqrt6=5\sqrt3$ and $\alpha=\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$.
Projection on $3\hat i+4\hat j$: $\frac{\vec b\cdot(3\hat i+4\hat j)}{5}=\pm\frac{5}{\sqrt2}\cdot\frac{-6+4}{5}=\mp\sqrt2$.
The two directions of rotation give $\pm\sqrt2$; the value that appears among the options is $\sqrt2$, option (B).
questions.correction_note: The PDF's last line shows $\pm\frac{5}{\sqrt2}\cdot\frac{-6+4}{5}=\pm\sqrt2$, but the arithmetic gives $\mp\sqrt2$ (the factor $\frac{-6+4}{5}=-\frac25$ flips the sign). The set of values $\{\sqrt2,-\sqrt2\}$ and the answer (B) are unchanged. Also noted that the question does not fix the rotation sense, so $-\sqrt2$ is equally possible; only $\sqrt2$ is among the options.

alternate_solutions.idea: $\vec b$ is along the component of $\hat i$ perpendicular to $\vec a$ (Gram-Schmidt), scaled to length $|\vec a|$.
solution: As before $\vec a=5(\hat i+\hat j+\hat k)$, $|\vec a|=5\sqrt3$.
$\vec b\perp\vec a$ and $\vec b$ is in the plane of $\vec a,\hat i$, so $\vec b$ is parallel to the component of $\hat i$ perpendicular to $\vec a$.
$\hat i-\frac{\hat i\cdot\vec a}{|\vec a|^2}\vec a=\hat i-\frac{5}{75}\cdot5(\hat i+\hat j+\hat k)=\hat i-\frac13(\hat i+\hat j+\hat k)=\frac13(2\hat i-\hat j-\hat k)$.
The vector $(2,-1,-1)$ has length $\sqrt6$, so $\vec b=\pm5\sqrt3\cdot\frac{2\hat i-\hat j-\hat k}{\sqrt6}=\pm\frac{5}{\sqrt2}(2\hat i-\hat j-\hat k)$.

useful_results: A vector making equal angles with the axes is $\lambda(\hat i+\hat j+\hat k)/\sqrt3$ (direction cosines $\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$).
A vector coplanar with $\vec a$ and $\hat i$ has the form $p\vec a+q\hat i$; imposing $\vec b\cdot\vec a=0$ fixes $q/p$ and $|\vec b|=|\vec a|$ fixes the scale.

Component of $\vec u$ perpendicular to $\vec a$: $\vec u-\frac{\vec u\cdot\vec a}{|\vec a|^2}\vec a$; rotating $\vec a$ by $90^\circ$ inside the plane of $\vec a,\vec u$ gives $\pm|\vec a|$ times its unit vector.
A rotation by $90^\circ$ in a plane has two senses, so the projection of $\vec b$ comes with both signs unless the sense is specified.

concepts: Vector triple product

questions.question: If $\vec a\cdot\vec b=1$, $\vec b\cdot\vec c=2$ and $\vec c\cdot\vec a=3$, then the value of $\left[\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c),\ \vec b\times(\vec c\times\vec a),\ \vec c\times(\vec b\times\vec a)\right]$ is:
questions.key_idea: BAC-CAB reduces each term; repeated vectors then kill most terms of the triple product.
solution: $\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c)=(\vec a\cdot\vec c)\vec b-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)\vec c=3\vec b-\vec c$.
$\vec b\times(\vec c\times\vec a)=(\vec b\cdot\vec a)\vec c-(\vec b\cdot\vec c)\vec a=\vec c-2\vec a$.
$\vec c\times(\vec b\times\vec a)=(\vec c\cdot\vec a)\vec b-(\vec c\cdot\vec b)\vec a=3\vec b-2\vec a$.
So the required value is $\left[3\vec b-\vec c,\ \vec c-2\vec a,\ 3\vec b-2\vec a\right]=(3\vec b-\vec c)\cdot\left[(\vec c-2\vec a)\times(3\vec b-2\vec a)\right]$.
$(\vec c-2\vec a)\times(3\vec b-2\vec a)=3(\vec c\times\vec b)-2(\vec c\times\vec a)-6(\vec a\times\vec b)$, since $\vec a\times\vec a=\vec 0$.

Dot with $3\vec b-\vec c$: every term having a repeated vector vanishes ($\vec b\cdot(\vec c\times\vec b)=0$, $\vec b\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)=0$, $\vec c\cdot(\vec c\times\vec b)=0$, $\vec c\cdot(\vec c\times\vec a)=0$).
Remaining: $3\vec b\cdot\left(-2\,\vec c\times\vec a\right)-\vec c\cdot\left(-6\,\vec a\times\vec b\right)=-6[\vec b\,\vec c\,\vec a]+6[\vec c\,\vec a\,\vec b]$.
By cyclic symmetry $[\vec b\,\vec c\,\vec a]=[\vec c\,\vec a\,\vec b]$, so the value is $0$: option (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: The Jacobi identity makes the three vectors linearly dependent ($\vec t_3=\vec t_1+\vec t_2$), so the triple product is $0$ without the dot products.
solution: Let $\vec t_1=\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c)$, $\vec t_2=\vec b\times(\vec c\times\vec a)$, $\vec t_3=\vec c\times(\vec b\times\vec a)$.
Jacobi identity: $\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c)+\vec b\times(\vec c\times\vec a)+\vec c\times(\vec a\times\vec b)=\vec 0$.
Since $\vec c\times(\vec b\times\vec a)=-\vec c\times(\vec a\times\vec b)$, this reads $\vec t_1+\vec t_2=\vec t_3$.
Three vectors with $\vec t_3=\vec t_1+\vec t_2$ are coplanar, so $[\vec t_1,\vec t_2,\vec t_3]=0$.
Check with the given data: $\vec t_1+\vec t_2=(3\vec b-\vec c)+(\vec c-2\vec a)=3\vec b-2\vec a=\vec t_3$. Answer (A) $0$.

useful_results: BAC-CAB rule: $\vec x\times(\vec y\times\vec z)=(\vec x\cdot\vec z)\vec y-(\vec x\cdot\vec y)\vec z$.
Jacobi identity: $\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c)+\vec b\times(\vec c\times\vec a)+\vec c\times(\vec a\times\vec b)=\vec 0$ for all vectors.
$[\vec u,\vec v,\vec w]=0$ whenever one of the vectors is a linear combination of the other two; repeated vectors in a triple product give $0$.
Cyclic symmetry: $[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c]=[\vec b\,\vec c\,\vec a]=[\vec c\,\vec a\,\vec b]$ and swapping two entries changes the sign.

questions.question: If the lines $\vec r=(\hat i-\hat j+\hat k)+\lambda(3\hat j-\hat k)$ and $\vec r=(\alpha\hat i-\hat j)+\mu(2\hat i-3\hat k)$ are coplanar, then the distance of the plane containing these two lines from the point $(\alpha,0,0)$ is:
questions.key_idea: Coplanarity of two lines gives $\alpha$ through a $3\times3$ determinant; then $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$ is the plane normal.
solution: Line 1 passes through $A(1,-1,1)$ with direction $(0,3,-1)$; line 2 passes through $B(\alpha,-1,0)$ with direction $(2,0,-3)$.
Normal of the plane: $\vec n=(0,3,-1)\times(2,0,-3)=(-9,-2,-6)$, so take $(9,2,6)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Non-parallel coplanar lines must intersect, so equate the two position vectors to get $\alpha$ and the point of intersection.
solution: The directions $(0,3,-1)$ and $(2,0,-3)$ are not parallel, so coplanar lines must meet at a point.
The $z$-component gives $1=-3\mu$, so $\mu=-\frac13$; the $x$-component gives $1=\alpha-\frac23$, so $\alpha=\frac53$.
The lines meet at $(1,-1,1)$. The plane through it has normal $(9,2,6)$ (from $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$): $9x+2y+6z=13$.
Distance of $\left(\frac53,0,0\right)$: $\frac{|\vec n\cdot(Q-A)|}{|\vec n|}$ with $Q-A=\left(\frac23,1,-1\right)$ gives $\frac{|6+2-6|}{11}=\frac{2}{11}$, option (B).

useful_results: Lines $A+\lambda\vec d_1$ and $B+\mu\vec d_2$ are coplanar iff $[\overrightarrow{AB},\vec d_1,\vec d_2]=0$; if also $\vec d_1\not\parallel\vec d_2$ they intersect.
The plane containing two such lines has normal $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$ and passes through $A$.
Distance of $Q$ from the plane $\vec n\cdot\vec x=k$ is $\frac{|\vec n\cdot Q-k|}{|\vec n|}$; with $|\vec n|=\sqrt{121}=11$ here (a clean norm signals a correct normal).
A $3\times3$ determinant with a column of zeros in two rows expands quickly along those zeros.
