questions.question: Let $\vec a=\hat i+\hat j+2\hat k$, $\vec b=2\hat i-3\hat j+\hat k$ and $\vec c=\hat i-\hat j+\hat k$ be three given vectors. Let $\vec v$ be a vector in the plane of $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ whose projection on $\vec c$ is $\frac{2}{\sqrt3}$. If $\vec v\cdot\hat j=7$, then $\vec v\cdot(\hat i+\hat k)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: A vector in the plane of $\vec a,\vec b$ is $x\vec a+y\vec b$; two conditions fix $x$ and $y$.
solution: Let $\vec v=x\vec a+y\vec b=x(\hat i+\hat j+2\hat k)+y(2\hat i-3\hat j+\hat k)=(x+2y)\hat i+(x-3y)\hat j+(2x+y)\hat k$.
Projection on $\vec c$ ($|\vec c|=\sqrt3$) is $\frac{\vec v\cdot\vec c}{|\vec c|}=\frac{2}{\sqrt3}$, so $\vec v\cdot\vec c=2$.
$\vec v=4\vec a-\vec b=(4-2)\hat i+(4+3)\hat j+(8-1)\hat k=2\hat i+7\hat j+7\hat k$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's second line reads $\frac{\vec v\cdot\vec c}{|\vec c|}=2\sqrt3$, but the question gives the projection as $\frac{2}{\sqrt3}$ (and the next line correctly uses $\vec v\cdot\vec c=2$). Corrected to $\frac{2}{\sqrt3}$ with $|\vec c|=\sqrt3$; the answer 9 is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: A vector lies in the plane of $\vec a,\vec b$ iff it is perpendicular to $\vec a\times\vec b$; use this normal instead of the parameters $x,y$.
solution: Let $\vec v=(p,7,r)$ using $\vec v\cdot\hat j=7$. In the plane of $\vec a,\vec b$: $\vec v\cdot\vec n=0$, so $7p+21-5r=0$.
$\vec v=(2,7,7)$ and $\vec v\cdot(\hat i+\hat k)=2+7=9$, option (D).

useful_results: A vector lies in the plane of $\vec a,\vec b$ iff $\vec v=x\vec a+y\vec b$ iff $\vec v\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)=0$.
Projection of $\vec v$ on $\vec c$ is the scalar $\frac{\vec v\cdot\vec c}{|\vec c|}$; the vector projection is $\frac{\vec v\cdot\vec c}{|\vec c|^2}\vec c$. Do not confuse the two.
A plane vector has 2 degrees of freedom, so two scalar conditions (projection and one component) determine it.
Here $\vec a\times\vec b=(7,3,-5)$ and $\vec v=(2,7,7)$: $14+21-35=0$ confirms $\vec v$ is in the plane.

concepts: Vector (cross) product and its perpendicularity
questions.question: Let $\vec a=\hat i+\hat j-\hat k$ and $\vec c=2\hat i-3\hat j+2\hat k$. Then the number of vectors $\vec b$ such that $\vec b\times\vec c=\vec a$ and $|\vec b|\in\{1,2,\ldots,10\}$ is:
questions.key_idea: A cross product is perpendicular to both factors, so $\vec b\times\vec c=\vec a$ requires $\vec a\cdot\vec c=0$.
solution: The equation is $\vec b\times\vec c=\vec a$, an equality of vectors (not merely parallel).
A cross product is perpendicular to each of its factors, so $\vec a=\vec b\times\vec c$ must be perpendicular to $\vec c$: we need $\vec a\cdot\vec c=0$.
$\vec a\cdot\vec c=(\hat i+\hat j-\hat k)\cdot(2\hat i-3\hat j+2\hat k)=2-3-2=-3\neq0$.
This is a contradiction, so no vector $\vec b$ satisfies $\vec b\times\vec c=\vec a$ (even $\vec b=\vec 0$ gives $\vec 0\neq\vec a$).
Hence the number of such vectors $\vec b$, with any magnitude in $\{1,\ldots,10\}$, is $0$: option (A).
questions.correction_note: The PDF says '$\vec b\times\vec c\parallel\vec a$ $\Rightarrow$ $\vec c\perp\vec a$' and ends 'no of vectors $\vec b=0$'. The condition is an equality $\vec b\times\vec c=\vec a$ (not just parallel), and the last line means the NUMBER of vectors is 0, not that $\vec b$ is the zero vector. Wording fixed; conclusion unchanged.
useful_results: $\vec b\times\vec c$ is perpendicular to both $\vec b$ and $\vec c$; so $\vec b\times\vec c=\vec a$ is solvable only if $\vec a\cdot\vec c=0$.
If $\vec a\cdot\vec c=0$ and $\vec c\neq\vec 0$, the solutions are $\vec b=\frac{\vec c\times\vec a}{|\vec c|^2}+t\vec c$, $t\in\mathbb R$ (infinitely many).
Check of that formula: $(\vec c\times\vec a)\times\vec c=\vec a|\vec c|^2-\vec c(\vec c\cdot\vec a)=\vec a|\vec c|^2$ when $\vec a\cdot\vec c=0$.
Always test the necessary perpendicularity before searching for $\vec b$ in such existence or counting questions.

concepts: Area of a parallelogram and vector product

questions.question: Let $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ be the vectors along the diagonals of a parallelogram having area $2\sqrt2$. Let the angle between $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ be acute, $|\vec a|=1$ and $|\vec a\cdot\vec b|=|\vec a\times\vec b|$. If $\vec c=2\sqrt2(\vec a\times\vec b)-2\vec b$, then an angle between $\vec b$ and $\vec c$ is:
questions.key_idea: Diagonals $\vec a,\vec b$ give area $\frac12|\vec a\times\vec b|$; $\vec b\perp\vec a\times\vec b$ gives $|\vec c|$ and $\vec b\cdot\vec c$.
solution: $|\vec a\cdot\vec b|=|\vec a\times\vec b|$ gives $\cos\theta=\sin\theta$, so $\tan\theta=1$ and $\theta=\frac\pi4$ (acute angle between $\vec a$ and $\vec b$).
The diagonals are $\vec a,\vec b$, so the area of the parallelogram is $\frac12|\vec a\times\vec b|=2\sqrt2$, hence $|\vec a\times\vec b|=4\sqrt2$.
$|\vec a||\vec b|\sin\theta=4\sqrt2$ with $|\vec a|=1$ and $\sin\theta=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$: $|\vec b|\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt2}=4\sqrt2$, so $|\vec b|=8$.
$\vec a\times\vec b\perp\vec b$, so $|\vec c|^2=8|\vec a\times\vec b|^2+4|\vec b|^2=8\cdot32+4\cdot64=256+256=512$.
$\vec b\cdot\vec c=2\sqrt2\,\vec b\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)-2\vec b\cdot\vec b=0-2|\vec b|^2=-128$.
Let $\phi$ be the angle between $\vec b$ and $\vec c$: $|\vec b||\vec c|\cos\phi=-2|\vec b|^2$, so $\cos\phi=\frac{-2\cdot8}{16\sqrt2}=-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: $\vec b$ and $\vec a\times\vec b$ are perpendicular, so use them as orthogonal axes and read off the angle of $\vec c$ from its two components.
solution: As before $\theta=\frac\pi4$, $|\vec a\times\vec b|=4\sqrt2$ and $|\vec b|=8$.
$\vec b$ and $\vec n=\vec a\times\vec b$ are perpendicular; take axes along $\hat b$ and $\hat n$.
$\vec c=2\sqrt2\,\vec n-2\vec b$ has component $-2|\vec b|=-16$ along $\hat b$ and $2\sqrt2|\vec n|=2\sqrt2\cdot4\sqrt2=16$ along $\hat n$.
So $\vec c=(-16,\,16)$ in this frame, a vector at $45^\circ$ above the negative $\hat b$ axis.
The angle between $\vec b$ (the positive axis) and $\vec c$ is $\pi-\frac\pi4=\frac{3\pi}{4}$, and $|\vec c|=16\sqrt2$ agrees. Option (D).

useful_results: If $\vec a,\vec b$ are the diagonals of a parallelogram, its area is $\frac12|\vec a\times\vec b|$ (not $|\vec a\times\vec b|$, which is the area when they are adjacent sides).
$|\vec a\cdot\vec b|=|\vec a\times\vec b|\iff|\tan\theta|=1$; acute $\theta$ gives $\theta=\frac\pi4$.
$\vec a\times\vec b$ is perpendicular to both $\vec a$ and $\vec b$, so $|p\vec b+q(\vec a\times\vec b)|^2=p^2|\vec b|^2+q^2|\vec a\times\vec b|^2$ and $\vec b\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)=0$.
Angle between $\vec b$ and $p\vec b+q\vec n$ (with $\vec n\perp\vec b$): $\tan\phi=\frac{q|\vec n|}{p|\vec b|}$; here $\frac{16}{-16}=-1$, so $\phi=\frac{3\pi}{4}$.

concepts: Plane through the line of intersection of two planes (family of planes)
questions.question: Let the plane $P:\vec{r}\cdot\vec{a}=d$ contain the line of intersection of the two planes $\vec{r}\cdot(\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-\hat{k})=6$ and $\vec{r}\cdot(-6\hat{i}+5\hat{j}-\hat{k})=7$. If the plane $P$ passes through the point $\left(2,3,\frac{1}{2}\right)$, then the value of $\frac{|13\vec{a}|^2}{d^2}$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Every plane through the line of intersection is $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$; the given point fixes $\lambda$.
solution: A plane containing their line of intersection has the form $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$, i.e. $(x+3y-z-6)+\lambda(-6x+5y-z-7)=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Take the direction of the common line and one point on it, then build the plane through the given point directly.
solution: Direction of the line of intersection: $\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2=(1,3,-1)\times(-6,5,-1)=(2,7,23)$.
A point on it: put $z=0$ in $x+3y=6$ and $-6x+5y=7$, giving $\left(\frac{9}{23},\frac{43}{23},0\right)$.
Join this point to $\left(2,3,\frac{1}{2}\right)$: vector $\left(\frac{37}{23},\frac{26}{23},\frac{1}{2}\right)$ lies in the plane.

useful_results: Planes through the line $\{P_1=0,P_2=0\}$ are exactly $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$ (with $\lambda$ possibly $\infty$ for $P_2$ itself); one extra condition fixes $\lambda$.
Keep both planes in the form $\vec{n}\cdot\vec{r}-d=0$ before forming the family so the constants are combined correctly.
The line's direction is $\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2$, and the normal of any plane containing it is perpendicular to this direction.
For $\vec{r}\cdot\vec{a}=d$, the scale of $(\vec{a},d)$ is arbitrary but $\frac{|\vec{a}|^2}{d^2}$ is scale-free, so any proportional form gives the same answer.

concepts: Cross product and area of a parallelogram
Dot product and magnitude of a vector
questions.question: Let $\vec{a}=\alpha\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b}=-2\hat{i}+\alpha\hat{j}+\hat{k}$, where $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$. If the area of the parallelogram whose adjacent sides are represented by the vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ is $\sqrt{15(\alpha^2+4)}$, then the value of $2|\vec{a}|^2+(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})|\vec{b}|^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Area $=|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|$ gives a quartic in $\alpha$ that is quadratic in $\alpha^2$; reject the negative root.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use Lagrange's identity $|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|^2=|\vec{a}|^2|\vec{b}|^2-(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})^2$ instead of expanding the determinant.
solution: Then $|\vec{a}|^2=|\vec{b}|^2=14$ and $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=-1$, so the value is $28-14=14$.

useful_results: Lagrange's identity: $|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|^2=|\vec{a}|^2|\vec{b}|^2-(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})^2$ avoids computing a determinant when only the magnitude is needed.
Area of the parallelogram on $\vec{a},\vec{b}$ is $|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|$; area of the triangle is half of it.
When the equation is in $\alpha^2$ only, factor it as a quadratic in $\alpha^2$ and discard negative values.
Here $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=-1$ for every $\alpha$ because the $\alpha$-terms cancel; look for such cancellations before solving.

concepts: Cross product, perpendicular vectors and projection of a vector
questions.question: Let $\vec{a}$ be a vector which is perpendicular to the vector $3\hat{i}+\frac{1}{2}\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$. If $\vec{a}\times(2\hat{i}+\hat{k})=2\hat{i}-13\hat{j}-4\hat{k}$, then the projection of the vector $\vec{a}$ on the vector $2\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ is:
questions.key_idea: $\vec{a}\times(2\hat{i}+\hat{k})$ yields $a_2$ and $a_1-2a_3$ at once; perpendicularity gives the last equation.
questions.correction_note: PDF wrote the perpendicularity condition with a minus sign, 3i - (1/2)j + 2k, giving 6a1 - a2 + 4a3 = 0 as equation (1); the stem has +1/2, so (1) must be 6a1 + a2 + 4a3 = 0. With the wrong sign the quoted solution a=(3,2,-5) does not satisfy (1) (gives -4). Corrected sign; a and the answer 5/3 are unchanged. PDF also skipped the substitution step.

alternate_solutions.idea: Since $\vec{a}\times\vec{w}=\vec{v}$, the part of $\vec{a}$ perpendicular to $\vec{w}$ is $\frac{\vec{w}\times\vec{v}}{|\vec{w}|^2}$; the rest is a multiple of $\vec{w}$.
solution: Let $\vec{w}=2\hat{i}+\hat{k}$ and $\vec{v}=2\hat{i}-13\hat{j}-4\hat{k}$. Note $\vec{v}\cdot\vec{w}=0$, as it must be.

useful_results: If $\vec{a}\times\vec{w}=\vec{v}$ is solvable then $\vec{v}\perp\vec{w}$; check this to detect inconsistent data, and $\vec{a}$ is determined only up to adding a multiple of $\vec{w}$.
Crossing with a coordinate-aligned vector such as $2\hat{i}+\hat{k}$ gives each component directly (no determinant of unknowns needed).
Scalar projection of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{b}$ is $\frac{\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|}$; vector projection is that times $\hat{b}$.
To clear fractions in a perpendicularity condition, scale the fixed vector, as $\left(3,\frac{1}{2},2\right)\to(6,1,4)$.

concepts: Projection of a vector and vector (cross) product
questions.question: Let $\vec{a}=\alpha\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-\hat{k}$, $\vec{b}=3\hat{i}-\beta\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ where $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}$, be three vectors. If the projection of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{c}$ is $\frac{10}{3}$ and $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}=-6\hat{i}+10\hat{j}+7\hat{k}$, then the value of $\alpha+\beta$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The projection condition involves only $\alpha$ and one component of $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$ involves only $\beta$.

alternate_solutions.idea: $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{b}$, so dotting with $\vec{b}$ gives $\beta$ without expanding a determinant.

useful_results: $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$ is perpendicular to both $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$; dotting the given cross product with $\vec{b}$ or $\vec{c}$ yields linear equations in the unknowns (and checks consistency).
Scalar projection of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{c}$: $\frac{\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}}{|\vec{c}|}$; remember to divide by $|\vec{c}|$.
Check: $(-6,10,7)\cdot(1,2,-2)=0$, confirming the given cross product is consistent with $\vec{c}$.

concepts: Collinearity of points and position vectors
Median of a triangle and midpoint formula
questions.question: Let $A,B,C$ be three points whose position vectors respectively are $\vec{a}=\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$, $\vec{b}=2\hat{i}+\alpha\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$, $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$, $\vec{c}=3\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+5\hat{k}$. If $\alpha$ is the smallest positive integer for which $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$ are non-collinear, then the length of the median, in $\triangle ABC$, through $A$ is:
questions.key_idea: Find the single value of $\alpha$ making the points collinear; the smallest positive integer other than it is $\alpha=2$.
solution: Hence the points are collinear only for $\alpha=1$; they are non-collinear for $\alpha=2$, the smallest positive integer.

alternate_solutions.idea: Apply the median-length (Apollonius) formula $AM^2=\frac{2AB^2+2AC^2-BC^2}{4}$ with $\alpha=2$.

useful_results: Points $A,B,C$ are collinear iff $\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}=\vec{0}$, i.e. the vectors are proportional (here exactly at $\alpha=1$).
Apollonius: median to side $a$ has $m_a^2=\frac{2b^2+2c^2-a^2}{4}$.
Read 'smallest positive integer for which ...' carefully: exclude the bad value ($\alpha=1$) first, then take the next integer.

concepts: Vector product identities and Lagrange's identity
questions.question: Let $\theta$ be the angle between the vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$, where $|\vec{a}|=4$, $|\vec{b}|=3$ and $\theta\in\left(\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{\pi}{3}\right)$. Then $\left|(\vec{a}-\vec{b})\times(\vec{a}+\vec{b})\right|^2+4(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})^2$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: Expanding gives $(\vec{a}-\vec{b})\times(\vec{a}+\vec{b})=2(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})$, so the $\theta$-dependence cancels.

alternate_solutions.idea: Put $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ in a coordinate plane with the given lengths and compute directly.
solution: Their cross product has only a $z$-component: $(4-3\cos\theta)(3\sin\theta)+3\sin\theta(4+3\cos\theta)=24\sin\theta$.
So the first term is $576\sin^2\theta$, and $4(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})^2=4(12\cos\theta)^2=576\cos^2\theta$.

useful_results: $(\vec{a}-\vec{b})\times(\vec{a}+\vec{b})=2(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})$ for all vectors; more generally $(\vec{a}+\vec{b})\times(\vec{a}-\vec{b})=-2(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})$.
Lagrange's identity: $|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|^2+(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})^2=|\vec{a}|^2|\vec{b}|^2$.
A restriction such as $\theta\in\left(\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{\pi}{3}\right)$ is often a distractor: if the final value is constant, $\theta$ plays no role.

concepts: Skew and intersecting lines in 3D, plane parallel to two lines
questions.question: Let the lines $L_1:\vec{r}=\lambda(\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}),\ \lambda\in\mathbb{R}$ and $L_2:\vec{r}=(\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+\hat{k})+\mu(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+5\hat{k});\ \mu\in\mathbb{R}$, intersect at the point $S$. If a plane $ax+by-z+d=0$ passes through $S$ and is parallel to both the lines $L_1$ and $L_2$, then the value of $a+b+d$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: The lines meet at $S$, so they span one plane; the required plane is that plane, with normal $\vec{d}_1\times\vec{d}_2$.
solution: $L_1$ passes through the origin with direction $(1,2,3)$; $L_2$ has direction $(1,1,5)$. They intersect at $S$, so they lie in one plane.
The plane through $S$ parallel to both lines is this common plane; it contains $(0,0,0)$ and has directions $(1,2,3)$ and $(1,1,5)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Find $S$ explicitly, take the normal $\vec{d}_1\times\vec{d}_2$, and fix $d$ by substituting $S$.
solution: Equate $\lambda(1,2,3)=(1+\mu,3+\mu,1+5\mu)$: $\lambda=1+\mu$ and $2\lambda=3+\mu$ give $\lambda=2$, $\mu=1$; the third coordinate checks ($6=6$).

useful_results: A plane parallel to two non-parallel directions $\vec{d}_1,\vec{d}_2$ has normal $\vec{d}_1\times\vec{d}_2$.
Two lines intersect iff they are coplanar and not parallel, i.e. $(\vec{a}_2-\vec{a}_1)\cdot(\vec{d}_1\times\vec{d}_2)=0$; here $(1,3,1)\cdot(7,-2,-1)=0$.
If the plane passes through the meeting point of the lines, it equals their common plane, so it passes through any point on either line.

concepts: Vector product, dot product and solving for an unknown vector
questions.question: Let $\vec{b}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\lambda\hat{k},\ \lambda\in\mathbb{R}$. If $\vec{a}$ is a vector such that $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}=13\hat{i}-\hat{j}-4\hat{k}$ and $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}+21=0$, then $(\vec{b}-\vec{a})\cdot(\hat{k}-\hat{j})+(\vec{b}+\vec{a})\cdot(\hat{i}-\hat{k})$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}\perp\vec{b}$ forces $\lambda$; then the three cross-product components and $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=-21$ give $\vec{a}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}\perp\vec{b}$ to get $\lambda$, then recover $\vec{a}$ from $\vec{b}\times(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})$ and simplify the target expression first.

useful_results: Given $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}=\vec{v}$ and $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=s$: $\vec{a}=\frac{\vec{b}\times\vec{v}+s\,\vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|^2}$ (since $\vec{b}\times(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})=|\vec{b}|^2\vec{a}-(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})\vec{b}$).
$\vec{v}=\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$ must satisfy $\vec{v}\cdot\vec{b}=0$; this pins down an unknown parameter in $\vec{b}$ immediately.
Dot products are linear: expand $(\vec{b}-\vec{a})\cdot\vec{u}+(\vec{b}+\vec{a})\cdot\vec{w}$ into $\vec{b}\cdot(\vec{u}+\vec{w})+\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{w}-\vec{u})$ to cut computation.

concepts: Coplanar vectors and scalar triple product
Dot product and perpendicular vectors
questions.question: If $\vec{a}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$, $\vec{b}=3\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c}=c_1\hat{i}+c_2\hat{j}+c_3\hat{k}$ are coplanar vectors and $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}=5$, $\vec{b}\perp\vec{c}$, then $122(c_1+c_2+c_3)$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: Coplanarity means $[\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{c}]=0$, a third linear equation to pair with $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}=5$ and $\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c}=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Coplanar with $\vec{a},\vec{b}$ and perpendicular to $\vec{b}$ means $\vec{c}$ is a multiple of the component of $\vec{a}$ perpendicular to $\vec{b}$.

useful_results: A vector coplanar with $\vec{a},\vec{b}$ and perpendicular to $\vec{b}$ is parallel to $|\vec{b}|^2\vec{a}-(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})\vec{b}=\vec{b}\times(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})$ (up to sign).
Three vectors are coplanar iff their scalar triple product is zero.
For three linear conditions on an unknown vector, use elimination to a 2x2 system; check by substituting back (here $a\cdot c=\frac{20-85+675}{122}=5$).

concepts: Plane through three points and line of intersection of two planes
questions.question: Let $P_1:\vec{r}\cdot(2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-3\hat{k})=4$ be a plane. Let $P_2$ be another plane which passes through the points $(2,-3,2)$, $(2,-2,-3)$ and $(1,-4,2)$. If the direction ratios of the line of intersection of $P_1$ and $P_2$ be $16,\alpha,\beta$, then the value of $\alpha+\beta$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: The line of intersection is perpendicular to both normals, so its direction is $\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2$.
solution: Direction of the line of intersection: $\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat{i}&\hat{j}&\hat{k}\\ 2&1&-3\\ -5&5&1\end{matrix}\right|$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Find two actual points on the common line by setting $z=0$ and $z=1$, and subtract.

useful_results: Direction of the line of intersection of two planes is $\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2$; direction ratios are defined up to a common factor.
Normal to the plane through $A,B,C$ is $\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}$; check it by substituting all three points into the resulting equation.
When one direction ratio is given (here $16$), scale the computed vector to match before reading the other two.

concepts: Scalar triple product and properties of the vector product
questions.question: Let $\vec{a}=\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$, $\vec{b}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c}$ be a vector such that $\vec{a}+(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})=\vec{0}$ and $\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c}=5$. Then the value of $3(\vec{c}\cdot\vec{a})$ is equal to ________. (*Data error in question)
questions.key_idea: Dotting $\vec{a}+\vec{b}\times\vec{c}=\vec{0}$ with $\vec{c}$ kills $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$ because $\vec{c}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})=0$.
solution: Take the dot product of both sides with $\vec{c}$: $\vec{c}\cdot\vec{a}+\vec{c}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})=0$.
$\vec{c}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})=[\vec{c}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{c}]=0$, as two rows of the triple product are equal (the vector $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{c}$).

(The printed data are inconsistent: $\vec{a}=-(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$ would be perpendicular to $\vec{b}$, but $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=2\neq0$; hence the '*Data error' note. The answer follows from the identity alone.)
questions.correction_note: PDF first line wrote a x (b x c) = 0 and then 'c.a + c.(a x c) = 0', which does not follow from the stem (the stem is a + (b x c) = 0, a sum, not a cross product). Replaced by dotting a + b x c = 0 with c and using c.(b x c) = 0. Answer 0 unchanged. Question data is inconsistent (a.b = 2, not 0).
useful_results: For any vectors, $\vec{c}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})=0$ and $\vec{b}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})=0$: a cross product is perpendicular to both factors.
If $\vec{a}=-(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$ then $\vec{a}\perp\vec{b}$ and $\vec{a}\perp\vec{c}$; always check that given data satisfy this before solving for $\vec{c}$.
A scalar triple product with a repeated vector is zero.

concepts: Shortest distance between skew lines
questions.question: If the shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-2}{3}=\frac{z-3}{\lambda}$ and $\frac{x-2}{1}=\frac{y-4}{4}=\frac{z-5}{5}$ is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$, then the sum of all possible values of $\lambda$ is:
questions.key_idea: Use $d=\frac{|\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot(\vec{p}\times\vec{q})|}{|\vec{p}\times\vec{q}|}$; squaring gives a quadratic in $\lambda$ and the sum of roots follows from Vieta.
solution: Lines pass through $A(1,2,3)$ and $B(2,4,5)$ with directions $\vec{p}=2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+\lambda\hat{k}$ and $\vec{q}=\hat{i}+4\hat{j}+5\hat{k}$; $\overrightarrow{AB}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$.
Roots $\lambda=5,11$ (both give non-parallel lines); sum of roots $=16$.
useful_results: Shortest distance between lines $\vec{r}=\vec{a}_1+s\vec{p}$ and $\vec{r}=\vec{a}_2+t\vec{q}$ is $\frac{|(\vec{a}_2-\vec{a}_1)\cdot(\vec{p}\times\vec{q})|}{|\vec{p}\times\vec{q}|}$; it is $0$ iff the lines are coplanar.
With a parameter, square both sides to get a polynomial equation and use Vieta for sum or product of roots.
Check the solutions do not make $\vec{p}\parallel\vec{q}$ (here $\vec{p}\times\vec{q}\neq\vec{0}$ at $\lambda=5,11$).

concepts: Plane (perpendicular bisector) and angle between two planes
questions.question: Let the points on the plane $P$ be equidistant from the points $(-4,2,1)$ and $(2,-2,3)$. Then the acute angle between the plane $P$ and the plane $2x+y+3z=1$ is:
questions.key_idea: The locus of points equidistant from two points is the perpendicular bisector plane, with normal along the line joining them.
solution: Let $P_0(-4,2,1)$ and $Q(2,-2,3)$; the plane $P$ is the perpendicular bisector of $P_0Q$.
Midpoint $M=(-1,0,2)$ lies on $P$, and the normal is $\overrightarrow{P_0Q}=6\hat{i}-4\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$.
Angle between the planes with normals $(6,-4,2)$ and $(2,1,3)$: $\cos\theta=\left|\frac{12-4+6}{\sqrt{36+16+4}\,\sqrt{4+1+9}}\right|$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write the locus $|X-P_0|=|X-Q|$ algebraically; squaring gives the plane directly.
solution: Expand and cancel the squares: $12x-8y+4z+4=0$, i.e. $3x-2y+z+1=0$.

useful_results: Locus of points equidistant from $A$ and $B$ is the plane through the midpoint with normal $\overrightarrow{AB}$.
Angle between planes equals the angle between normals; take $|\cos\theta|$ for the acute angle.
Squaring $|X-A|^2=|X-B|^2$ cancels the quadratic terms and gives the plane at once.

concepts: Image of a point in a plane
Line and plane intersection in 3D
questions.question: Let $Q$ be the mirror image of the point $P(1,0,1)$ with respect to the plane $S:x+y+z=5$. If a line $L$ passing through $(1,-1,-1)$, parallel to the line $PQ$ meets the plane $S$ at $R$, then $QR^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $PQ$ is along the normal $(1,1,1)$ of $S$, so $L$ is the normal line through $(1,-1,-1)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: $L$ is perpendicular to $S$, so $R$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $T(1,-1,-1)$ on $S$; no need for the equation of $L$.
solution: $PQ$ is perpendicular to $S$ (reflection), so $L\parallel PQ$ is a line along the normal; $R$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $T(1,-1,-1)$.

useful_results: Image of $(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ in $ax+by+cz+d=0$: $\frac{x-x_1}{a}=\frac{y-y_1}{b}=\frac{z-z_1}{c}=\frac{-2(ax_1+by_1+cz_1+d)}{a^2+b^2+c^2}$.
The segment joining a point and its mirror image is along the plane's normal; so any line parallel to it is perpendicular to the plane.
Foot of the perpendicular from $T$ to the plane uses the same formula with $-1$ instead of $-2$.

concepts: Family of planes through the intersection of two planes
Position of points relative to a plane
questions.question: Let $P$ be the plane passing through the intersection of the planes $\vec{r}\cdot(\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-\hat{k})=5$ and $\vec{r}\cdot(2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k})=3$ and the point $(2,1,-2)$. Let the position vectors of the points $X$ and $Y$ be $\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$ and $5\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ respectively. Then the points:
options: $X$ and $X+Y$ are on the same side of $P$
$Y$ and $Y-X$ are on the opposite side of $P$
$X$ and $Y$ are on the opposite side of $P$
$X+Y$ and $X-Y$ are on the same side of $P$
questions.answer: (C) $X$ and $Y$ are on the opposite side of $P$
questions.key_idea: A plane through the intersection of $P_1=0$ and $P_2=0$ is $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$; two points lie on opposite sides exactly when the plane's expression has opposite signs at them.
solution: Write the planes in Cartesian form: $P_1: x+3y-z-5=0$ and $P_2: 2x-y+z-3=0$.
A plane through their line of intersection is $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$, i.e. $(x+3y-z-5)+\lambda(2x-y+z-3)=0$.
It passes through $(2,1,-2)$: $P_1=2+3+2-5=2$ and $P_2=4-1-2-3=-2$, so $2-2\lambda=0$ and $\lambda=1$.
The signs differ, so $X$ and $Y$ are on opposite sides of $P$: option (C).

Check of the rest: $f(X+Y)=f(6,-3,6)=4>0$ is opposite to $f(X)<0$, so (A) fails; $f(Y-X)=f(4,1,-2)=6>0$ has the same sign as $f(Y)$, so (B) fails; $f(X-Y)=f(-4,-1,2)=-22<0$ is opposite to $f(X+Y)>0$, so (D) fails.

alternate_solutions.idea: Find where the segment $XY$ meets the plane: a parameter strictly between $0$ and $1$ means $X$ and $Y$ are on opposite sides.
solution: This vanishes at $t=\frac{9}{14}$, which lies in $(0,1)$, so the segment $XY$ crosses $P$ at an interior point.
Hence $X$ and $Y$ are on opposite sides of $P$: option (C).

useful_results: Plane through the line of $P_1=0,\ P_2=0$: $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$; one extra point fixes $\lambda$ (the $\lambda$ family misses only $P_2$ itself).
Points $A,B$ lie on opposite sides of $ax+by+cz+d=0$ iff $f(A)f(B)<0$; same side iff $f(A)f(B)>0$.
For position vectors, $f$ is affine, not linear: $f(X+Y)\ne f(X)+f(Y)$ unless $d=0$, so evaluate $f$ at the new point.
The segment $AB$ meets the plane at ratio $AM:MB=|f(A)|:|f(B)|$; here $9:5$.

concepts: Direction ratios of lines and perpendicularity
Angle between two lines in 3D
questions.question: If the two lines $l_1:\ \frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y+1}{-2},\ z=2$ and $l_2:\ \frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{2y+3}{\alpha}=\frac{z+5}{2}$ are perpendicular, then an angle between the lines $l_2$ and $l_3:\ \frac{1-x}{3}=\frac{2y-1}{-4}=\frac{z}{4}$ is:
questions.key_idea: Rewrite every line as $\frac{x-x_0}{a}=\frac{y-y_0}{b}=\frac{z-z_0}{c}$ with unit coefficient on $y$; the factor $2$ in $2y+3$ halves the $y$-direction ratio.
useful_results: Always normalise to $\frac{x-x_0}{a}=\dots$ with coefficient $1$ on each variable: $\frac{2y+3}{\alpha}=\frac{y+3/2}{\alpha/2}$ gives direction ratio $\frac{\alpha}{2}$, not $\alpha$.

Lines with direction ratios $(a_1,b_1,c_1),(a_2,b_2,c_2)$ are perpendicular iff $a_1a_2+b_1b_2+c_1c_2=0$; the angle between them satisfies $\cos\theta=\frac{|a_1a_2+b_1b_2+c_1c_2|}{\sqrt{\sum a_1^2}\sqrt{\sum a_2^2}}$.
$\cos^{-1}\frac{1}{u}=\sec^{-1}u$ for $u\ge1$; here $\cos\theta=\frac{4}{29}$ gives $\sec\theta=\frac{29}{4}$ (option (A) $\cos^{-1}\frac{29}{4}$ is not even defined).
A line given as $z=k$ has third direction ratio $0$.

concepts: Family of planes through the intersection of two planes
Image of a point in a plane
questions.question: Let the plane $2x+3y+z+20=0$ be rotated through a right angle about its line of intersection with the plane $x-3y+5z=8$. If the mirror image of the point $\left(2,-\frac{1}{2},2\right)$ in the rotated plane is $B(a,b,c)$, then:
questions.key_idea: A plane rotated through $90^\circ$ about the common line is the member of the family $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$ perpendicular to $P_1$.
solution: The rotated plane contains the line of intersection, so it is $(2x+3y+z+20)+\lambda(x-3y+5z-8)=0$.
A right-angle rotation makes it perpendicular to $2x+3y+z+20=0$: $(2+\lambda)\cdot2+(3-3\lambda)\cdot3+(1+5\lambda)\cdot1=0$, i.e. $14-2\lambda=0$, so $\lambda=7$.
Let $A=\left(2,-\frac{1}{2},2\right)$. The line $AB$ is along the normal $(1,-2,4)$: $\frac{x-2}{1}=\frac{y+\frac{1}{2}}{-2}=\frac{z-2}{4}=k$.
The midpoint of $AB$, $\left(2+\frac{k}{2},\,-\frac{1}{2}-k,\,2+2k\right)$, lies on $x-2y+4z-4=0$: $7+\frac{21k}{2}=0$, so $k=-\frac{2}{3}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The rotated plane has normal $\vec{n}_1\times(\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2)$ (perpendicular to $\vec{n}_1$ and inside the pencil); then use the image-point formula.
solution: The line of intersection has direction $\vec{d}=\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2$; the rotated plane contains $\vec{d}$ and is perpendicular to $\vec{n}_1$, so its normal is $\vec{n}_1\times\vec{d}=\vec{n}_1(\vec{n}_1\cdot\vec{n}_2)-\vec{n}_2|\vec{n}_1|^2=(-18,36,-72)\parallel(1,-2,4)$.
A point on the line: put $z=0$ in both planes: $2x+3y=-20$ and $x-3y=8$ give $(-4,-4,0)$.

useful_results: Plane through the line of $P_1=0$, $P_2=0$ and perpendicular to a given plane $P_1$: take $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$ and impose normal $\cdot\ \vec{n}_1=0$ (only the normal matters, not the constant).
Its normal is also $\vec{n}_1\times(\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2)=\vec{n}_1(\vec{n}_1\cdot\vec{n}_2)-\vec{n}_2|\vec{n}_1|^2$, the part of $\vec{n}_2$ perpendicular to $\vec{n}_1$ (reversed).
Image of $A$ in plane $\vec{n}\cdot\vec{r}=d$: $B=A-\frac{2(\vec{n}\cdot A-d)}{|\vec{n}|^2}\vec{n}$.
If the rotation angle is $\varphi$ (not $90^\circ$), use the angle formula between $P_1+\lambda P_2$ and $P_1$ instead.

concepts: Family of planes through the intersection of two planes
questions.question: If the plane $2x+y-5z=0$ is rotated about its line of intersection with the plane $3x-y+4z-7=0$ by an angle of $\frac{\pi}{2}$, then the plane after the rotation passes through the point:
questions.key_idea: The rotated plane belongs to the family $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$ and, being turned by $90^\circ$, is perpendicular to $P_1$.
solution: The rotated plane contains the line of intersection: $(2x+y-5z)+\lambda(3x-y+4z-7)=0$.
Rotation by $\frac{\pi}{2}$ makes it perpendicular to $2x+y-5z=0$; only the normals matter: $2(2+3\lambda)+1(1-\lambda)-5(-5+4\lambda)=0$.
Test $(1,0,2)$: $8-0+6-14=0$, so it lies on the plane. The others give $(2,-2,0)\to4$, $(-2,2,0)\to-32$, $(-1,0,-2)\to-28$, none zero.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's perpendicularity line was printed as $2(2+3\lambda)+1-(1-\lambda)-5(-5+4\lambda)-7\lambda=0$: it wrongly includes the constant term $-7\lambda$ (a perpendicularity test uses only the normal) and has a sign slip on the $y$-term; that expression does not simplify to the printed $30=15\lambda$. Corrected to $2(2+3\lambda)+(1-\lambda)-5(-5+4\lambda)=30-15\lambda=0$. Also the PDF prints the final plane as '8x - y + 32 - 14' (the $3z$ lost its symbol). Result $\lambda=2$ and answer unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: The new plane's normal is $\vec{n}_1\times(\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2)$; add a point of the line of intersection.
solution: A point on the line of intersection: put $z=0$: $2x+y=0$ and $3x-y=7$ give $\left(\frac{7}{5},-\frac{14}{5},0\right)$.

useful_results: Rotating plane $P_1$ about its intersection with $P_2$ keeps it in the pencil $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$; a $90^\circ$ turn needs $\vec{n}(\lambda)\cdot\vec{n}_1=0$.
Never include the constant term in a perpendicularity or angle condition: only the normals $(a,b,c)$ count.
Normal of the member perpendicular to $P_1$: $\vec{n}_1\times(\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2)\propto\vec{n}_2|\vec{n}_1|^2-\vec{n}_1(\vec{n}_1\cdot\vec{n}_2)$.
Quick sanity check for the final plane: it must contain a point of the common line, e.g. $\left(\frac{7}{5},-\frac{14}{5},0\right)$: $8\cdot\frac{7}{5}+\frac{14}{5}=14$.

concepts: Direction cosines and direction ratios of a line
questions.question: If two straight lines whose direction cosines $l,m,n$ are given by the relations $l+m-n=0$ and $3l^2+m^2+cnl=0$ are parallel, then the positive value of $c$ is:
questions.key_idea: Eliminating $m$ gives a quadratic in $\frac{l}{n}$; the two lines coincide in direction exactly when its two roots are equal.
solution: The two lines correspond to the two roots $\frac{l_1}{n_1},\frac{l_2}{n_2}$ of this quadratic.
Parallel lines have equal direction cosines up to sign, so $\frac{l_1}{n_1}=\frac{l_2}{n_2}$ (then $\frac{m}{n}=1-\frac{l}{n}$ also agrees): the roots are equal and $D=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Eliminate $n=l+m$ instead, getting a quadratic in $\frac{l}{m}$ with a simpler discriminant condition.
solution: Parallel lines need equal $t$ for both, i.e. equal roots: $c^2-4(3+c)=0$.
$c^2-4c-12=0$, so $(c-6)(c+2)=0$ and the positive value is $c=6$.

useful_results: Two lines with direction cosines given by a linear and a quadratic relation correspond to the two roots of a quadratic in a ratio such as $\frac{l}{n}$; they are perpendicular when $l_1l_2+m_1m_2+n_1n_2=0$ and parallel when the roots coincide ($D=0$).
Always eliminate the variable that leaves the simplest coefficients; any of $l,m,n$ may be removed (here $n=l+m$ gives $c^2-4c-12=0$ directly).
The sign ambiguity of direction cosines does not matter for parallelism: ratios are what must agree.
For perpendicular lines, use Vieta on the quadratic in $\frac{l}{n}$ together with $m=n-l$ to evaluate $l_1l_2+m_1m_2+n_1n_2$.

concepts: Foot of the perpendicular from a point to a line
Distance of a point from a plane
questions.question: Let the foot of the perpendicular from the point $(1,2,4)$ on the line $\frac{x+2}{4}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z+1}{3}$ be $P$. Then the distance of $P$ from the plane $3x+4y+12z+23=0$ is:
questions.key_idea: A general point of the line is $(4\lambda-2,\,2\lambda+1,\,3\lambda-1)$; perpendicularity of $\overrightarrow{AP}$ to the direction fixes $\lambda$.
solution: $\overrightarrow{AP}=(4\lambda-3,\,2\lambda-1,\,3\lambda-5)$ must be perpendicular to the direction $4\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$.
useful_results: Foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to a line with point $B$ and direction $\vec{d}$: $\lambda=\frac{(A-B)\cdot\vec{d}}{|\vec{d}|^2}$; here $\frac{29}{29}=1$.
Distance of $(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ from $ax+by+cz+d=0$ is $\frac{|ax_1+by_1+cz_1+d|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}$; $(3,4,12)$ is a Pythagorean quadruple with $|\vec{n}|=13$.
Distance from a point to a line: $|\overrightarrow{AP}|$, or $\frac{|(A-B)\times\vec{d}|}{|\vec{d}|}$.

concepts: Shortest distance between two skew lines
questions.question: The shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x-3}{2}=\frac{y-2}{3}=\frac{z-1}{-1}$ and $\frac{x+3}{2}=\frac{y-6}{1}=\frac{z-5}{3}$ is:
questions.key_idea: For skew lines the shortest distance is the projection of the join of two points on the common normal $\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2$.
solution: $\overrightarrow{AB}=(-6,4,4)$ (the PDF uses $(6,-4,-4)$, the sign is immaterial because of the modulus).

alternate_solutions.idea: Take the plane through line 1 parallel to line 2 and measure the distance of a point of line 2 from it.
solution: The plane through $A(3,2,1)$ containing direction $\vec{b}_1$ and parallel to $\vec{b}_2$ has normal $\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2=(10,-8,-4)\parallel(5,-4,-2)$.
Line 2 is parallel to this plane, so every point of it is at the same distance; take $B(-3,6,5)$: $|{-15}-24-10-5|=54$.

useful_results: Shortest distance between skew lines $\vec{r}=\vec{a}_1+t\vec{b}_1$, $\vec{r}=\vec{a}_2+s\vec{b}_2$: $\frac{|(\vec{a}_2-\vec{a}_1)\cdot(\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2)|}{|\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2|}$; it is $0$ iff the lines are coplanar.
Equivalent picture: the distance between two parallel planes, each containing one line and parallel to the other.
For parallel lines use $\frac{|(\vec{a}_2-\vec{a}_1)\times\vec{b}|}{|\vec{b}|}$ instead (the formula above gives $0/0$).
Scaling $\vec{n}=(10,-8,-4)$ to $(5,-4,-2)$ before dividing saves arithmetic.

concepts: Line of intersection of two planes and distance between points in 3D
Area of a triangle (isosceles)
questions.question: If two distinct points $Q$, $R$ lie on the line of intersection of the planes $-x+2y-z=0$ and $3x-5y+2z=0$ and $PQ=PR=\sqrt{18}$ where the point $P$ is $(1,-2,3)$, then the area of the triangle $PQR$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The line of intersection passes through the origin along $(1,1,1)$, so its points are $(k,k,k)$; the two points at distance $\sqrt{18}$ from $P$ are the two roots of a quadratic in $k$.
solution: Line of intersection: direction $(-1,2,-1)\times(3,-5,2)=(-1,-1,-1)$ and it passes through the origin, so a general point is $(k,k,k)$.
As $PQ=PR$, the foot $S$ of the perpendicular from $P$ is the midpoint of $QR$: $S=\left(\frac{2}{3},\frac{2}{3},\frac{2}{3}\right)$.
Base $QR=\sqrt{3}\cdot\frac{8}{3}$ (the $k$-values differ by $\frac{8}{3}$ and each coordinate step is $\sqrt{3}$ along the line).
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes the distance equation as $(k-2)^2+(k+2)^2+(k-3)^2=18$; the first term should be $(k-1)^2$ because $P=(1,-2,3)$ (with $(k-2)^2$ the equation would be $3k^2-6k+17=18$, not $3k^2-4k-4=0$). Corrected. Everything after it is unchanged. The PDF also states $R(k,k,k)$ and the direction $(1,1,1)$ without derivation; the derivation is added.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the perpendicular distance from $P$ to the line and Pythagoras in the isosceles triangle instead of finding $Q$ and $R$.
solution: In the isosceles triangle, $QS^2=PQ^2-PS^2=18-\frac{38}{3}=\frac{16}{3}$, so $QS=\frac{4}{\sqrt{3}}$ and $QR=\frac{8}{\sqrt{3}}$.

useful_results: Line of intersection of $\vec{n}_1\cdot\vec{r}=0$ and $\vec{n}_2\cdot\vec{r}=0$ passes through the origin with direction $\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2$.
Distance of $P$ from the line through $A$ with direction $\vec{d}$: $\frac{|\overrightarrow{AP}\times\vec{d}|}{|\vec{d}|}$.
Two points of a line at the same distance $r$ from $P$ are symmetric about the foot $S$ of the perpendicular, with $QS=\sqrt{r^2-PS^2}$.
Area of triangle $=\frac{1}{2}|\overrightarrow{PQ}\times\overrightarrow{PR}|$ also works directly: here it equals $\frac{4}{3}\sqrt{38}$.

concepts: Family of planes through the intersection of two planes
Angle between two planes
questions.question: The acute angle between the planes $P_1$ and $P_2$, when $P_1$ and $P_2$ are the planes passing through the intersection of the planes $5x+8y+13z-29=0$ and $8x-7y+z-20=0$ and the points $(2,1,3)$ and $(0,1,2)$ respectively, is:
questions.key_idea: Each required plane is a member of the pencil $(5x+8y+13z-29)+\lambda(8x-7y+z-20)=0$, with $\lambda$ fixed by its point.

alternate_solutions.idea: Find a point and the direction of the common line, then get each plane's normal as $\vec{d}\times(\text{point}-\text{line point})$.
solution: A point on it: put $z=0$: $5x+8y=29$, $8x-7y=20$ give $L_0=\left(\frac{11}{3},\frac{4}{3},0\right)$.

$P_1$ contains the line and $A=(2,1,3)$, so its normal is $\vec{d}\times(A-L_0)=(1,1,-1)\times\left(-\frac{5}{3},-\frac{1}{3},3\right)=\left(\frac{8}{3},-\frac{4}{3},\frac{4}{3}\right)\parallel(2,-1,1)$.
$P_2$ contains the line and $B=(0,1,2)$, so its normal is $\vec{d}\times(B-L_0)=\left(\frac{5}{3},\frac{5}{3},\frac{10}{3}\right)\parallel(1,1,2)$.

useful_results: Every plane through the line $P_1=0=P_2$ (except $P_2$ itself) is $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$; one extra point gives $\lambda$ by substitution.
Angle between planes $=$ angle between normals; take the acute value via $\cos\theta=\frac{|\vec{n}_1\cdot\vec{n}_2|}{|\vec{n}_1||\vec{n}_2|}$.
Plane through a line (point $L_0$, direction $\vec{d}$) and an external point $A$: normal $=\vec{d}\times\overrightarrow{L_0A}$.
Always simplify each plane to integer coefficients before comparing normals ($\frac{33}{2}(2,-1,1)$ is just $(2,-1,1)$).

concepts: Equation of a plane perpendicular to given planes
questions.question: Let the plane $ax+by+cz=d$ pass through $(2,3,-5)$ and be perpendicular to the planes $2x+y-5z=10$ and $3x+5y-7z=12$. If $a,b,c,d$ are integers, $d>0$ and $\gcd(|a|,|b|,|c|,d)=1$, then the value of $a+7b+c+20d$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: A plane perpendicular to two planes contains the directions of their normals, so its normal is the cross product of those normals.
solution: The required plane passes through $(2,3,-5)$ and is parallel to the normals $(2,1,-5)$ and $(3,5,-7)$ of the given planes.
useful_results: A plane perpendicular to two planes with normals $\vec{n}_1,\vec{n}_2$ has normal $\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2$ (it is spanned by $\vec{n}_1$ and $\vec{n}_2$).
Plane through $\vec{a}$ with normal $\vec{N}$: $\vec{N}\cdot(\vec{r}-\vec{a})=0$; fix the sign by $d>0$.

concepts: Image of a point in a plane
questions.question: If the mirror image of the point $(2,4,7)$ in the plane $3x-y+4z=2$ is $(a,b,c)$, then $2a+b+2c$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The midpoint of $PQ$ lies on the plane and $PQ$ is parallel to the normal, so $Q=P+k(3,-1,4)$ with $k$ fixed by the midpoint condition.
solution: Let $P=(2,4,7)$ and its image $Q=(a,b,c)$; the midpoint $M=\left(\frac{a+2}{2},\frac{b+4}{2},\frac{c+7}{2}\right)$ lies on the plane.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the image formula $Q=P-\frac{2(\vec{n}\cdot P-d)}{|\vec{n}|^2}\vec{n}$ and take the required combination before computing the point.

useful_results: Image of $P$ in plane $\vec{n}\cdot\vec{r}=d$: $Q=P-\frac{2(\vec{n}\cdot P-d)}{|\vec{n}|^2}\vec{n}$; the foot is $P-\frac{\vec{n}\cdot P-d}{|\vec{n}|^2}\vec{n}$.
A linear combination $\vec{w}\cdot Q$ is $\vec{w}\cdot P-\frac{2(\vec{n}\cdot P-d)}{|\vec{n}|^2}(\vec{w}\cdot\vec{n})$: no need to find $Q$ itself.
Here $\vec{w}=(2,1,2)$ and $\vec{w}\cdot\vec{n}=13=|\vec{n}|^2/2$, which is why the answer comes out clean.

concepts: Line lying in a plane
Distance of a point from a plane
questions.question: Let $\frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y+1}{-2}=\frac{z+3}{-1}$ lie on the plane $px-qy+z=5$, for some $p,q\in\mathbb{R}$. The shortest distance of the plane from the origin is:
questions.key_idea: A line lies on a plane iff every point $(3\lambda+2,\,-2\lambda-1,\,-\lambda-3)$ satisfies it for all $\lambda$, so the coefficient of $\lambda$ and the constant term must both vanish.
solution: A general point of the line is $(3\lambda+2,\,-2\lambda-1,\,-\lambda-3)$.
useful_results: A line lies in a plane iff (i) its direction is perpendicular to the plane's normal and (ii) one of its points lies on the plane; equivalently the identity in the parameter holds for all values.
For $px-qy+z=5$ the normal is $(p,-q,1)$ (note the sign of $q$); direction $(3,-2,-1)$ gives $3p+2q-1=0$ and the point $(2,-1,-3)$ gives $2p+q-3=5$.
Distance of the plane $\vec{n}\cdot\vec{r}=d$ from the origin is $\frac{|d|}{|\vec{n}|}$, here $\frac{5}{\sqrt{710}}$; simplify $\frac{5}{\sqrt{710}}=\sqrt{\frac{5}{142}}$ to match options.

concepts: Straight lines: triangle, orthocentre and centroid
questions.question: The distance of the origin from the centroid of the triangle whose two sides have the equations $x-2y+1=0$ and $2x-y-1=0$ and whose orthocenter is $\left(\frac{7}{3},\frac{7}{3}\right)$ is:
questions.key_idea: The vertices on the two given sides come from the altitudes through the orthocentre, which are perpendicular to the opposite sides.
solution: The altitude from $B$ passes through $H\left(\frac{7}{3},\frac{7}{3}\right)$ and is perpendicular to $AC$ (slope $2$), so $BH: x+2y-7=0$.
The altitude from $C$ is perpendicular to $AB$ (slope $\frac{1}{2}$): $CH: 2x+y-7=0$.
Distance of the origin from $G$: $\sqrt{(2-0)^2+(2-0)^2}=2\sqrt{2}$: option (C).
useful_results: Orthocentre $H$ lies on all three altitudes; the altitude from $B$ has slope $-\frac{1}{m_{AC}}$ and passes through $H$.
Centroid $G=\left(\frac{x_1+x_2+x_3}{3},\frac{y_1+y_2+y_3}{3}\right)$.
Euler line: $O$, $G$, $H$ are collinear with $OG:GH=1:2$; given $H$ and $G$ one gets the circumcentre $O=\frac{3G-H}{2}$ (here $\left(\frac{11}{6},\frac{11}{6}\right)$ - a useful check).
Verify: $HB\perp AC$ gives $\left(3-\frac{7}{3}\right)(1)+\left(2-\frac{7}{3}\right)(2)=\frac{2}{3}-\frac{2}{3}=0$.

concepts: Image of a point in a plane
Plane containing a line and a point
questions.question: Let $Q$ be the mirror image of the point $P(1,2,1)$ with respect to the plane $x+2y+2z=16$. Let $T$ be a plane passing through the point $Q$ and containing the line $\vec{r}=-\hat{k}+\lambda(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+2\hat{k}),\ \lambda\in\mathbb{R}$. Then, which of the following points lies on $T$?
questions.key_idea: The normal of the plane through a point $Q$ and a line is $\overrightarrow{AQ}\times\vec{d}$, with $A$ a point and $\vec{d}$ the direction of the line.
solution: The line passes through $A(0,0,-1)$ with direction $\vec{d}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$.
Test the options: $(1,2,1)$ gives $2-1-1=0$, while $(2,1,0)\to3$, $(1,2,2)\to-1$, $(1,3,2)\to-1$. Hence option (B).
questions.correction_note: The PDF's last steps are wrong as printed: it simplifies the plane $2(x-0)+0(y-0)-1(z+1)=0$ to '$2x-2=0$' (it should be $2x-z-1=0$; '$2x-2=0$' would make $z$ irrelevant and give $x=1$ for every point) and labels $Q$ as '$a=(3,8,5)$' in one line ($Q=(3,6,5)$). With the correct plane only $(1,2,1)$ lies on $T$ among the options. Answer (B) unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Test each option by coplanarity: the scalar triple product $[\overrightarrow{AQ},\vec{d},\overrightarrow{AX}]$ vanishes iff $X$ lies on $T$.
solution: For the others the determinant is non-zero: $(2,1,0)\to9$, $(1,2,2)\to-3$, $(1,3,2)\to-3$ (using $\overrightarrow{AX}=(2,1,1),(1,2,3),(1,3,3)$).

useful_results: Plane through a point $Q$ and a line (point $A$, direction $\vec{d}$): normal $\overrightarrow{AQ}\times\vec{d}$; point $X$ lies on it iff $[\overrightarrow{AQ},\vec{d},\overrightarrow{AX}]=0$.
Image of $P$ in $\vec{n}\cdot\vec{r}=d$: $P-\frac{2(\vec{n}\cdot P-d)}{|\vec{n}|^2}\vec{n}$ (here $P-\frac{2(-9)}{9}(1,2,2)=P+2(1,2,2)$).
Here $\overrightarrow{AQ}=3(1,2,2)$ is parallel to the mirror's normal, so $A$, $P$, $Q$ are collinear and $P$ lies on $T$ - which is why $(1,2,1)$ is the answer.
Always keep all three coordinates when simplifying a plane equation; dropping a term changes the plane.

concepts: Lines in 3D: direction ratios and intersection of a line with two given lines
questions.question: Let a line having direction ratios $1,-4,2$ intersect the lines $\frac{x-7}{3}=\frac{y-1}{-1}=\frac{z+2}{1}$ and $\frac{x}{2}=\frac{y-7}{3}=\frac{z}{1}$ at the points $A$ and $B$. Then $(AB)^2$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Take general points $A$, $B$ on the two lines and impose $\overrightarrow{AB}\parallel(1,-4,2)$; two proportion equations fix both parameters.
solution: Let $A$ lie on the first line and $B$ on the second: $A(3\lambda+7,\,-\lambda+1,\,\lambda-2)$ and $B(2\mu,\,3\mu+7,\,\mu)$.
First and second ratios: $-12\lambda+8\mu-28=-\lambda-3\mu-6$, which gives $\lambda-\mu+2=0$.
Second and third ratios: $-2\lambda-6\mu-12=-4\lambda+4\mu+8$, which gives $\lambda-5\mu-10=0$.
Subtracting the two equations: $-4\mu-12=0$, so $\mu=-3$ and $\lambda=-5$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The line $AB$ lies in the plane through line 1 parallel to $(1,-4,2)$; that plane meets line 2 at $B$ directly.
solution: Normal of the plane containing line 1 (direction $(3,-1,1)$) and direction $(1,-4,2)$: $(3,-1,1)\times(1,-4,2)=(2,-5,-11)$.
$AB$ lies in this plane, so $B$ is where line 2, $(2\mu,3\mu+7,\mu)$, meets it: $4\mu-5(3\mu+7)-11\mu-31=0$.
Points of the line through $B$ with ratios $1,-4,2$ are $(-6+s,-2-4s,-3+2s)$; $A$ is where it meets line 1.

useful_results: A line with given direction $\vec d$ meeting two skew lines: write $A(\lambda)$, $B(\mu)$ and impose $\overrightarrow{AB}\times\vec d=\vec 0$ (two independent equations for two unknowns).
Equivalent geometric view: the plane through one line parallel to $\vec d$ meets the other line exactly at the required point.
If $\overrightarrow{AB}=s\,\vec d$, then $AB=|s|\,|\vec d|$, so $(AB)^2=s^2|\vec d|^2$; here $s=-2$, $|\vec d|^2=21$.

concepts: Shortest distance between skew lines
questions.question: If the shortest distance between the lines $\vec r=(-\hat i+3\hat k)+\lambda(\hat i-a\hat j)$ and $\vec r=(-\hat j+2\hat k)+\mu(\hat i-\hat j+\hat k)$ is $\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}$, then the integral value of $a$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Use $d=\frac{|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)|}{|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|}$ and solve the resulting quadratic in $a$.
solution: Line 1: point $\vec a_1=(-1,0,3)$, direction $\vec b_1=(1,-a,0)$. Line 2: point $\vec a_2=(0,-1,2)$, direction $\vec b_2=(1,-1,1)$.
$\vec b_1\times\vec b_2=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\1&-a&0\\1&-1&1\end{matrix}\right|=-a\hat i-\hat j+(a-1)\hat k$.
useful_results: Shortest distance between skew lines $\vec r=\vec a_1+\lambda\vec b_1$, $\vec r=\vec a_2+\mu\vec b_2$ is $\frac{|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)|}{|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|}$.
Distance is zero (lines coplanar) exactly when the scalar triple product $[\vec a_2-\vec a_1,\vec b_1,\vec b_2]=0$.
With a parameter in the direction, expect a quadratic after squaring; read the question for the constraint (here integral value) to select the root.

concepts: Shortest distance between skew lines
Intercept form of a line in a plane
questions.question: Let $l_1$ be the line in the $xy$-plane with $x$ and $y$ intercepts $\frac18$ and $\frac{1}{4\sqrt2}$ respectively and $l_2$ be the line in the $zx$-plane with $x$ and $z$ intercepts $-\frac18$ and $-\frac{1}{6\sqrt3}$ respectively. If $d$ is the shortest distance between the lines $l_1$ and $l_2$, then $d^{-2}$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Intercept form gives each line's point and direction; both lines pass through the $x$-axis, so $\overrightarrow{AB}$ is along $\hat i$ and $d$ is its projection on $\vec p\times\vec q$.
solution: Direction of $l_1$: $\left(-\frac18,\frac{1}{4\sqrt2},0\right)\propto(\sqrt2,-2,0)$, so $\vec p=\sqrt2\hat i-2\hat j$.
Direction of $l_2$: $\left(\frac18,0,-\frac{1}{6\sqrt3}\right)\propto(3\sqrt3,0,-4)$, so $\vec q=3\sqrt3\hat i-4\hat k$.
$\overrightarrow{AB}=-\frac14\hat i$, and $\vec p\times\vec q=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\\sqrt2&-2&0\\3\sqrt3&0&-4\end{matrix}\right|=8\hat i+4\sqrt2\hat j+6\sqrt3\hat k$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF takes $\vec q=3\sqrt3\hat i+4\hat k$ for $l_2$, but the printed $z$-intercept $-\frac{1}{6\sqrt3}$ gives $\vec q=3\sqrt3\hat i-4\hat k$; its $p\times q$ line is also garbled. The sign change does not alter $d$ (only the $\hat i$-component of $p\times q$ and its magnitude matter), so the answer 51 stands.
useful_results: A line with intercepts $a$ on $x$ and $b$ on $y$ in the $xy$-plane is $\frac xa+\frac yb=1$, $z=0$; its direction is $(a,-b,0)$.
If both lines meet the same axis, the join of those points lies along that axis, which simplifies $\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot(\vec p\times\vec q)$ to one component.
Shortest distance is unaffected by reversing the sign of a direction vector, since only $|\vec p\times\vec q|$ and a dot product magnitude are used.

concepts: Image of a point in a plane
questions.question: Let the mirror image of the point $(a,b,c)$ with respect to the plane $3x-4y+12z+19=0$ be $(a-6,\beta,\gamma)$. If $a+b+c=5$, then $7\beta-9\gamma$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: The join of a point and its mirror image is parallel to the normal and its midpoint lies on the plane; this gives $\beta-b$, $\gamma-c$ and one more relation.
solution: Let $A(a,b,c)$ and $C(a-6,\beta,\gamma)$ be mirror images; $\overrightarrow{AC}=(-6,\beta-b,\gamma-c)$ is parallel to the normal $(3,-4,12)$.
The midpoint $B\left(a-3,\frac{b+\beta}{2},\frac{c+\gamma}{2}\right)$ lies on the plane.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the reflection formula: the displacement is $-2\frac{ax_1+by_1+cz_1+d}{a^2+b^2+c^2}(a,b,c)$, so one scalar $k$ determines everything.

useful_results: A point and its image differ by a multiple of the normal, so their displacements are proportional to $(a,b,c)$.
If one coordinate of the shift is given (here $-6$ in $x$), the scalar multiplier is fixed at once.

concepts: Image of a point in a line
Section formula
questions.question: Let the image of the point $P(1,2,3)$ in the line $L:\ \frac{x-6}{3}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z-2}{3}$ be $Q$. Let $R(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ be a point that divides internally the line segment $PQ$ in the ratio $1:3$. Then the value of $22(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: $R$ divides $PQ$ in $1:3$ and the foot $P'$ is the midpoint of $PQ$, so $R$ is the midpoint of $PP'$.
solution: Let $P'$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P(1,2,3)$ on $L$: $P'(3\lambda+6,\,2\lambda+1,\,3\lambda+2)$.
$P'$ is the midpoint of $PQ$. $R$ divides $PQ$ in $1:3$, so $PR=\frac14PQ=\frac12PP'$, i.e. $R$ is the midpoint of $PP'$.
useful_results: Foot of the perpendicular from $P$ on a line with direction $\vec d$: impose $\overrightarrow{PP'}\cdot\vec d=0$ on the general point $P'$.
Image $Q=2P'-P$; any point dividing $PQ$ in the ratio $1:3$ from $P$ is $\frac{3P+Q}{4}=\frac{P+P'}{2}$.
Reflection through the line preserves distances: $QP'=PP'$ and $Q,P,P'$ are collinear.

concepts: Foot of perpendicular from a point to a plane
questions.question: Let $d$ be the distance between the foot of perpendiculars of the points $P(1,2,-1)$ and $Q(2,-1,3)$ on the plane $-x+y+z=1$. Then $d^2$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Apply the foot-of-perpendicular formula to both points and take the distance between the feet.

alternate_solutions.idea: The distance between the feet is the length of $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ with its normal component removed.
solution: The feet are the projections of $P$, $Q$ on the plane, so $d$ is the length of the component of $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ parallel to the plane.
$\overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot\vec n=-1-3+4=0$, so $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ is already parallel to the plane.

useful_results: Distance between the feet of perpendiculars from $P$, $Q$ on a plane with unit normal $\hat n$: $d^2=|PQ|^2-(\overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot\hat n)^2$.
Here $\overrightarrow{PQ}\perp$ normal, so the projection leaves its length unchanged.

concepts: Vector algebra: triangle law, cross product and dot product

questions.question:
Let $ABC$ be a triangle such that $\overrightarrow{BC}=\vec{a}$, $\overrightarrow{CA}=\vec{b}$, $\overrightarrow{AB}=\vec{c}$, $|\vec{a}|=6\sqrt2$, $|\vec{b}|=2\sqrt3$ and $\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c}=12$. Consider the statements:
(S1): $|(\vec{a}	imes\vec{b})+(\vec{c}	imes\vec{b})|-|\vec{c}|=6\left(2\sqrt2-1ight)$
(S2): $\angle ACB=\cos^{-1}\left(\sqrt{ rac23}ight)$
Then:
questions.key_idea: Since $\vec a+\vec b+\vec c=\vec 0$, we get $\vec a+\vec c=-\vec b$, which makes the cross-product sum in (S1) vanish.
solution: The sides form a closed triangle: $\vec a+\vec b+\vec c=\vec 0$, so $\vec b+\vec c=-\vec a$.
Squaring: $|\vec b|^2+|\vec c|^2+2\vec b\cdot\vec c=|\vec a|^2$, i.e. $12+|\vec c|^2+24=72$, so $|\vec c|^2=36$ and $|\vec c|=6$.
(S1): $(\vec a\times\vec b)+(\vec c\times\vec b)=(\vec a+\vec c)\times\vec b=(-\vec b)\times\vec b=\vec 0$.
So the left side of (S1) is $0-|\vec c|=-6$, whereas $6(2\sqrt2-1)\approx10.97$. (S1) is false.
(S2): $\angle ACB$ is the angle between sides $CA$ and $CB$ of lengths $2\sqrt3$ and $6\sqrt2$, opposite side $AB=6$.
Cosine rule: $|\vec c|^2=|\vec a|^2+|\vec b|^2-2|\vec a||\vec b|\cos\angle ACB$, i.e. $36=72+12-2(6\sqrt2)(2\sqrt3)\cos\angle ACB$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's own working shows (S1) false (value $-6$) and gets $\cos\angle ACB=\sqrt{2/3}$, so (S2) is true, but it prints the answer (D) 'both false'. The correct option is (C) 'only (S2) is true'; the working is reproduced and the final answer fixed.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the given $\vec b\cdot\vec c=12$ to get $\vec a\cdot\vec b$, then take the angle between $\overrightarrow{CA}=\vec b$ and $\overrightarrow{CB}=-\vec a$ directly.
solution: From $\vec c=-\vec a-\vec b$: $\vec b\cdot\vec c=-\vec a\cdot\vec b-|\vec b|^2=12$, so $\vec a\cdot\vec b=-24$.
$\overrightarrow{CA}=\vec b$ and $\overrightarrow{CB}=-\vec a$, so $\cos\angle ACB=\frac{\vec b\cdot(-\vec a)}{|\vec a||\vec b|}=\frac{24}{12\sqrt6}=\frac{2}{\sqrt6}=\sqrt{\frac23}$.
(S1): $(\vec a+\vec c)\times\vec b=-\vec b\times\vec b=\vec 0$ and $|\vec c|^2=72+12-48=36$; LHS $=-6\neq6(2\sqrt2-1)$, so (S1) is false.

useful_results: For a closed triangle $\vec a+\vec b+\vec c=\vec 0$: any two of them sum to minus the third, so $\vec a\times\vec b=\vec b\times\vec c=\vec c\times\vec a$.
Angle at a vertex is the angle between the two vectors leaving it, e.g. $\angle ACB$ is between $\overrightarrow{CA}=\vec b$ and $\overrightarrow{CB}=-\vec a$, not between $\vec a$ and $\vec b$.
Cosine rule in vector form: $|\vec c|^2=|\vec a|^2+|\vec b|^2+2\vec a\cdot\vec b$ since $\vec c=-(\vec a+\vec b)$.

concepts: Vector product and scalar product
Projection of a vector
questions.question: Let $\vec{a}=\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ and let $\vec{b}$ be a vector such that $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}=2\hat{i}-\hat{k}$ and $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=3$. Then the projection of $\vec{b}$ on the vector $\vec{a}-\vec{b}$ is:
questions.key_idea: Lagrange's identity $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2+(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2$ gives $|\vec b|$ without solving for the components of $\vec b$.
solution: Use $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2+(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2$.
$|\vec a-\vec b|=\sqrt{|\vec a|^2+|\vec b|^2-2\vec a\cdot\vec b}=\sqrt{6+\frac73-6}=\sqrt{\frac73}$.
Projection of $\vec b$ on $\vec a-\vec b$ is $\frac{\vec b\cdot(\vec a-\vec b)}{|\vec a-\vec b|}=\frac{\vec a\cdot\vec b-|\vec b|^2}{|\vec a-\vec b|}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Recover $\vec b$ explicitly from $\vec b\,|\vec a|^2=(\vec a\cdot\vec b)\vec a+(\vec a\times\vec b)\times\vec a$.
solution: $(\vec a\times\vec b)\times\vec a=\vec b|\vec a|^2-\vec a(\vec a\cdot\vec b)$, so $\vec b=\frac{(\vec a\cdot\vec b)\vec a+(\vec a\times\vec b)\times\vec a}{|\vec a|^2}$.

useful_results: Lagrange's identity: $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2+(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2$.
$\vec a\times\vec b$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec b$ together determine $\vec b$ uniquely when $\vec a\ne\vec 0$: $\vec b=\frac{(\vec a\cdot\vec b)\vec a+(\vec a\times\vec b)\times\vec a}{|\vec a|^2}$.
Projection of $\vec p$ on $\vec q$ is $\frac{\vec p\cdot\vec q}{|\vec q|}$ (signed scalar).

concepts: Vector product and projection
questions.question: Let $\vec{a}=\alpha\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\alpha\hat{k}$, $\alpha>0$. If the projection of $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$ on the vector $-\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ is $30$, then $\alpha$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Projection of $\vec a\times\vec b$ on $\vec n$ is $\frac{(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot\vec n}{|\vec n|}$, a quadratic in $\alpha$; positivity picks the root.
solution: $\vec a\times\vec b=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\\alpha&1&-1\\2&1&-\alpha\end{matrix}\right|=(1-\alpha)\hat i+(\alpha^2-2)\hat j+(\alpha-2)\hat k$.
Let $\vec n=-\hat i+2\hat j-2\hat k$; $|\vec n|=3$.
useful_results: Projection (scalar component) of $\vec p$ on $\vec n$: $\frac{\vec p\cdot\vec n}{|\vec n|}$; the sign carries direction.
$(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot\vec n=[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec n]$, so the projection is a determinant divided by $|\vec n|$.
Always use stated sign conditions (here $\alpha>0$) to discard the extra quadratic root.

concepts: Planes: line of intersection of two planes
Angle between vectors
questions.question: A vector $\vec{a}$ is parallel to the line of intersection of the plane determined by the vectors $\hat{i},\hat{i}+\hat{j}$ and the plane determined by the vectors $\hat{i}-\hat{j},\hat{i}+\hat{k}$. The obtuse angle between $\vec{a}$ and the vector $\vec{b}=\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ is:
questions.key_idea: The intersection line of two planes is parallel to $\vec n_1\times\vec n_2$, and the two angles with $\vec b$ are supplementary, so pick the obtuse one.
solution: Plane 1 contains $\hat i$ and $\hat i+\hat j$: $\vec n_1=\hat i\times(\hat i+\hat j)=\hat k$.
Plane 2 contains $\hat i-\hat j$ and $\hat i+\hat k$: $\vec n_2=(\hat i+\hat k)\times(\hat i-\hat j)=\hat i+\hat j-\hat k$.
The line of intersection is along $\vec n_1\times\vec n_2=\hat k\times(\hat i+\hat j-\hat k)=\hat j-\hat i=-\hat i+\hat j$.
So $\vec a$ has direction ratios $(-1,1,0)$ (or the opposite direction).
With $\vec b=(1,-2,2)$: $\vec a\cdot\vec b=-1-2+0=-3$, $|\vec a|=\sqrt2$, $|\vec b|=3$.
Reversing $\vec a$ gives the acute angle $\frac\pi4$, so the obtuse angle is $\frac{3\pi}{4}$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes $\vec n_1=\hat i\times(\hat i+\hat j)=\hat i$ (it is $\hat k$; its next line does use $\hat k$) and writes $\vec n_2$ as $(\hat i+\hat j)\times(\hat i-\hat j)$, which is not the product of the plane's two vectors; the intended product $(\hat i+\hat k)\times(\hat i-\hat j)=\hat i+\hat j-\hat k$ matches its result. Answer (A) unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write both planes through the origin as equations; their intersection direction is read off immediately.
solution: Plane 1 through $\hat i$ and $\hat i+\hat j$ is the $xy$-plane: $z=0$.
Plane 2 through $\hat i-\hat j$ and $\hat i+\hat k$ has normal $(1,1,-1)$: $x+y-z=0$ (check: $1-1=0$ and $1-1=0$).
$\cos\theta=\frac{(1,-1,0)\cdot(1,-2,2)}{\sqrt2\cdot3}=\frac{3}{3\sqrt2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$, angle $\frac\pi4$; the opposite direction gives the obtuse angle $\frac{3\pi}{4}$.

useful_results: Two planes with normals $\vec n_1,\vec n_2$ meet in a line parallel to $\vec n_1\times\vec n_2$.
Plane through the origin containing vectors $\vec u,\vec v$ has normal $\vec u\times\vec v$ and equation $(\vec u\times\vec v)\cdot\vec r=0$.
A line direction $\vec a$ has two angles with $\vec b$, $\theta$ and $\pi-\theta$; the sign of $\vec a\cdot\vec b$ decides which one is obtuse.

concepts: Vector product and projection
questions.question: Let $\vec{a}=\alpha\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\beta\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b}=3\hat{i}-5\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$ be two vectors, such that $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}=-\hat{i}+9\hat{j}+12\hat{k}$. Then the projection of $\vec{b}-2\vec{a}$ on $\vec{b}+\vec{a}$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Equate components of $\vec a\times\vec b$ to find $\alpha,\beta$, then use $|\vec a+\vec b|$ and dot-product expansion for the projection.
solution: $\vec a\times\vec b=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\\alpha&1&\beta\\3&-5&4\end{matrix}\right|=(4+5\beta)\hat i+(3\beta-4\alpha)\hat j+(-5\alpha-3)\hat k$.
$\vec a=-3\hat i+\hat j-\hat k$; $\vec a+\vec b=-4\hat j+3\hat k$, so $|\vec a+\vec b|=5$.
$(\vec b-2\vec a)\cdot(\vec a+\vec b)=|\vec b|^2-2|\vec a|^2-\vec a\cdot\vec b=50-22+18=46$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's working line says 'projection of $(2\vec b-2\vec a)$' by a typo (it computes the projection of $\vec b-2\vec a$, as in the question) and writes $|\vec b|^2-2|\vec a|^2-\vec a\cdot\vec b$ correctly; only the notation was fixed. Answer (D) unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use that $\vec a\times\vec b$ is perpendicular to $\vec a$ to get $\beta$ from one component equation and the orthogonality $\vec a\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)=0$.
solution: The third component gives $-5\alpha-3=12$, so $\alpha=-3$ directly.
$(\vec b-2\vec a)\cdot(\vec a+\vec b)=0+28+18=46$; divide by $|\vec a+\vec b|=5$ to get $\frac{46}{5}$.

useful_results: $\vec a\times\vec b$ is perpendicular to both $\vec a$ and $\vec b$, giving two extra scalar equations: $\vec a\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)=0$ and $\vec b\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)=0$.
Here $\vec b\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)=-3-45+48=0$ confirms consistency of the given data.
Projection of $\vec p$ on $\vec q$ is $\frac{\vec p\cdot\vec q}{|\vec q|}$; expand $(\vec b-2\vec a)\cdot(\vec a+\vec b)$ using $\vec a\cdot\vec b$, $|\vec a|^2$, $|\vec b|^2$.

concepts: Vector triple product
Vector product and magnitude
questions.question: Let $\vec{a}=2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+5\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b}=\alpha\hat{i}+\beta\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$. If $\left((\vec{a}\times\vec{b})\times\hat{i}\right)\cdot\hat{k}=\frac{23}{2}$, then $\left|\vec{b}\times2\hat{j}\right|$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Expand $(\vec a\times\vec b)\times\hat i=(\vec a\cdot\hat i)\vec b-(\vec b\cdot\hat i)\vec a$; only its $\hat k$-component is needed, and it fixes $\alpha$ alone.
solution: $(\vec a\times\vec b)\times\hat i=(\vec a\cdot\hat i)\vec b-(\vec b\cdot\hat i)\vec a$.
$\vec a\cdot\hat i=2$ and $\vec b\cdot\hat i=\alpha$, so the expression is $2\vec b-\alpha\vec a$.
$\vec b\times2\hat j=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\\alpha&\beta&2\\0&2&0\end{matrix}\right|=-4\hat i+2\alpha\hat k$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Avoid the triple-product formula: compute $\vec a\times\vec b$ component-wise and use $\vec v\times\hat i=(0,v_z,-v_y)$.
solution: For any $\vec v$, $\vec v\times\hat i=(0,\,v_z,\,-v_y)$, so the $\hat k$-component of $(\vec a\times\vec b)\times\hat i$ is $-(5\alpha-4)=4-5\alpha$.

useful_results: Vector triple product: $(\vec a\times\vec b)\times\vec c=(\vec a\cdot\vec c)\vec b-(\vec b\cdot\vec c)\vec a$ and $\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c)=(\vec a\cdot\vec c)\vec b-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)\vec c$.
For a unit axis vector the triple product reduces to picking components, e.g. $\vec v\times\hat i=(0,v_z,-v_y)$.
$|\vec b\times\vec c|$ with $\vec c=2\hat j$ equals $2\sqrt{b_x^2+b_z^2}$; $\beta$ never matters.

concepts: Linear independence of vectors and scalar triple product
questions.question: Let the vectors $\vec{a}=(1+t)\hat{i}+(1-t)\hat{j}+\hat{k}$, $\vec{b}=(1-t)\hat{i}+(1+t)\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c}=t\hat{i}-t\hat{j}+\hat{k}$, $t\in\mathbb R$ be such that for $\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in\mathbb R$, $\alpha\vec{a}+\beta\vec{b}+\gamma\vec{c}=\vec{0}\Rightarrow\alpha=\beta=\gamma=0$. Then the set of all values of $t$ is:
questions.key_idea: The condition means $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ are linearly independent, i.e. the scalar triple product $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]\ne0$.
solution: $\alpha\vec a+\beta\vec b+\gamma\vec c=\vec0\Rightarrow\alpha=\beta=\gamma=0$ means $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ are linearly independent.
Three vectors are linearly independent iff $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]\ne0$.
Apply $C_2\to C_1+C_2$: the second column becomes $(2,2,0)$. Taking the factor 2 out of that column gives $2\left|\begin{matrix}1+t&1&1\\1-t&1&2\\t&0&1\end{matrix}\right|$.
The set of all such $t$ is $\mathbb R-\{0\}$: option (C).
questions.correction_note: The PDF takes the factor 2 out of $C_2$ but still prints 2 in that column, and its expansion line $2[(1+t)-(1-t)+t]$ does not match the determinant it shows (the value $6t$ is right). The expansion was rewritten correctly; the answer (C) is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Solve $\alpha\vec a+\beta\vec b+\gamma\vec c=\vec0$ component-wise; a non-zero solution exists only when $t=0$.
solution: If $t\ne0$ then $\alpha=0$, so $\alpha=\beta=\gamma=0$; if $t=0$ then $\alpha=1,\beta=-1,\gamma=1$ is a non-trivial solution (indeed $\vec b-\vec a=\vec c$).
Hence the condition holds exactly for $t\ne0$: $\mathbb R-\{0\}$.

useful_results: Vectors $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ are linearly independent (non-coplanar) iff $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]\ne0$; the condition '$\alpha\vec a+\beta\vec b+\gamma\vec c=\vec0\Rightarrow\alpha=\beta=\gamma=0$' is the definition.
Column operation $C_2\to C_1+C_2$ does not change a determinant; use it to create a zero or common factor.
Here at $t=0$: $\vec b-\vec a=\hat k=\vec c$, a direct check that dependence occurs only at $t=0$.

concepts: Scalar product and perpendicular vectors
