questions.question: Let a vector $\vec{a}$ has magnitude $9$. Let a vector $\vec{b}$ be such that for every $(x,y)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R-\{(0,0)\}$, the vector $(x\vec{a}+y\vec{b})$ is perpendicular to the vector $(6y\vec{a}-18x\vec{b})$. Then the value of $|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The dot product must vanish identically in $x,y$, so the coefficients of $xy$ and $y^2-3x^2$ vanish separately: $|\vec a|^2=3|\vec b|^2$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec b=0$.
solution: Perpendicular for all $(x,y)$: $(x\vec a+y\vec b)\cdot(6y\vec a-18x\vec b)=0$.
Expand: $6xy|\vec a|^2-18x^2(\vec a\cdot\vec b)+6y^2(\vec a\cdot\vec b)-18xy|\vec b|^2=0$.
This holds for every $x,y$, and $xy$ and $y^2-3x^2$ are independent polynomials, so $|\vec a|^2=3|\vec b|^2$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec b=0$.
$|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2=81\cdot27$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF drops the factor 6 in front of $(\vec a\cdot\vec b)(y^2-3x^2)$ and writes the last step garbled ('$\vec a\cdot|\vec a|^2/3$'); the corrected grouping $6xy(|\vec a|^2-3|\vec b|^2)+6(\vec a\cdot\vec b)(y^2-3x^2)$ gives the same conditions. Answer (B) unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Plug in two convenient pairs $(x,y)$ instead of comparing coefficients.
solution: Take $(x,y)=(1,0)$: $\vec a\cdot(-18\vec b)=0$, so $\vec a\cdot\vec b=0$.
Take $(x,y)=(1,1)$: $(\vec a+\vec b)\cdot(6\vec a-18\vec b)=6|\vec a|^2-18|\vec b|^2-12\,\vec a\cdot\vec b=0$.
With $\vec a\cdot\vec b=0$: $|\vec a|^2=3|\vec b|^2$, so $|\vec b|^2=27$.
Since $\vec a\perp\vec b$, $|\vec a\times\vec b|=|\vec a||\vec b|=9\cdot3\sqrt3=27\sqrt3$.

useful_results: If a polynomial identity holds for all $x,y$, then each coefficient (after grouping independent monomials) must vanish; or substitute special values.
$|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2$ (Lagrange); for perpendicular vectors $|\vec a\times\vec b|=|\vec a||\vec b|$.
Choosing $(x,y)=(1,0)$ or $(0,1)$ isolates pure dot products at once.

concepts: Angle between vectors and scalar product
Sign of a quadratic expression for all $t>0$
questions.question: Let $S$ be the set of all $a\in\mathbb{R}$ for which the angle between the vectors $\vec{u}=a\left(\log_e b\right)\hat{i}-6\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ and $\vec{v}=\left(\log_e b\right)\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2a\left(\log_e b\right)\hat{k}$, $(b>1)$ is acute. Then $S$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The angle is acute iff $\vec{u}\cdot\vec{v}>0$; as $\log_e b\to0^+$ the product tends to $-12$, so no $a$ works.
solution: The angle between $\vec{u}$ and $\vec{v}$ is acute exactly when $\vec{u}\cdot\vec{v}>0$.
But $y\to-12<0$ as $t\to0^+$, so $y>0$ cannot hold for every $t>0$ whatever the value of $a$.
Hence there is no such $a$, i.e. $S=\Phi$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Split on the sign of $a$: the term $at(t+6)$ cannot rescue the constant $-12$ near $t=0$.
solution: If $a\le0$, then $at(t+6)\le0$ for $t>0$, so $\vec{u}\cdot\vec{v}\le-12<0$ and the angle is never acute.
If $a>0$, then $at(t+6)$ is increasing in $t>0$ and equals $0$ at $t=0$; it is below $12$ for $0<t<t_0$, where $at_0(t_0+6)=12$.
So for $b$ with $0<\log_e b<t_0$ we get $\vec{u}\cdot\vec{v}<0$ (obtuse angle).
Thus for every real $a$ some $b>1$ gives a non-acute angle, so $S=\Phi$.

useful_results: For $\vec{p},\vec{q}\ne\vec{0}$: acute iff $\vec{p}\cdot\vec{q}>0$, obtuse iff $\vec{p}\cdot\vec{q}<0$ (and not anti-parallel).
A condition required 'for all $t>0$' is first tested at the boundary $t\to0^+$ and $t\to\infty$; a negative limit kills the condition at once.
A quadratic $at^2+bt+c$ with $c<0$ takes a negative value near $t=0$, so it is never positive on all of $t>0$.

concepts: Vector triple product
questions.question: Let $\vec{a}=3\hat{i}+\hat{j}$ and $\vec{b}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$. Let $\vec{c}$ be a vector satisfying $\vec{a}\times\left(\vec{b}\times\vec{c}\right)=\vec{b}+\lambda\vec{c}$. If $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ are non-parallel, then the value of $\lambda$ is:
questions.key_idea: Expanding $\vec{a}\times(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$ gives a combination of $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$; non-parallel vectors let us equate coefficients.
solution: Since $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ are non-parallel, both coefficients vanish: $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}=1$ and $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=-\lambda$.
useful_results: BAC-CAB: $\vec{a}\times(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})=(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c})\vec{b}-(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})\vec{c}$; the result lies in the plane of $\vec{b},\vec{c}$.
If $\vec{b},\vec{c}$ are non-parallel and $x\vec{b}+y\vec{c}=\vec{0}$ then $x=y=0$: this is how coefficients are compared.
$\vec{a}\times(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})\ne(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})\times\vec{c}$ in general; bracket position matters.

concepts: Scalar and vector product of unit vectors
Angle between two vectors
questions.question: Let $\hat{a}$ and $\hat{b}$ be two unit vectors such that the angle between them is $\frac{\pi}{4}$. If $\theta$ is the angle between the vectors $\left(\hat{a}+\hat{b}\right)$ and $\left(\hat{a}+2\hat{b}+2\left(\hat{a}\times\hat{b}\right)\right)$, then the value of $164\cos^2\theta$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $\hat{c}=\hat{a}\times\hat{b}$ is perpendicular to both $\hat{a}$ and $\hat{b}$ with $|\hat{c}|=\sin\frac{\pi}{4}$, which kills every cross term.

alternate_solutions.idea: Pick coordinates: $\hat{a}=(1,0,0)$, $\hat{b}=\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},0\right)$, so $\hat{a}\times\hat{b}=\left(0,0,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$.
solution: Denominator: $(2+\sqrt{2})(7+2\sqrt{2})=18+11\sqrt{2}$. Multiply top and bottom by $18-11\sqrt{2}$; $(18+11\sqrt{2})(18-11\sqrt{2})=324-242=82$.

useful_results: For any $\vec{a},\vec{b}$: $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}\perp\vec{a}$, $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}\perp\vec{b}$ and $|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|=|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\sin\phi$.
$\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$ form a right-handed orthogonal triad: a convenient coordinate frame is $\hat{i},\hat{j},\hat{k}$ with $\vec{a}$ along $\hat{i}$ and $\vec{b}$ in the $xy$-plane.
For unit vectors at angle $\phi$: $|\hat{a}+\hat{b}|^2=2+2\cos\phi$, $|\hat{a}-\hat{b}|^2=2-2\cos\phi$.
Rationalising $\frac{1}{p+q\sqrt{2}}$ uses $(p+q\sqrt{2})(p-q\sqrt{2})=p^2-2q^2$.

concepts: Coplanarity of four points (scalar triple product)
questions.question: If $(2,3,9)$, $(5,2,1)$, $(1,\lambda,8)$ and $(\lambda,2,3)$ are coplanar, then the product of all possible values of $\lambda$ is:
questions.key_idea: Four points are coplanar iff the scalar triple product $\left[\overrightarrow{AB}\ \overrightarrow{AC}\ \overrightarrow{AD}\right]=0$.
solution: The discriminant $57^2-4\cdot8\cdot95=209>0$, so both roots are real and the product of the values is $\lambda_1\lambda_2=\frac{95}{8}$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's expansion line ends with '=8' (3(-6lambda+17)-8(-lambda^2+5lambda-5)+(lambda+4)=8) although the equation being solved is [AB AC AD]=0; the right side must be 0 (the left side simplifies to 8lambda^2-57lambda+95). The expansion is rewritten with the right side 0. Quadratic and answer 95/8 are unchanged.

concepts: Scalar product of two cross products
Coplanar vectors and angle between them
questions.question: Let $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$ be three coplanar concurrent vectors such that angles between any two of them is same. If the product of their magnitudes is $14$ and $\left(\vec{a}\times\vec{b}\right)\cdot\left(\vec{b}\times\vec{c}\right)+\left(\vec{b}\times\vec{c}\right)\cdot\left(\vec{c}\times\vec{a}\right)+\left(\vec{c}\times\vec{a}\right)\cdot\left(\vec{a}\times\vec{b}\right)=168$, then $|\vec{a}|+|\vec{b}|+|\vec{c}|$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: For coplanar vectors with equal pairwise angles the angle is $120^\circ$, and $(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})=(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})(\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c})-(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c})(\vec{b}\cdot\vec{b})$.
solution: Let $|\vec{a}|=a$, $|\vec{b}|=b$, $|\vec{c}|=c$, so $abc=14$. Coplanar with equal pairwise angles means each angle is $\frac{2\pi}{3}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Coplanar vectors give cross products all along one normal $\hat{n}$, so each dot product is just a product of magnitudes.
solution: All vectors lie in one plane, so $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$, $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$, $\vec{c}\times\vec{a}$ are all parallel to the same unit normal $\hat{n}$ (angles measured in the same sense).
Each angle is $120^\circ$, so $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}=ab\sin120^\circ\,\hat{n}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}ab\,\hat{n}$, and likewise for the others.
Parallel and in the same direction, so $(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})=\frac{3}{4}ab\cdot bc=\frac{3}{4}ab^2c$.
The other two terms are $\frac{3}{4}abc^2$ and $\frac{3}{4}a^2bc$, so the sum is $\frac{3}{4}abc(a+b+c)$.

useful_results: Three coplanar vectors with equal pairwise angles are at $120^\circ$ to each other (and then $\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}=\vec{0}$ iff magnitudes are equal).
Lagrange/Binet-Cauchy identity: $(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})\cdot(\vec{c}\times\vec{d})=(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c})(\vec{b}\cdot\vec{d})-(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{d})(\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c})$.
Cross products of coplanar vectors are all parallel to the plane's normal, so their dot products are products of magnitudes with a sign.
Numerical check: magnitudes $3,2,\frac{7}{3}$ at $120^\circ$ give $abc=14$ and the sum $\frac{3}{4}\cdot14\cdot\frac{22}{3}=77$.

concepts: Equation of a plane containing two lines
Distance of a point from a plane
questions.question: The largest value of $a$, for which the perpendicular distance of the plane containing the lines $\vec{r}=(\hat{i}+\hat{j})+\lambda\left(\hat{i}+a\hat{j}-\hat{k}\right)$ and $\vec{r}=(\hat{i}+\hat{j})+\mu\left(-\hat{i}+\hat{j}-a\hat{k}\right)$ from the point $(2,1,4)$ is $\sqrt{3}$, is ______.
questions.key_idea: Both lines pass through $(1,1,0)$, so the plane's normal is the cross product of the two direction vectors.
solution: Both lines pass through the point $(1,1,0)$, with direction vectors $(1,a,-1)$ and $(-1,1,-a)$.
useful_results: Two lines through a common point with directions $\vec{d}_1,\vec{d}_2$ lie in the plane through that point with normal $\vec{d}_1\times\vec{d}_2$.
Distance of $(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ from $px+qy+rz+s=0$ is $\frac{|px_1+qy_1+rz_1+s|}{\sqrt{p^2+q^2+r^2}}$.
A parametric cross product that factorises, as $(1+a)(\ldots)$ here, signals the degenerate case $a=-1$ (parallel lines, no unique plane); always test it.
If the point is $Q$ and the lines meet at $M$, then $d=|\overrightarrow{MQ}\cdot\hat{n}|$.

concepts: Cross product of mutually perpendicular vectors
Magnitudes from vector product relations
questions.question: Let $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$ be three non-coplanar vectors such that $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}=4\vec{c}$, $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}=9\vec{a}$ and $\vec{c}\times\vec{a}=\alpha\vec{b}$, $\alpha>0$. If $|\vec{a}|+|\vec{b}|+|\vec{c}|=36$, then $\alpha$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: A cross product is perpendicular to both factors, so $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$ are mutually perpendicular and their magnitudes satisfy simple product relations.
solution: So $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$ are mutually perpendicular, and the magnitudes satisfy $|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|=4|\vec{c}|$, $|\vec{b}||\vec{c}|=9|\vec{a}|$, $|\vec{c}||\vec{a}|=\alpha|\vec{b}|$.
Divide the first two: $\frac{|\vec{a}|}{|\vec{c}|}=\frac{4|\vec{c}|}{9|\vec{a}|}$, so $9|\vec{a}|^2=4|\vec{c}|^2$ and $\frac{|\vec{c}|}{|\vec{a}|}=\frac{3}{2}$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF first writes the sum condition as |a|+|b|+|c| = 1/36 (a misreading of 36), gets a negative |a| = -43/18 and declares the data wrong; it then redoes it with 36. The data are fine. The wrong 1/36 attempt is removed, and the step |b| = 6 (not derived in the PDF) is derived from |b||c| = 9|a|. Final answer 36 is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Multiply the first two magnitude relations: the factors $|\vec{a}||\vec{c}|$ cancel and $|\vec{b}|=6$ falls out at once.
solution: Multiply the first two: $xy^2z=36xz$, and since $xz\ne0$, $y^2=36$, so $y=6$.

useful_results: If $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}=k\vec{c}$ with $k\ne0$, then $\vec{c}\perp\vec{a}$ and $\vec{c}\perp\vec{b}$; a cyclic set of three such relations makes $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$ mutually perpendicular.
For perpendicular vectors $|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|=|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|$, so each relation turns into a product of magnitudes.
Multiplying (or dividing) cyclic product relations such as $xy=4z$, $yz=9x$ isolates one variable ($y^2=36$ here).
Right-handed orthogonal triple: $\vec{a}=x\hat{i}$, $\vec{b}=y\hat{j}$, $\vec{c}=z\hat{k}$, which makes the data easy to check.

concepts: Scalar and vector product of two vectors (Lagrange identity)
questions.question: Let $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ be two vectors such that $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}|^2=|\vec{a}|^2+2|\vec{b}|^2$, $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=3$ and $|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|^2=75$. Then $|\vec{a}|^2$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Expand $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}|^2$ to get $|\vec{b}|^2$, then use $|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|^2=|\vec{a}|^2|\vec{b}|^2-(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})^2$.
solution: $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}|^2=|\vec{a}|^2+|\vec{b}|^2+2\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}$, and it is given to equal $|\vec{a}|^2+2|\vec{b}|^2$.
useful_results: Lagrange's identity: $|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|^2+(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})^2=|\vec{a}|^2|\vec{b}|^2$ (it is $\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$ scaled).
$|\vec{a}\pm\vec{b}|^2=|\vec{a}|^2+|\vec{b}|^2\pm2\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}$.
Given $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}$ and $|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|$, the angle satisfies $\tan\theta=\frac{|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|}{\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}}$; here $\tan\theta=\frac{5\sqrt{3}}{3}$.

concepts: Plane containing a line and perpendicular to a plane
Distance of a point from a plane
questions.question: Let $P$ be the plane containing the straight line $\frac{x-3}{9}=\frac{y+4}{-1}=\frac{z-7}{-5}$ and perpendicular to the plane containing the straight lines $\frac{x}{2}=\frac{y}{3}=\frac{z}{5}$ and $\frac{x}{3}=\frac{y}{7}=\frac{z}{8}$. If $d$ is the distance of $P$ from the point $(2,-5,11)$, then $d^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The normal of $P$ is perpendicular both to the given line's direction and to the normal of the other plane.
solution: The plane containing $\frac{x}{2}=\frac{y}{3}=\frac{z}{5}$ and $\frac{x}{3}=\frac{y}{7}=\frac{z}{8}$ has direction ratios $\langle a,b,c\rangle$ with $2a+3b+5c=0$ and $3a+7b+8c=0$.
Let the normal of $P$ be $\langle a_1,b_1,c_1\rangle$. It is perpendicular to the line direction $(9,-1,-5)$ and to $(11,1,-5)$: $9a_1-b_1-5c_1=0$ and $11a_1+b_1-5c_1=0$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's cross-multiplication for the normal of P prints denominators -5-5, -45-55, -11-9, which would give <-10,-100,-20>; the correct middle value is -45+55 = 10, giving <-10,10,-20> ~ <1,-1,2> (the PDF's stated final direction). Its distance step is printed as |2+5+22-2|/sqrt6 = 27/sqrt6 but must be |2+5+22-21|/sqrt6 = 8/sqrt6 (the plane has constant -21). The final d^2 = 32/3 is correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Distance as $|[\overrightarrow{AR},\vec{d},\vec{n}_1]|/|\vec{d}\times\vec{n}_1|$ with $A(3,-4,7)$ on the line: no plane equation needed.
solution: $\vec{n}_1=(11,1,-5)$ is the normal of the second plane; $\vec{d}=(9,-1,-5)$ is the line direction; $A=(3,-4,7)$, $R=(2,-5,11)$.

useful_results: Plane containing a line (direction $\vec{d}$) and perpendicular to a plane (normal $\vec{n}_1$): normal $=\vec{d}\times\vec{n}_1$.
Plane through two lines/points through the origin with directions $\vec{p},\vec{q}$: normal $\vec{p}\times\vec{q}$.
Distance from $R$ to the plane through $A$ with normal $\vec{N}$: $d=\frac{|\overrightarrow{AR}\cdot\vec{N}|}{|\vec{N}|}$.
Check a normal against both conditions: $(1,-1,2)\cdot(9,-1,-5)=9+1-10=0$ and $(1,-1,2)\cdot(11,1,-5)=11-1-10=0$.

concepts: Plane perpendicular to two planes
Distance of a point from a plane
questions.question: A plane $E$ is perpendicular to the two planes $2x-2y+z=0$ and $x-y+2z=4$, and passes through the point $P(1,-1,1)$. If the distance of the plane $E$ from the point $Q(a,a,2)$ is $3\sqrt{2}$, then $(PQ)^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: A plane perpendicular to two planes has normal equal to the cross product of their normals.
solution: The normals are $\vec{n}_1=(2,-2,1)$ and $\vec{n}_2=(1,-1,2)$. The plane $E$ is perpendicular to both planes, so its normal is $\vec{n}_3=\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2$.
For $a=\pm3$ (both signs give the same value): $PQ^2=18+3=21$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes the point as Q = (+-3, +-3, 2) (suggesting independent signs; the two signs must agree since Q = (a,a,2)) and writes 'Distance 7Q = sqrt21' (a typo for PQ). Rewritten with Q = (a,a,2) and PQ^2 = 2a^2 + 3 = 21 for a = +-3. Answer 21 unchanged.
useful_results: A plane perpendicular to planes with normals $\vec{n}_1,\vec{n}_2$ has normal parallel to $\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2$ (it contains both normal directions).
Distance from $(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ to $px+qy+rz+s=0$: $\frac{|px_1+qy_1+rz_1+s|}{\sqrt{p^2+q^2+r^2}}$.
When a point depends on a parameter and the distance is given, the absolute value gives two symmetric parameter values; check whether the final quantity depends on the sign (here $PQ^2$ does not).

concepts: Shortest distance between skew lines
questions.question: The shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x+7}{-6}=\frac{y-6}{7}=z$ and $\frac{7-x}{2}=y-2=z-6$ is:
questions.key_idea: Write both lines as point plus direction (the second has direction $(-2,1,1)$) and use the shortest-distance formula for skew lines.

alternate_solutions.idea: Minimise $|P_1P_2|^2$ over the two line parameters $s,t$ (calculus); at the minimum $P_1P_2$ is perpendicular to both lines.
solution: $P_1P_2=(6,4,8)$ is parallel to $\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2$ as expected, and $D_{\min}=36+16+64=116$.

useful_results: Shortest distance between $\vec{r}=\vec{a}_1+s\vec{b}_1$ and $\vec{r}=\vec{a}_2+t\vec{b}_2$ is $\frac{|(\vec{a}_2-\vec{a}_1)\cdot(\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2)|}{|\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2|}$; it is $0$ iff the lines intersect (or are parallel and coincide).
Normalise each line to $\frac{x-x_0}{l}=\frac{y-y_0}{m}=\frac{z-z_0}{n}$ with unit coefficients on $x,y,z$ before reading the direction: $\frac{7-x}{2}$ means direction component $-2$.
Scaling $\vec{b}_1\times\vec{b}_2$ by any non-zero constant does not change the ratio, so halve it to keep numbers small.
For parallel lines use $\frac{|\vec{b}\times(\vec{a}_2-\vec{a}_1)|}{|\vec{b}|}$ instead.

concepts: Direction of a line from two planes
Length of perpendicular from a point to a line
questions.question: The length of the perpendicular from the point $(1,-2,5)$ on the line passing through $(1,2,4)$ and parallel to the line $x+y-z=0=x-2y+3z-5$ is:
questions.key_idea: A line given as the intersection of two planes is parallel to the cross product of their normals.
solution: Let $Q=(1,-2,5)$ and $P=(1,2,4)$. The line $x+y-z=0=x-2y+3z-5$ is parallel to $\vec{b}=(1,1,-1)\times(1,-2,3)$.
The required line through $P(1,2,4)$ with direction $\vec{b}$: $\frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{y-2}{-4}=\frac{z-4}{-3}$.
Let the foot of the perpendicular be $N=(\lambda+1,\ -4\lambda+2,\ -3\lambda+4)$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF prints the cross product as (1,4,-3) (the correct j-component is -4, as its own line equation (y-2)/(-4) uses), writes the through-point as P(1,2,3) instead of (1,2,4) in one line, and the dot product with (1,4,-3) would not give lambda = 1/2. With b = (1,-4,-3) the condition is 26*lambda - 13 = 0, lambda = 1/2, so the final length sqrt(21/2) is correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Point-to-line distance via $\dfrac{|\overrightarrow{QP}\times\vec{b}|}{|\vec{b}|}$ - no foot needed.

useful_results: The line $\{a_1x+b_1y+c_1z+d_1=0,\ a_2x+b_2y+c_2z+d_2=0\}$ has direction $\vec{n}_1\times\vec{n}_2$.
Distance from $Q$ to the line through $P$ with direction $\vec{b}$: $\frac{|\overrightarrow{PQ}\times\vec{b}|}{|\vec{b}|}$ (Pythagoras on $|PQ|^2$ also works).
Foot of the perpendicular: $N=P+\frac{\overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot\vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|^2}\vec{b}$; here $\frac{(0,-4,1)\cdot(1,-4,-3)}{26}=\frac{13}{26}=\frac{1}{2}$.

concepts: Family of planes through the intersection of two planes
Intercepts of a plane on the axes
questions.question: If the plane $P$ passes through the intersection of two mutually perpendicular planes $2x+ky-5z=1$ and $3kx-ky+z=5$, $k<3$, and intercepts a unit length on positive $x$-axis, then the intercept made by the plane $P$ on the $y$-axis is:
questions.key_idea: A plane through the intersection of two planes is $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$; imposing the x-intercept gives $\lambda$, then read the y-intercept.
solution: The planes are perpendicular, so $2(3k)+k(-k)+(-5)(1)=0$, i.e. $k^2-6k+5=0$ and $k=1$ or $5$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Pass the plane through three explicit points: $(1,0,0)$ and two points of the line of intersection.
solution: With $k=1$ the planes are $2x+y-5z=1$ and $3x-y+z=5$. Adding: $5x-4z=6$.
Two points of the common line: $z=0$ gives $x=\frac{6}{5}$, $y=1-\frac{12}{5}=-\frac{7}{5}$; and $z=1$ gives $x=2$, $y=2$.
The x-intercept $1$ means $P$ also passes through $(1,0,0)$. So $P$ contains $A(1,0,0)$, $B\left(\frac{6}{5},-\frac{7}{5},0\right)$, $C(2,2,1)$.

useful_results: Plane through the line of intersection of $P_1=0$ and $P_2=0$: $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$.
Intercept form: $px+qy+rz=s$ has intercepts $\frac{s}{p},\frac{s}{q},\frac{s}{r}$ on the axes.
Planes $a_1x+b_1y+c_1z=d_1$ and $a_2x+b_2y+c_2z=d_2$ are perpendicular iff $a_1a_2+b_1b_2+c_1c_2=0$.

concepts: Foot of perpendicular and image of a point in a line
questions.question: If the length of the perpendicular drawn from the point $P(a,4,2)$, $a>0$ on the line $\frac{x+1}{2}=\frac{y-3}{3}=\frac{z-1}{-1}$ is $2\sqrt{6}$ units and $Q(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3)$ is the image of the point $P$ in this line, then $a+\sum_{i=1}^{3}\alpha_i$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Take the foot as a point on the line with parameter $\lambda$, use the perpendicularity and the given length, then the image is the reflection through the foot.
solution: A point on the line (the foot $M$) is $(2\lambda-1,\ 3\lambda+3,\ -\lambda+1)$, and $\overrightarrow{PM}\perp$ direction $(2,3,-1)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Point-to-line distance $\frac{|\overrightarrow{AP}\times\vec{d}|}{|\vec{d}|}=2\sqrt{6}$ gives $a$ directly, without a foot parameter.
solution: Take $A(-1,3,1)$ on the line and $\vec{d}=(2,3,-1)$, $|\vec{d}|^2=14$. Then $\overrightarrow{AP}=(a+1,1,1)$.

useful_results: Image of $P$ in a line: $Q=2M-P$ where $M$ is the foot of the perpendicular.
Foot of perpendicular from $P$ to the line through $A$ with direction $\vec{d}$: $M=A+\frac{\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\vec{d}}{|\vec{d}|^2}\vec{d}$.
Distance from $P$ to the line: $\frac{|\overrightarrow{AP}\times\vec{d}|}{|\vec{d}|}$, which avoids a parameter altogether.
A condition like $a>0$ is there to discard one root of the quadratic; always test the other root against it.

concepts: Line of intersection of two planes
Angle between a line and a plane
questions.question: If the line of intersection of the planes $ax+by=3$ and $ax+by+cz=0$, $a>0$, makes an angle $30^\circ$ with the plane $y-z+2=0$, then the direction cosines of the line are:
questions.key_idea: The line of intersection is parallel to $\vec n_1\times\vec n_2$, so its direction ratios are $(b,-a,0)$ and the angle condition reduces to $b=\pm a$.
solution: Direction of the line $=\vec n_1\times\vec n_2=(a,b,0)\times(a,b,c)=bc\,\hat{i}-ac\,\hat{j}$, i.e. direction ratios $b,\,-a,\,0$.
The normal of the plane $y-z+2=0$ has direction ratios $0,\,1,\,-1$.
The line makes $30^\circ$ with the plane, so it makes $60^\circ$ with the normal: $\cos60^\circ=\frac{|-a|}{\sqrt2\sqrt{b^2+a^2}}=\frac12$.
Remark: for $b=-a$ the ratios $(-a,-a,0)$ give $\pm\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt2},\frac{1}{\sqrt2},0\right)$, option (A), which also satisfies the data; the intended key is (B).
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes $b=\pm a$ and then lists only $\pm(1/\sqrt2,-1/\sqrt2,0)$; $b=-a$ actually gives $\pm(1/\sqrt2,1/\sqrt2,0)$ (option A) as well, so the question has two valid options. Remark added; intended key (B) kept.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write the direction as $(l,m,0)$ (it lies in $z=0$) and use only the angle condition, without finding $a,b$.
solution: Both planes contain the line, so its direction $(l,m,n)$ is perpendicular to $(a,b,0)$ and to $(a,b,c)$; hence $n=0$ (as $c\ne0$) and $l^2+m^2=1$.
The angle with the plane $y-z+2=0$ is $30^\circ$: $\sin30^\circ=\frac{|m\cdot1+0\cdot(-1)|}{\sqrt2}$, so $|m|=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$.
Then $|l|=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$ too, so the direction cosines are $\left(\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt2},\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt2},0\right)$.
The sign pattern follows from the planes: the line is perpendicular to $(a,b)$, and the choice $b=a>0$ gives $\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt2},-\frac{1}{\sqrt2},0\right)$, option (B).

useful_results: The line of intersection of $\vec n_1\cdot\vec r=d_1$ and $\vec n_2\cdot\vec r=d_2$ has direction $\vec n_1\times\vec n_2$.
Angle $\theta$ between a line (direction $\vec d$) and a plane (normal $\vec n$): $\sin\theta=\frac{|\vec d\cdot\vec n|}{|\vec d||\vec n|}$, i.e. the angle with the normal is $90^\circ-\theta$.
A plane containing the $z$-axis direction, like $ax+by+cz=0$ with the other plane $ax+by=3$, forces the common line to lie parallel to $z=0$.
Check for sign ambiguity: $|a|=|b|$ gives two directions; always test whether more than one option fits.

concepts: Foot of perpendicular from a point to a plane
Locus
questions.question: The foot of the perpendicular from a point on the circle $x^2+y^2=1$, $z=0$ to the plane $2x+3y+z=6$ lies on which one of the following curves?
questions.key_idea: Parametrise the circle point as $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta,0)$, find its foot $(h,k,w)$, and eliminate $\theta$ by solving for $\cos\theta,\sin\theta$ linearly.
solution: Let the point be $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta,0)$ and the foot $(h,k,w)$; the foot lies along the normal $(2,3,1)$: $\frac{h-\cos\theta}{2}=\frac{k-\sin\theta}{3}=\frac{w-0}{1}$.
The common ratio equals $-\frac{2\cos\theta+3\sin\theta-6}{14}$ (plane value at the point divided by $|\vec n|^2=14$).
The foot lies on the plane, so $w=6-2h-3k$; hence the locus is option (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: Test two convenient points of the circle against the options instead of eliminating $\theta$.
solution: For $(1,0,0)$: the plane value is $2-6=-4$, so the foot is $(1,0,0)+\frac{4}{14}(2,3,1)=\left(\frac{11}{7},\frac{6}{7},\frac27\right)$.
For $(0,1,0)$: the plane value is $3-6=-3$, so the foot is $(0,1,0)+\frac{3}{14}(2,3,1)=\left(\frac37,\frac{23}{14},\frac{3}{14}\right)$.
Option (B) at $\left(\frac{11}{7},\frac67\right)$: $5h+6k-12=1$ and $3h+5k-9=0$, so LHS $=1$. At $\left(\frac37,\frac{23}{14}\right)$: $5h+6k-12=0$, $3h+5k-9=\frac12$, LHS $=4\cdot\frac14=1$.
Options (A), (C), (D) give values far from $1$ at the first point, so they fail; (B) is the answer.

useful_results: Foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $\vec n\cdot\vec r=d$: $F=P-\frac{\vec n\cdot P-d}{|\vec n|^2}\vec n$.

questions.question: Let the lines $\frac{x-1}{\lambda}=\frac{y-2}{1}=\frac{z-3}{2}$ and $\frac{x+26}{-2}=\frac{y+18}{3}=\frac{z+28}{\lambda}$ be coplanar and $P$ be the plane containing these two lines. Then which of the following points does NOT lie on $P$?
questions.key_idea: Coplanarity of two lines is the vanishing of the triple product of the joining vector and the two directions; then the plane normal is the cross product of the directions.
solution: $L_1$ passes through $(1,2,3)$ with direction $(\lambda,1,2)$; $L_2$ passes through $(-26,-18,-28)$ with direction $(-2,3,\lambda)$.
Joining vector $=(27,20,31)$ (difference of the points, up to sign). Coplanarity: $\begin{vmatrix}27&20&31\\ \lambda&1&2\\ -2&3&\lambda\end{vmatrix}=0$.
Directions are now $(3,1,2)$ and $(-2,3,3)$; the normal of $P$ is $\begin{vmatrix}\hat{i}&\hat{j}&\hat{k}\\3&1&2\\-2&3&3\end{vmatrix}=-3\hat{i}-13\hat{j}+11\hat{k}$.
Test $(0,4,5)$: $52-55+4=1\ne0$, so it does not lie on $P$. The other three points give $0$.
Hence the required point is $(0,4,5)$, option (D).
useful_results: Lines through $A,B$ with directions $\vec d_1,\vec d_2$ are coplanar iff $[\overrightarrow{AB},\vec d_1,\vec d_2]=0$.
The plane containing two coplanar (non-parallel) lines has normal $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$ and passes through any point of either line.
Quick test of an option: substitute the points into the plane equation; exactly one fails in a 'does NOT lie' question.
Sign of the joining vector does not matter in the triple product (the determinant only changes sign).

questions.question: A plane $P$ is parallel to two lines whose direction ratios are $-2,1,-3$ and $-1,2,-2$ and it contains the point $(2,2,-2)$. Let $P$ intersect the coordinate axes at the points $A,B,C$ making the intercepts $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$. If $V$ is the volume of the tetrahedron $OABC$, where $O$ is the origin, and $p=\alpha+\beta+\gamma$, then the ordered pair $(V,p)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: A plane parallel to two lines has normal $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$; the volume of $OABC$ with perpendicular axes is $\frac16|\alpha\beta\gamma|$.
useful_results: Plane parallel to lines with directions $\vec d_1,\vec d_2$ through a point $P_0$: $(\vec r-P_0)\cdot(\vec d_1\times\vec d_2)=0$.
Plane $ax+by+cz=d$ ($abc\ne0$) has intercepts $\frac da,\frac db,\frac dc$ and cuts a tetrahedron of volume $\frac{|d|^3}{6|abc|}$ with the origin.
Here $\frac{12^3}{6\cdot12}=24$, matching the answer.
Intercepts may be negative; $p=\alpha+\beta+\gamma$ keeps signs while the volume uses the modulus.

questions.question: If the foot of the perpendicular from the point $A(-1,4,3)$ on the plane $P:2x+my+nz=4$ is $\left(-2,\frac72,\frac32\right)$, then the distance of the point $A$ from the plane $P$, measured parallel to a line with direction ratios $3,-1,-4$, is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $A$ and its foot $B$ lie along the normal, so $\overrightarrow{AB}\propto(2,m,n)$ fixes $m,n$; the slanted distance is $AC$ with $C$ on the plane.
solution: $AB$ is along the normal $(2,m,n)$, so $m=1$ and $n=3$; the plane is $2x+y+3z=4$ (it contains $B$: $-4+\frac72+\frac92=4$).
The line through $A$ with direction ratios $(3,-1,-4)$ is $\frac{x+1}{3}=\frac{y-4}{-1}=\frac{z-3}{-4}=\lambda$.
$C$ lies on the plane: $2(3\lambda-1)+(4-\lambda)+3(3-4\lambda)=4$, i.e. $11-7\lambda=4$, so $\lambda=1$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Slanted distance $=$ perpendicular distance divided by the cosine of the angle between the line and the normal.
solution: Angle $\phi$ between the line $(3,-1,-4)$ and the normal $(2,1,3)$: $\cos\phi=\frac{|6-1-12|}{\sqrt{26}\sqrt{14}}=\frac{7}{\sqrt{26}\sqrt{14}}$.

useful_results: Distance from $A$ to a plane measured along direction $\vec d$: $\frac{|\vec n\cdot A-p|}{|\vec n\cdot\hat d|}$ where $\hat d$ is the unit direction.
The foot of the perpendicular from $A$ lies on the line through $A$ parallel to $\vec n$, so $\overrightarrow{AB}\parallel\vec n$ gives unknown coefficients of the plane.
The slanted distance is always at least the perpendicular distance; here $\sqrt{26}>\sqrt{7/2}$. It is undefined if $\vec n\cdot\vec d=0$ (line parallel to the plane).

questions.question: Let $Q$ be the foot of perpendicular drawn from the point $P(1,2,3)$ to the plane $x+2y+z=14$. If $R$ is a point on the plane such that $\angle PRQ=60^\circ$, then the area of $\triangle PQR$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $PQ$ is perpendicular to the plane, so $PQ\perp QR$ and the triangle is right-angled at $Q$; use $\tan60^\circ=\frac{PQ}{QR}$.
solution: $PQ$ is the distance of $P$ from the plane: $PQ=\frac{|1+4+3-14|}{\sqrt{1+4+1}}=\frac{6}{\sqrt6}=\sqrt6$.
$PQ$ is perpendicular to every line of the plane through $Q$, so $\angle PQR=90^\circ$ and the angle at $R$ is $60^\circ$.
useful_results: The foot $Q$ of the perpendicular makes $\triangle PQR$ right-angled at $Q$ for every $R$ in the plane; $R$ then lies on a circle of radius $QR$ about $Q$.
For $\angle PRQ=\theta$: $QR=PQ\cot\theta$ and $PR=PQ/\sin\theta$.
Distance of $(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ from $ax+by+cz=d$: $\frac{|ax_1+by_1+cz_1-d|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}$.

questions.question: The line of shortest distance between the lines $\frac{x-2}{0}=\frac{y-1}{1}=\frac z1$ and $\frac{x-3}{2}=\frac{y-5}{2}=\frac{z-1}{1}$ makes an angle of $\cos^{-1}\left(\sqrt{\frac{2}{27}}\right)$ with the plane $P:ax-y-z=0$, $(a>0)$. If the image of the point $(1,1,-5)$ in the plane $P$ is $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$, then $\alpha+\beta-\gamma$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: The shortest-distance line is parallel to $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$; the intended condition is $\cos$ of the angle with the normal $=\sqrt{2/27}$, which gives $a$.
solution: Directions $(0,1,1)$ and $(2,2,1)$; the line of shortest distance has direction $\vec d=\begin{vmatrix}\hat{i}&\hat{j}&\hat{k}\\0&1&1\\2&2&1\end{vmatrix}=-\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$, $|\vec d|=3$.
The plane normal is $\vec n=(a,-1,-1)$; $\vec d\cdot\vec n=-a-2+2=-a$ and $|\vec n|=\sqrt{a^2+2}$.
Taken literally, $\sin\phi=\frac{a}{3\sqrt{a^2+2}}$ with $\cos\phi=\sqrt{2/27}$ gives $3a^2=25a^2+50$, which has no real solution. So the data is meant as the angle with the normal.
So $3a^2=2a^2+4$, giving $a^2=4$ and $a=2$ (as $a>0$). The plane is $2x-y-z=0$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF computes $\cos\alpha=\frac{5}{3\sqrt3}$ (wrong: the dot product is $-a$, not 5), reaches $3a^2=25a^2+50$ and writes 'No value of a', yet gives answer 3. As printed ('angle with the plane has cosine $\sqrt{2/27}$') no $a$ exists; reading the given cosine as that of the angle with the normal gives $a=2$ and the key 3. Written out the intended working.
useful_results: Direction of the common perpendicular of skew lines is $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$.
Image of $P$ in $\vec n\cdot\vec r=d$: $P'=P-\frac{2(\vec n\cdot P-d)}{|\vec n|^2}\vec n$.
Angle $\theta$ between a line and a plane: $\sin\theta=\frac{|\vec d\cdot\vec n|}{|\vec d||\vec n|}$; the angle with the normal has this as its cosine. Do not mix them up.

questions.question: Let $Q$ and $R$ be two points on the line $\frac{x+1}{2}=\frac{y+2}{3}=\frac{z-1}{2}$ at a distance $\sqrt{26}$ from the point $P(4,2,7)$. Then the square of the area of the triangle $PQR$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: Parametrise the line as $(2\lambda-1,3\lambda-2,2\lambda+1)$ and impose $PQ^2=26$; the cross product then gives the area.
solution: A general point of the line is $(2\lambda-1,\,3\lambda-2,\,2\lambda+1)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: $PQ=PR$, so the foot $F$ of the perpendicular from $P$ is the midpoint of $QR$; use Pythagoras for $QR$.
solution: $PQ=PR=\sqrt{26}$, so $F$ (foot of the perpendicular from $P$) is the midpoint of $QR$, and $F$ corresponds to $\lambda=2$ (average of the two roots), $F=(3,4,5)$.

useful_results: If two points of a line are equidistant from $P$, the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ is their midpoint.
Area of $\triangle PQR=\frac12|\overrightarrow{PQ}\times\overrightarrow{PR}|$; for numerical answers ask for the square to avoid surds.
Points on $\frac{x-x_0}{l}=\frac{y-y_0}{m}=\frac{z-z_0}{n}$ at distance $r$ from the point $P$ on it: $\lambda=\pm\frac{r}{\sqrt{l^2+m^2+n^2}}$ in the ratio parameter.
Check: $\lambda^2-4\lambda+3=0$ has roots summing to $4$, so the midpoint is at $\lambda=2$.

questions.key_idea: Since $L$ lies in $3x-8y+7z=4$, its direction $\vec n_1\times\vec n_2$ is perpendicular to $(3,-8,7)$; this fixes $\ell$.
solution: $L$ lies in the plane $3x-8y+7z=4$, so its direction is perpendicular to $(3,-8,7)$: $3(6\ell-5)-8(3-2\ell)+7(2\ell+1)=0$.

A point of the given line is $(7t+3,\,-t+2,\,-4t+3)$; on the plane: $7t+3-2t+4-12t+9-2=0$, so $-7t+14=0$ and $t=2$.

Normal of the required plane $=(1,-2,1)\times(13,7,-9)=(11,22,33)\propto(1,2,3)$; through $(4,-1,0)$: $x+2y+3z=2$.

questions.question: Let $P(-2,-1,1)$ and $Q\left(\frac{56}{17},\frac{43}{17},\frac{111}{17}\right)$ be the vertices of the rhombus $PRQS$. If the direction ratios of the diagonal $RS$ are $\alpha,-1,\beta$, where both $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are integers of minimum absolute values, then $\alpha^2+\beta^2$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: The diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular, so $(\alpha,-1,\beta)\cdot\overrightarrow{PQ}=0$, a linear equation solved in integers of least size.
solution: $PQ$ and $RS$ are the diagonals of the rhombus, so $RS\perp PQ$.
The smallest $|\alpha|$ occurs for $3\alpha-2=-47$, i.e. $\alpha=-15$, giving $\beta=15$ (the next solution is $\alpha=32,\beta=-30$, which is larger).

The sum of squares $450$ is unaffected. The PDF's garbled line $\beta=\frac{3\alpha-2}{47}$ was written out as the divisibility condition.

General integer solution of $pX+qY=r$ with $\gcd(p,q)=1$: $X=X_0+qt,\ Y=Y_0-pt$; successive solutions are $q$ apart in $X$.

questions.question: Let a line with direction ratios $a,-4a,-7$ be perpendicular to the lines with direction ratios $3,-1,2b$ and $b,a,-2$. If the point of intersection of the line $\frac{x+1}{a^2+b^2}=\frac{y-2}{a^2-b^2}=\frac z1$ and the plane $x-y+z=0$ is $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$, then $\alpha+\beta+\gamma$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Perpendicularity means zero dot products; the two equations in $a,b$ give $a^2$ and $b^2$, which then define the second line.
useful_results: Two lines with direction ratios $(l_1,m_1,n_1)$ and $(l_2,m_2,n_2)$ are perpendicular iff $l_1l_2+m_1m_2+n_1n_2=0$.
